skin.blood_supply: A dense network of small arteries in the dermis, fed by the arteries of each body region.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 5 The Integumentary System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Skin and its appendages

skeleton.name: Skeleton
skeleton.tagline: The body's bony framework: support, protection, movement and blood-cell production.
skeleton.overview: The adult skeleton has about 206 bones joined at joints. On CT, bone is the densest tissue apart from metal, so a simple brightness threshold can outline it as one surface. That surface includes the skull, spine, ribs, pelvis and limb bones, and sometimes calcified cartilage or contrast-filled vessels that are similarly bright.
functions: Supporting the body and giving it shape
Protecting the brain, heart, lungs and other organs
Acting as levers for muscles to produce movement
Making blood cells in the bone marrow
Storing calcium and phosphate
connections: Muscles, through tendons
Other bones, through joints and ligaments
Bone marrow inside the bones
clinical: Bone density falls with age, especially after menopause (osteoporosis), making fractures more likely.
Fractures are the most common bone injury and usually heal well with time.
A threshold-based bone surface is approximate: thin bone may be missed and bright non-bone may be included.
skeleton.lateralization: Mostly paired on both sides, with midline bones such as the spine, sternum and skull base.
skeleton.fact: A newborn has close to 300 bony pieces; many fuse during childhood.
skeleton.blood_supply: Each bone has its own nutrient arteries plus vessels from the surrounding membrane (periosteum).
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 6 Bone Tissue and the Skeletal System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 7 Axial Skeleton
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Skeletal system

lung.name: Lung
lung.tagline: The paired organs of breathing, where oxygen enters the blood.
lung.overview: The two lungs fill most of the chest on either side of the heart. They are light and spongy because they are made of millions of tiny air sacs (alveoli) surrounded by fine blood vessels. On CT the lungs look dark because they are mostly air; this simple surface shows each whole lung without splitting it into lobes.
functions: Taking oxygen into the blood
Removing carbon dioxide from the blood
Helping keep the blood's acid-base balance
Filtering small clots from the circulation
Supplying the airflow used for speech
connections: Trachea and bronchi
Heart, through the pulmonary arteries and veins
Diaphragm and chest wall, via the pleura
clinical: Pneumonia is an infection that fills some air sacs with fluid.
Smoking damages the air sacs and airways over time (for example in COPD).
Chest CT is a common way to look at the lungs in detail.
lung.lateralization: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two; the left is a little smaller to make room for the heart.
lung.fact: Spread flat, the air sacs of both lungs would cover roughly the area of a tennis court.
lung.blood_supply: Pulmonary arteries bring blood to be oxygenated; small bronchial arteries nourish the lung tissue itself.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

airway.name: Central airway
airway.tagline: The large air tubes: the windpipe and its first two branches.
airway.overview: This surface shows the central airway as a single shape: the trachea and the right and left main bronchi that it splits into. These large tubes are held open by cartilage and carry all the air that moves in and out of the lungs. Inside the lungs they keep branching into ever smaller airways.
functions: Conducting air between the throat and the lungs
Warming, moistening and filtering air
Clearing mucus with cilia
Triggering the cough reflex when irritated
connections: Larynx above
Lobar bronchi inside each lung
Oesophagus behind the trachea
clinical: Inhaled objects more often enter the right main bronchus, which is wider and more vertical.
Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial lining, often after a cold.
airway.lateralization: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more upright than the left.
airway.fact: The point where the trachea divides is called the carina, a sensitive spot that strongly triggers coughing.
airway.blood_supply: Inferior thyroid arteries for the trachea; bronchial arteries from the aorta for the bronchi.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

spinal_cord.name: Spinal cord
spinal_cord.tagline: The nerve cable inside the spine linking the brain with the body.
spinal_cord.overview: The spinal cord is a cylinder of nerve tissue about as thick as a finger, running from the base of the brain down the spinal canal to around the first or second lumbar vertebra. Grey matter in its core holds nerve cells; white matter around it carries signals up and down. Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves leave it to reach the body.
functions: Carrying sensations from the body to the brain
Carrying movement commands from the brain to muscles
Producing reflexes, such as the knee jerk
Controlling bladder, bowel and other automatic functions
Coordinating basic rhythmic patterns like walking
connections: Brainstem (medulla) above
Spinal nerve roots on both sides
Cauda equina below its end
Protective coverings (meninges) and spinal fluid around it
clinical: Injury to the cord can cause weakness and loss of feeling below the level of damage.
Narrowing of the spinal canal can press on the cord, most often in the neck.
Inflammation of the cord (myelitis) and conditions such as multiple sclerosis can affect it.
spinal_cord.lateralization: Each side of the cord mainly serves the same side of the body for movement; many sensory pathways cross.
spinal_cord.fact: In adults the cord is only about 45 cm long, shorter than the spine, because the spine grows faster in childhood.
spinal_cord.blood_supply: One anterior spinal artery and two posterior spinal arteries, reinforced by segmental arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 13 Anatomy of the Nervous System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)

spinal_csf.name: Spinal CSF space
spinal_csf.tagline: The fluid-filled sleeve around the spinal cord that cushions it.
spinal_csf.overview: The spinal cord floats in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inside a sleeve of membranes called the dural or thecal sac. The fluid fills the space between the inner membranes (subarachnoid space) and is continuous with the fluid around the brain. Below the end of the cord the sac continues to about the second sacral level, holding the nerve roots.
functions: Cushioning the spinal cord against knocks
Letting the cord float, reducing its effective weight
Carrying nutrients and removing waste
Housing the nerve roots below the end of the cord
connections: Fluid spaces around the brain and the ventricles
Spinal cord and nerve roots
Dura and arachnoid membranes
clinical: A lumbar puncture takes a sample of this fluid from the lower back, below the end of the cord.
Narrowing of the canal can reduce the fluid space around the cord or nerve roots.
spinal_csf.lateralization: A midline space surrounding the cord.
spinal_csf.fact: The body makes roughly half a litre of CSF a day and replaces it several times over.
spinal_csf.blood_supply: CSF is made mainly by the choroid plexus in the brain's ventricles; it contains no blood vessels of its own.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)

intervertebral_disc.name: Intervertebral disc
intervertebral_disc.tagline: A cushion between two vertebrae that absorbs shocks and lets the spine bend.
intervertebral_disc.overview: Intervertebral discs are the cushions between the vertebral bodies, from the second neck vertebra down to the sacrum. Each has a tough outer ring of fibrous cartilage (annulus fibrosus) around a soft, gel-like centre (nucleus pulposus). Together they make up about a quarter of the spine's length. In spine MR this label marks the discs found between the segmented vertebrae.
functions: Absorbing shocks between vertebrae
Allowing the spine to bend and twist
Spreading load evenly over the vertebral bodies
Keeping space for the nerve roots to exit
Holding the vertebrae together
connections: Vertebral bodies above and below (through the endplates)
Longitudinal ligaments in front and behind
Spinal nerve roots close behind them
clinical: With age the discs lose water and height, a normal process often called disc degeneration.
Part of the soft centre can bulge or push out (disc herniation) and press on a nerve root, causing leg or arm pain.
Disc changes are very common on scans of people without any symptoms.
intervertebral_disc.lateralization: Midline structures, one between each pair of vertebrae.
intervertebral_disc.fact: You are slightly taller in the morning because the discs regain water while you lie down.
intervertebral_disc.blood_supply: Adult discs have almost no blood vessels; they are nourished by diffusion through the vertebral endplates.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

vertebral_column.name: Vertebral column
vertebral_column.tagline: The backbone: a flexible stack of vertebrae protecting the spinal cord.
vertebral_column.overview: The vertebral column is a flexible stack of 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (lower back), 5 fused sacral and about 4 small coccygeal. Discs between them act as cushions. Seen from the side it has four gentle curves that help absorb shocks, and its central canal shelters the spinal cord. This label is used when individual vertebral levels cannot be told apart.
functions: Supporting the head and trunk
Protecting the spinal cord
Allowing bending and twisting
Carrying weight down to the pelvis
Anchoring back muscles and the ribs
connections: Skull at the top
Ribs along the thoracic part
Hip bones through the sacrum
Spinal cord and nerve roots inside the canal
clinical: Back pain is very common and usually comes from muscles, joints or discs rather than serious disease.
Bone thinning can lead to vertebral compression fractures, especially in the thoracic and lumbar spine.
Abnormal curves can develop sideways (scoliosis) or as an exaggerated rounding (kyphosis).
vertebral_column.lateralization: A midline column; nerves leave it in pairs to the left and right.
vertebral_column.fact: Whether a giraffe or a human, almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae.
vertebral_column.blood_supply: Segmental branches of the vertebral, intercostal, lumbar and sacral arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

vertebrae_c1.name: C1 vertebra (Atlas)
vertebrae_c1.tagline: The first cervical (neck) vertebra. Known as the atlas.
vertebrae_c1.overview: It is number 1 of the cervical vertebrae, counted from the top. C1, the atlas, has no body and no spine: it is a ring that cradles the skull. The nodding 'yes' movement happens at the joints between it and the skull. Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile. Each has a hole in its side (transverse foramen) for the vertebral artery, and most have a forked spine at the back. The C1 nerve leaves above it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Supporting the skull and allowing the nodding movement
Protecting the vertebral artery in its side holes
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: Skull (occipital condyles) above, C2 below
Joints with its neighbours; no disc lies above or below it
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: A ring fracture of the atlas can follow a heavy load on the top of the head.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_c1.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_c1.fact: It is named after Atlas, the figure of Greek myth who held up the heavens.
vertebrae_c1.blood_supply: Branches of the vertebral arteries, with the ascending and deep cervical arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

vertebrae_c2.name: C2 vertebra (Axis)
vertebrae_c2.tagline: The second cervical (neck) vertebra. Known as the axis.
vertebrae_c2.overview: It is number 2 of the cervical vertebrae, counted from the top. C2, the axis, has a tooth-like peg (the dens) that rises into the ring of the atlas. The atlas turns around this peg, giving about half of the head's 'no' rotation. Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile. Each has a hole in its side (transverse foramen) for the vertebral artery, and most have a forked spine at the back. The C2 nerve leaves above it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Providing the pivot for turning the head
Protecting the vertebral artery in its side holes
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: C1 above (around the dens), C3 below
Disc below it; no disc between it and C1
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: Fractures of the dens are among the more common neck fractures in older people after a fall.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_c2.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_c2.fact: Its spine is the first large bony bump you can feel below the skull.
vertebrae_c2.blood_supply: Branches of the vertebral arteries, with the ascending and deep cervical arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

vertebrae_c3.name: C3 vertebra
vertebrae_c3.overview: It is number 3 of the cervical vertebrae, counted from the top. Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile. Each has a hole in its side (transverse foramen) for the vertebral artery, and most have a forked spine at the back. The C3 nerve leaves above it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Allowing the wide movements of the neck
Protecting the vertebral artery in its side holes
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: C2 above, C4 below
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: Neck pain and stiffness are common and usually come from muscles, joints or discs.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_c3.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_c3.fact: Seven cervical vertebrae support a head that weighs about 5 kg.
vertebrae_c3.blood_supply: Branches of the vertebral arteries, with the ascending and deep cervical arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column

vertebrae_c4.name: C4 vertebra
vertebrae_c4.overview: It is number 4 of the cervical vertebrae, counted from the top. Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile. Each has a hole in its side (transverse foramen) for the vertebral artery, and most have a forked spine at the back. The C4 nerve leaves above it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Allowing the wide movements of the neck
Protecting the vertebral artery in its side holes
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: C3 above, C5 below
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: Neck pain and stiffness are common and usually come from muscles, joints or discs.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_c4.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_c4.fact: Seven cervical vertebrae support a head that weighs about 5 kg.
vertebrae_c4.blood_supply: Branches of the vertebral arteries, with the ascending and deep cervical arteries.

vertebrae_c7.name: C7 vertebra (Vertebra prominens)
vertebrae_c7.tagline: The seventh cervical (neck) vertebra. Known as the vertebra prominens.
vertebrae_c7.overview: It is number 7 of the cervical vertebrae, counted from the top. C7, the vertebra prominens, has a long, single spine that makes the obvious bump at the base of the back of the neck. It is the transition to the thoracic spine. Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile. Each has a hole in its side (transverse foramen) for the vertebral artery, and most have a forked spine at the back. The C7 nerve leaves above it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Serving as a landmark for counting vertebrae
Protecting the vertebral artery in its side holes
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: C6 above, T1 below
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: Occasionally a small extra rib grows from C7 (cervical rib) and may press on nerves to the arm.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_c7.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_c7.fact: Its spine is the easiest vertebral landmark to find by touch.
vertebrae_c7.blood_supply: Branches of the vertebral arteries, with the ascending and deep cervical arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

vertebrae_t1.name: T1 vertebra
vertebrae_t1.overview: It is number 1 of the thoracic vertebrae, counted from the top. T1 joins the whole head of the first rib and links the neck to the chest; its spine is almost as prominent as C7's. Thoracic vertebrae carry joint surfaces (facets) for the ribs on their bodies and transverse processes, and have long spines that point downward, which limits bending but steadies the ribcage. The T1 nerve leaves below it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Forming joints with rib 1
Steadying the ribcage and allowing twisting
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: C7 above, T2 below; first rib
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: Compression fractures from bone thinning are most frequent in the mid and lower thoracic spine.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_t1.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_t1.fact: The apex of the lung rises just in front of the first rib and T1.
vertebrae_t1.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta (upper levels also from the supreme intercostal artery).
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back

vertebrae_t12.name: T12 vertebra
vertebrae_t12.overview: It is number 12 of the thoracic vertebrae, counted from the top. T12 is the transition to the lumbar spine: its lower joints face like lumbar ones, and it carries the twelfth rib. Thoracic vertebrae carry joint surfaces (facets) for the ribs on their bodies and transverse processes, and have long spines that point downward, which limits bending but steadies the ribcage. The T12 nerve leaves below it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Forming joints with rib 12
Steadying the ribcage and allowing twisting
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: T11 above, L1 below; twelfth rib
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: The junction of T12 and L1 is a common site of fractures after falls from height.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.

vertebrae_l1.name: L1 vertebra
vertebrae_l1.overview: It is number 1 of the lumbar vertebrae, counted from the top. L1 lies at about the level where the spinal cord ends in most adults; below it the canal holds a bundle of nerve roots. Lumbar vertebrae have the largest bodies of the movable spine because they carry the most weight, and short, thick spines; their joints favour bending forward and back. The L1 nerve leaves below it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Carrying the weight of the upper body
Allowing bending forward and backward
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: T12 above, L2 below
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: Low back pain is very common and is usually due to strain of muscles, joints or discs.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_l1.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_l1.fact: The lumbar spine curves forward (lordosis), bringing the body's weight over the pelvis.
vertebrae_l1.blood_supply: Lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta.

vertebrae_l4.name: L4 vertebra
vertebrae_l4.overview: It is number 4 of the lumbar vertebrae, counted from the top. L4 usually lies at the level of the top of the hip bones (iliac crests), a landmark used for procedures on the lower spine. Lumbar vertebrae have the largest bodies of the movable spine because they carry the most weight, and short, thick spines; their joints favour bending forward and back. The L4 nerve leaves below it.

vertebrae_l5.name: L5 vertebra
vertebrae_l5.overview: It is number 5 of the lumbar vertebrae, counted from the top. L5 is the lowest and largest lumbar vertebra, with a wedge-shaped body that forms the lumbosacral angle where the spine meets the sacrum. Lumbar vertebrae have the largest bodies of the movable spine because they carry the most weight, and short, thick spines; their joints favour bending forward and back. The L5 nerve leaves below it.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Carrying the weight of the upper body
Allowing bending forward and backward
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: L4 above, sacrum (S1) below
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: A defect in the arch of L5 (spondylolysis) can let it slip forward on the sacrum (spondylolisthesis).
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_l5.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_l5.fact: L5 sometimes partly fuses with the sacrum (sacralisation), a common harmless variant.
vertebrae_l5.blood_supply: Lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta.

vertebrae_s1.name: S1 vertebra (First sacral vertebra)
vertebrae_s1.tagline: The top segment of the sacrum, where the spine meets the pelvis.
vertebrae_s1.overview: S1 is the top segment of the sacrum. Its front upper edge (the sacral promontory) juts forward at the lumbosacral junction, and it carries the large joint surfaces for the hip bones.
functions: Protecting the spinal cord or nerve roots in its canal
Passing the weight of the spine to the pelvis
Letting the first sacral nerves out
Anchoring back muscles and ligaments
connections: L5 above (L5-S1 disc), rest of the sacrum below, hip bones at the sides
Intervertebral discs and facet joints
Spinal nerves leaving through the gaps beside it
clinical: The L5-S1 disc is one of the two discs most often affected by herniation, which can irritate the S1 nerve root.
Age-related wear of the discs and small joints at this level is common and often painless.
vertebrae_s1.lateralization: A midline bone; its nerves leave in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae_s1.fact: In some people S1 is partly separate from the rest of the sacrum (lumbarisation).
vertebrae_s1.blood_supply: Lateral sacral arteries and the median sacral artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

brain.name: Brain
brain.tagline: The control centre of the nervous system, shown here as one whole organ.
brain.overview: The brain fills most of the skull and weighs about 1.2 to 1.4 kg in adults. Its main parts are the two cerebral hemispheres, the cerebellum at the back and the brainstem, which continues down as the spinal cord. It is wrapped in three membranes (the meninges) and floats in cerebrospinal fluid. In body scans it is often outlined as one shape.
functions: Sensing and interpreting the world
Planning and controlling movement
Thinking, memory, language and emotion
Controlling breathing, heart rate and other automatic functions
Regulating hormones through the hypothalamus and pituitary
connections: Spinal cord through the brainstem
Cranial nerves to the head and neck
Skull and meninges around it
clinical: Stroke happens when part of the brain loses its blood supply or a vessel bleeds.
Head injury can affect the brain even without a skull fracture.
brain.lateralization: Each half of the brain mainly controls and senses the opposite side of the body.
brain.fact: The brain is about 2 per cent of body weight but uses about 20 per cent of the body's energy at rest.
brain.blood_supply: Two internal carotid arteries and two vertebral arteries, joined at the base of the brain in the circle of Willis.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.2 The Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

optic_nerve.name: Optic nerve
optic_nerve.tagline: The nerve that carries visual signals from the eye to the brain.
optic_nerve.overview: The optic nerve is a bundle of about a million nerve fibres from the retina. It leaves the back of the eye, runs through the orbit and enters the skull through the optic canal. Behind the eyes the two optic nerves meet at the optic chiasm, where fibres from the inner half of each retina cross to the other side. Strictly it is part of the brain.
functions: Carrying visual information from the retina to the brain
Carrying signals for the pupil light reflex
Sending part of each eye's view to both sides of the brain via the chiasm
Contributing to the body clock through light signals
connections: Retina of the eye
Optic chiasm and optic tracts
Thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus) and visual cortex
clinical: Optic neuritis, an inflammation of the nerve, can cause blurred vision and pain on moving the eye.
Raised pressure inside the skull can make the head of the optic nerve swell, which can be seen during an eye examination.
optic_nerve.lateralization: There is one for each eye; damage before the chiasm affects only that eye's vision.
optic_nerve.fact: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light receptors, creating a natural blind spot.
optic_nerve.blood_supply: Ophthalmic artery and its central retinal branch.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

eye.name: Eye
eye.tagline: The organ of sight: a fluid-filled ball that focuses light onto the retina.
eye.overview: The eye is a roughly 24 mm ball sitting in the bony eye socket (orbit), cushioned by fat and moved by six small muscles. Light passes through the clear cornea, the pupil and the lens and is focused onto the retina at the back, whose light-sensitive cells send signals along the optic nerve to the brain. Its tough white outer coat is the sclera.
functions: Focusing light onto the retina
Converting light into nerve signals
Seeing colour and fine detail (in the macula)
Adjusting to bright and dim light through the pupil
Providing depth perception together with the other eye
connections: Optic nerve at the back
Six extraocular muscles that move it
Bony orbit and eyelids around it
clinical: Short- and long-sightedness come from a mismatch between the eye's length and its focusing power.
Diabetes and high blood pressure can affect the small vessels of the retina, which is why eye checks are advised.
eye.lateralization: There is one on each side; each eye's view overlaps with the other's to give depth.
eye.fact: The retina is a direct outgrowth of the brain during development.
eye.blood_supply: Ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery, including the central retinal artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

eyeball.name: Eye
eyeball.tagline: The organ of sight: a fluid-filled ball that focuses light onto the retina.
eyeball.overview: The eye is a roughly 24 mm ball sitting in the bony eye socket (orbit), cushioned by fat and moved by six small muscles. Light passes through the clear cornea, the pupil and the lens and is focused onto the retina at the back, whose light-sensitive cells send signals along the optic nerve to the brain. Its tough white outer coat is the sclera.
functions: Focusing light onto the retina
Converting light into nerve signals
Seeing colour and fine detail (in the macula)
Adjusting to bright and dim light through the pupil
Providing depth perception together with the other eye
connections: Optic nerve at the back
Six extraocular muscles that move it
Bony orbit and eyelids around it
clinical: Short- and long-sightedness come from a mismatch between the eye's length and its focusing power.
Diabetes and high blood pressure can affect the small vessels of the retina, which is why eye checks are advised.
eyeball.lateralization: There is one on each side; each eye's view overlaps with the other's to give depth.
eyeball.fact: The retina is a direct outgrowth of the brain during development.
eyeball.blood_supply: Ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery, including the central retinal artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

eye_lens.name: Lens of the eye
eye_lens.tagline: The clear, flexible lens behind the pupil that fine-tunes focus.
eye_lens.overview: The lens is a clear, disc-shaped structure behind the iris and pupil, held in place by fine fibres attached to the ciliary muscle. When this muscle tightens, the lens becomes rounder to focus on near objects; when it relaxes, the lens flattens for distance. It has no blood vessels and is nourished by the fluid around it.
functions: Fine-tuning focus between near and far (accommodation)
Bending light onto the retina
Filtering some ultraviolet light
Staying transparent so light can pass
connections: Iris and pupil in front
Ciliary muscle through its suspensory fibres
Vitreous gel behind
clinical: Cataract is a clouding of the lens that is common with age and can be treated by replacing the lens.
The lens stiffens with age, which is why reading glasses are often needed after about 40 (presbyopia).
eye_lens.lateralization: There is one in each eye.
eye_lens.fact: The lens keeps growing slowly throughout life by adding new layers, a bit like an onion.
eye_lens.blood_supply: None directly: it has no blood vessels and is fed by the aqueous humour.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

auditory_canal.name: Ear canal
auditory_canal.tagline: The tube from the outer ear to the eardrum that funnels sound inwards.
auditory_canal.overview: The ear canal is an S-shaped tube about 2.5 cm long running from the opening of the outer ear to the eardrum. Its outer third has a cartilage wall with hairs and wax glands; its inner two-thirds is a channel through the temporal bone with thin, sensitive skin. Its skin slowly migrates outwards, carrying wax and debris with it.
functions: Carrying sound waves to the eardrum
Boosting some speech frequencies by resonance
Protecting the eardrum with wax and hairs
Self-cleaning as its skin moves outwards
connections: Outer ear (pinna)
Eardrum (tympanic membrane) and middle ear
Temporal bone around its inner part
clinical: Earwax build-up is common and can muffle hearing.
Infection of the ear canal skin (otitis externa, 'swimmer's ear') is common after water exposure.
auditory_canal.lateralization: There is one on each side of the head.
auditory_canal.fact: Earwax is normal and protective; the canal usually cleans itself.
auditory_canal.blood_supply: Branches of the external carotid artery, mainly the posterior auricular and superficial temporal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

ventricle_frontal_horn.name: Frontal horn of the lateral ventricle
ventricle_frontal_horn.tagline: The front part of the lateral ventricle, inside the frontal lobe.
ventricle_frontal_horn.overview: The frontal (anterior) horn is the forward extension of each lateral ventricle. It lies in the frontal lobe, with the corpus callosum above and in front, the head of the caudate nucleus on its outer wall and the thin septum pellucidum separating it from its partner. Unlike the rest of the ventricle, it contains no choroid plexus.
functions: Holding cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Housing choroid plexus that makes CSF
Passing CSF on towards the third ventricle
Helping to cushion the brain
connections: Body of the lateral ventricle behind
Head of the caudate nucleus
Septum pellucidum in the midline
clinical: The ventricles can enlarge if the flow or absorption of CSF is blocked (hydrocephalus).
Some difference in size between the left and right ventricles is a common normal variant.
ventricle_frontal_horn.lateralization: There is one lateral ventricle in each hemisphere; each has its own version of this part.
ventricle_frontal_horn.fact: The two frontal horns are separated only by the paper-thin septum pellucidum.
ventricle_frontal_horn.blood_supply: Choroid plexus is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

ventricle_body.name: Body of the lateral ventricle
ventricle_body.tagline: The central part of the lateral ventricle, under the corpus callosum.
ventricle_body.overview: The body is the main central section of each lateral ventricle, running backwards from the interventricular foramen to the trigone. The corpus callosum forms its roof, and the thalamus and caudate nucleus lie along its floor. Choroid plexus runs along its floor, and its front end connects to the third ventricle.
functions: Holding cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Housing choroid plexus that makes CSF
Passing CSF on towards the third ventricle
Helping to cushion the brain
connections: Third ventricle through the interventricular foramen
Corpus callosum above
Thalamus and caudate nucleus below
clinical: The ventricles can enlarge if the flow or absorption of CSF is blocked (hydrocephalus).
Some difference in size between the left and right ventricles is a common normal variant.
ventricle_body.lateralization: There is one lateral ventricle in each hemisphere; each has its own version of this part.
ventricle_body.fact: The interventricular foramen near its front end is the only route for CSF to leave the lateral ventricle.
ventricle_body.blood_supply: Choroid plexus is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

ventricle_trigone.name: Trigone of the lateral ventricle
ventricle_trigone.tagline: The wide junction where body, occipital and temporal horns of the ventricle meet.
ventricle_trigone.overview: The trigone (atrium) is the broad triangular area at the back of each lateral ventricle where the body, the occipital horn and the temporal horn meet. It contains a large tuft of choroid plexus (the glomus), which often calcifies with age and is a familiar normal landmark on scans.
functions: Holding cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Housing choroid plexus that makes CSF
Passing CSF on towards the third ventricle
Helping to cushion the brain
connections: Body of the lateral ventricle in front
Occipital horn behind and temporal horn below
Splenium of the corpus callosum above
clinical: The ventricles can enlarge if the flow or absorption of CSF is blocked (hydrocephalus).
Some difference in size between the left and right ventricles is a common normal variant.
ventricle_trigone.lateralization: There is one lateral ventricle in each hemisphere; each has its own version of this part.
ventricle_trigone.fact: Calcification of the choroid plexus in the trigone is common in adults and is a normal finding.
ventricle_trigone.blood_supply: Choroid plexus is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

ventricle_occipital_horn.name: Occipital horn of the lateral ventricle
ventricle_occipital_horn.tagline: The backward extension of the lateral ventricle into the occipital lobe.
ventricle_occipital_horn.overview: The occipital (posterior) horn extends backwards from the trigone into the occipital lobe. It is surrounded by white-matter fibres, including those of the visual pathway, and has no choroid plexus. Its size varies a great deal between people and between the two sides.
functions: Holding cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Housing choroid plexus that makes CSF
Passing CSF on towards the third ventricle
Helping to cushion the brain
connections: Trigone in front
Visual white-matter pathways (optic radiation) around it
Occipital lobe
clinical: The ventricles can enlarge if the flow or absorption of CSF is blocked (hydrocephalus).
Some difference in size between the left and right ventricles is a common normal variant.
ventricle_occipital_horn.lateralization: There is one lateral ventricle in each hemisphere; each has its own version of this part.
ventricle_occipital_horn.fact: The occipital horns are the most variable part of the ventricles and are often unequal on the two sides.
ventricle_occipital_horn.blood_supply: Choroid plexus is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

ventricle_temporal_horn.name: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle
ventricle_temporal_horn.tagline: The downward, forward extension of the lateral ventricle into the temporal lobe.
ventricle_temporal_horn.overview: The temporal (inferior) horn curves down and forwards from the trigone into the temporal lobe. The hippocampus forms much of its floor, and the amygdala lies near its front tip. It contains choroid plexus and is normally a thin slit.
functions: Holding cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Housing choroid plexus that makes CSF
Passing CSF on towards the third ventricle
Helping to cushion the brain
connections: Trigone above and behind
Hippocampus along its floor
Amygdala near its tip
clinical: The ventricles can enlarge if the flow or absorption of CSF is blocked (hydrocephalus).
Some difference in size between the left and right ventricles is a common normal variant.
ventricle_temporal_horn.lateralization: There is one lateral ventricle in each hemisphere; each has its own version of this part.
ventricle_temporal_horn.fact: Because the hippocampus forms its floor, a wider temporal horn can reflect hippocampal shrinkage in some conditions.
ventricle_temporal_horn.blood_supply: Choroid plexus is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neuroanatomy

trachea.name: Trachea
trachea.tagline: The windpipe: a stiffened tube carrying air from the throat to the lungs.
trachea.overview: The trachea is a tube about 10 to 12 cm long that runs from the larynx in the neck down into the chest. C-shaped rings of cartilage keep it open, with a soft muscular wall at the back where it touches the oesophagus. Behind the upper part of the heart it divides into the right and left main bronchi.
functions: Carrying air to and from the lungs
Staying open thanks to its cartilage rings
Warming and moistening inhaled air
Trapping dust in mucus
Moving mucus upward with tiny hairs (cilia)
connections: Larynx above
Right and left main bronchi below
Oesophagus directly behind it
clinical: Coughing is the body's way of clearing the trachea of mucus or foreign material.
Inflammation of the trachea (tracheitis) often comes with chest-cold infections.
A tracheostomy is a surgical opening into the trachea used to help breathing.
trachea.lateralization: A midline structure; its lower end turns slightly to the right.
trachea.fact: The lining is covered with cilia that beat many times a second to sweep mucus towards the throat.
trachea.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior thyroid arteries above and bronchial arteries below.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neck

lung_upper_lobe.name: Upper lobe of the lung
lung_upper_lobe.tagline: The top part of each lung, reaching up into the base of the neck.
lung_upper_lobe.overview: Each lung has an upper lobe that forms its top and much of its front. On the left it is separated from the lower lobe by the oblique fissure and includes a tongue-like part (the lingula) beside the heart. On the right the horizontal fissure separates it from the middle lobe.
functions: Gas exchange in its air sacs
Receiving air through its own lobar bronchus
Expanding and recoiling with each breath
Producing surfactant that keeps air sacs open
connections: Its lobar bronchus
Branches of the pulmonary artery and veins
Neighbouring lobes across a fissure
clinical: Some infections and smoking-related changes tend to favour the upper lobes.
Surgeons can remove a single lobe (lobectomy) and the rest of the lung keeps working.
lung_upper_lobe.lateralization: Present on both sides; the left upper lobe includes the lingula.
lung_upper_lobe.fact: The very top of the lung, the apex, rises a little above the collarbone.
lung_upper_lobe.blood_supply: Lobar branches of the pulmonary artery; bronchial arteries nourish the tissue.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

lung_middle_lobe.name: Middle lobe of the right lung
lung_middle_lobe.tagline: The small wedge-shaped middle lobe found only in the right lung.
lung_middle_lobe.overview: The middle lobe lies at the front of the right lung, between the upper and lower lobes, bounded by the horizontal and oblique fissures. It sits against the right side of the heart. The left lung has no middle lobe; its lingula plays a similar role.
functions: Gas exchange in its air sacs
Receiving air through its own lobar bronchus
Expanding and recoiling with each breath
Producing surfactant that keeps air sacs open
connections: Its lobar bronchus
Branches of the pulmonary artery and veins
Neighbouring lobes across a fissure
clinical: Its narrow bronchus can make mucus drainage from this lobe less efficient.
Infections here can blur the right edge of the heart on an X-ray.
lung_middle_lobe.fact: It is the smallest lobe of the right lung.
lung_middle_lobe.blood_supply: Lobar branches of the pulmonary artery; bronchial arteries nourish the tissue.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

lung_lower_lobe.name: Lower lobe of the lung
lung_lower_lobe.tagline: The large bottom and back part of each lung, resting on the diaphragm.
lung_lower_lobe.overview: Each lung has a lower lobe below and behind the oblique fissure. It forms most of the back of the lung and rests on the dome of the diaphragm. Because it is large and low, it does much of the breathing work when a person is upright.
functions: Gas exchange in its air sacs
Receiving air through its own lobar bronchus
Expanding and recoiling with each breath
Producing surfactant that keeps air sacs open
connections: Its lobar bronchus
Branches of the pulmonary artery and veins
Neighbouring lobes across a fissure
clinical: Inhaled material while lying down often reaches the lower lobes.
The lower lobes are a common site for pneumonia.
lung_lower_lobe.fact: Its base follows the curve of the diaphragm and moves several centimetres with each deep breath.
lung_lower_lobe.blood_supply: Lobar branches of the pulmonary artery; bronchial arteries nourish the tissue.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

lung_airways.name: Bronchial tree
lung_airways.tagline: The branching air tubes inside the lungs, like an upside-down tree.
lung_airways.overview: After the main bronchi enter the lungs they divide again and again into lobar, segmental and smaller bronchi, then into bronchioles that end at the air sacs. There are around twenty or more generations of branching. This structure shows the air inside the larger branches that imaging can resolve.
functions: Distributing air evenly to every part of the lung
Filtering and moistening air
Adjusting airflow by narrowing or widening
Clearing mucus towards the throat
connections: Main bronchi and trachea
Air sacs (alveoli) at the ends
Pulmonary arteries that run alongside
clinical: In asthma the smaller airways narrow and produce extra mucus.
Bronchiectasis is a long-term widening of airways that makes mucus harder to clear.
lung_airways.lateralization: Both lungs; the right tree has three lobar branches and the left has two.
lung_airways.fact: Each lung segment has its own segmental bronchus, which is why surgeons can remove one segment.
lung_airways.blood_supply: Bronchial arteries, mostly from the descending aorta.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

lung_airways_wall.name: Airway wall
lung_airways_wall.tagline: The layered wall of the lung's air tubes: lining, muscle and cartilage.
lung_airways_wall.overview: The walls of the bronchi are made of layers: an inner lining with mucus glands and cilia, a ring of smooth muscle, and plates of cartilage in the larger branches. The thickness of these walls can be seen on detailed CT. In the smallest airways the cartilage disappears and the wall is mostly muscle.
functions: Keeping larger airways open with cartilage
Changing airway width with smooth muscle
Producing protective mucus
Moving mucus with cilia
Forming a barrier against germs
connections: Air inside the bronchial tree
Surrounding lung tissue
Bronchial arteries and nerves
clinical: Long-term inflammation, as in chronic bronchitis or asthma, can thicken airway walls.
Medicines inhaled for asthma act mainly on the muscle in these walls.
lung_airways_wall.fact: The smooth muscle of the airways is controlled automatically by the autonomic nervous system.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

lung_trachea_bronchia.name: Trachea and bronchi
lung_trachea_bronchia.tagline: The windpipe together with its branching bronchi, shown as one airway tree.
lung_trachea_bronchia.overview: This structure combines the trachea and the bronchi that branch from it inside the lungs into a single airway tree. It runs from the neck, through the chest, and into both lungs, dividing at each step into narrower tubes. Together these tubes conduct air but do not exchange gases themselves.
functions: Conducting air into and out of the lungs
Filtering, warming and moistening air
Clearing mucus with the cilia escalator
Protecting the lungs through coughing
connections: Larynx above
Air sacs of both lungs
Pulmonary arteries alongside the bronchi
clinical: Infections can inflame the lining anywhere along the tree.
Doctors can look inside the larger branches with a thin camera (bronchoscopy).
lung_trachea_bronchia.lateralization: Midline trachea dividing into right and left trees.
lung_trachea_bronchia.fact: The airways from the trachea to the smallest bronchioles hold about 150 ml of air that never reaches the air sacs.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

lung_pleural.name: Pleura
lung_pleural.tagline: The thin double membrane that wraps each lung and lines the chest wall.
lung_pleural.overview: Each lung is wrapped in a smooth membrane (the visceral pleura), and the inside of the chest wall is lined by another (the parietal pleura). Between them is a very thin space with a little lubricating fluid. This lets the lungs glide as they move and keeps them stuck to the chest wall so they expand when it does.
functions: Letting the lungs slide smoothly during breathing
Coupling the lungs to the chest wall
Producing and absorbing a small amount of fluid
Separating the two lungs into their own compartments
connections: Surface of each lung
Inner chest wall and ribs
Upper surface of the diaphragm and the mediastinum
clinical: Pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura and can cause sharp pain on breathing.
Air or fluid can collect in the pleural space and press on the lung.
lung_pleural.lateralization: Right and left pleural sacs are separate.
lung_pleural.fact: The parietal pleura is sensitive to pain, but the visceral pleura on the lung surface is not.
lung_pleural.blood_supply: Parietal pleura from chest-wall arteries; visceral pleura from bronchial vessels.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 22 The Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

nasal_cavity.name: Nasal cavity
nasal_cavity.tagline: The air space inside the nose that warms, moistens and filters each breath.
nasal_cavity.overview: Each nasal cavity runs from the nostril back to the nasopharynx and is separated from its partner by the nasal septum. Three curled bony shelves (the conchae or turbinates) on the side wall increase its surface, and a moist, blood-rich lining covers it. The roof carries the smell receptors, and the paranasal sinuses drain into it.
functions: Warming and moistening inhaled air
Trapping dust and germs in mucus
Sense of smell
Draining the sinuses and tear ducts
Giving resonance to the voice
connections: Paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, sphenoid)
Nasopharynx behind
Hard palate below
clinical: A deviated nasal septum is common and can make one side feel more blocked.
Nosebleeds most often start from a network of vessels at the front of the septum.
nasal_cavity.lateralization: Left and right cavities are separated by the nasal septum; they often take turns being more congested (the nasal cycle).
nasal_cavity.fact: Air in the nose is warmed to close to body temperature within a fraction of a second.
nasal_cavity.blood_supply: Sphenopalatine and ethmoidal arteries, plus branches of the facial artery near the nostrils.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

nasopharynx.name: Nasopharynx
nasopharynx.tagline: The top part of the throat, behind the nose and above the soft palate.
nasopharynx.overview: The nasopharynx is the uppermost part of the pharynx. It lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate, and it carries only air. On each side wall is the opening of the auditory (Eustachian) tube leading to the middle ear, and on its back wall lies the adenoid, a patch of lymphoid tissue that is largest in childhood.
functions: Carrying air from the nose to the lower throat
Balancing middle-ear pressure through the auditory tubes
Immune defence through the adenoid
Acting as a resonating space for the voice
connections: Nasal cavity in front
Auditory (Eustachian) tubes on each side
Oropharynx below the soft palate
clinical: Enlarged adenoids in children can block nasal breathing and the auditory tubes.
Blockage of an auditory tube during a cold can cause a feeling of fullness in the ear.
nasopharynx.lateralization: A single midline space with an auditory-tube opening on each side.
nasopharynx.fact: The adenoid usually shrinks considerably after childhood.
nasopharynx.blood_supply: Branches of the external carotid artery, including the ascending pharyngeal and pharyngeal branches of the maxillary artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

larynx_air.name: Larynx (air space)
larynx_air.tagline: The air passage inside the voice box, containing the vocal folds.
larynx_air.overview: This is the air-filled inside of the larynx, from its entrance behind the epiglottis down to the start of the trachea. It is framed by the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, and near its middle the two vocal folds stretch from front to back. The gap between them, the glottis, is the narrowest part of the adult airway.
functions: Producing the voice as air vibrates the vocal folds
Closing tightly to protect the airway during swallowing
Allowing coughing to clear the airway
Controlling airflow into the trachea
connections: Thyroid and cricoid cartilages around it
Hypopharynx above and behind
Trachea below
clinical: Hoarseness often comes from swelling or strain of the vocal folds.
Laryngitis, an inflammation of the larynx, usually follows a common cold.
larynx_air.lateralization: A single midline airway with paired vocal folds.
larynx_air.fact: Vocal folds in adults vibrate roughly 100 to 250 times per second during ordinary speech.
larynx_air.blood_supply: Superior and inferior laryngeal arteries, from the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

thyroid_cartilage.name: Thyroid cartilage
thyroid_cartilage.tagline: The largest cartilage of the voice box, forming the Adam's apple.
thyroid_cartilage.overview: The thyroid cartilage is a shield-shaped cartilage made of two flat plates joined at the front. The ridge where they meet forms the laryngeal prominence, or Adam's apple, which is usually more marked after puberty in males. The vocal folds attach to its inner surface at the front. It often becomes partly bony (calcified) with age.
functions: Protecting the vocal folds and the larynx
Anchoring the front end of the vocal folds
Giving attachment to neck and throat muscles
Tilting against the cricoid cartilage to change voice pitch
connections: Hyoid bone above, joined by a membrane
Cricoid cartilage below, at a small joint on each side
Thyroid gland, which lies just below and to the sides
clinical: It is a useful landmark for finding other structures in the neck.
Calcification of the cartilage with age is normal.
thyroid_cartilage.lateralization: A single midline cartilage made of left and right plates.
thyroid_cartilage.fact: The thyroid cartilage gave its name to the thyroid gland, from the Greek for 'shield-shaped'.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

cricoid_cartilage.name: Cricoid cartilage
cricoid_cartilage.tagline: The only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, at the base of the larynx.
cricoid_cartilage.overview: The cricoid cartilage sits below the thyroid cartilage and above the first ring of the trachea. It is shaped like a signet ring: narrow at the front and tall at the back. Because it is a complete ring, it keeps the airway open at this level, and the small arytenoid cartilages that move the vocal folds sit on its upper back edge.
functions: Keeping the airway open as a complete ring
Supporting the arytenoid cartilages that move the vocal folds
Forming joints with the thyroid cartilage for pitch control
Marking the start of the trachea and oesophagus
connections: Thyroid cartilage above
Trachea below
Lower end of the pharynx and start of the oesophagus behind
clinical: Its level, at about the sixth cervical vertebra, is a standard landmark in the neck.
In young children the cricoid ring is the narrowest part of the airway.
cricoid_cartilage.blood_supply: Branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

sinus_frontal.name: Frontal sinus
sinus_frontal.tagline: An air space in the forehead bone, above the eyes, draining into the nose.
sinus_frontal.overview: The frontal sinuses are air-filled spaces inside the frontal bone, just above the eyebrows. They are lined by the same moist lining as the nose and drain into the nasal cavity through a narrow channel. They are absent at birth, start to develop in early childhood and reach adult size after puberty.
functions: Making the skull lighter
Adding resonance to the voice
Producing mucus that drains into the nose
Helping to cushion the face against blows
connections: Nasal cavity, through the frontonasal duct
Eye sockets below
Front of the brain (frontal lobes) behind
clinical: Sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinus lining, usually follows a cold.
Thickened lining or fluid in the sinuses is often seen on scans of people without symptoms.
sinus_frontal.lateralization: Left and right sinuses are separated by a thin wall and are often unequal in size; one may even be missing.
sinus_frontal.fact: The shape of the frontal sinuses is so individual that it has been used to help identify people.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

sinus_maxillary.name: Maxillary sinus
sinus_maxillary.tagline: The largest air sinus, inside the cheekbone area of the upper jaw.
sinus_maxillary.overview: The maxillary sinuses are the largest of the paranasal sinuses, one inside each upper jaw bone (maxilla), below the eye socket and above the upper back teeth. Each drains into the side of the nasal cavity through an opening high on its inner wall, so drainage relies partly on the beating of tiny hairs in its lining.
functions: Making the skull lighter
Adding resonance to the voice
Producing mucus that drains into the nose
Helping to cushion the face against blows
connections: Nasal cavity, through an opening in its inner wall
Eye socket (orbit) above
Roots of the upper premolars and molars below
clinical: Sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinus lining, usually follows a cold.
Because upper back-tooth roots are close to its floor, dental problems can sometimes affect the sinus.
sinus_maxillary.lateralization: There is one on each side; they are usually similar in size.
sinus_maxillary.fact: It is the first sinus to develop and is already present, though small, at birth.
sinus_maxillary.blood_supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, including the infraorbital and superior alveolar arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

maxillary_sinus.name: Maxillary sinus
maxillary_sinus.tagline: The largest air sinus, inside the cheekbone area of the upper jaw.
maxillary_sinus.overview: The maxillary sinuses are the largest of the paranasal sinuses, one inside each upper jaw bone (maxilla), below the eye socket and above the upper back teeth. Each drains into the side of the nasal cavity through an opening high on its inner wall, so drainage relies partly on the beating of tiny hairs in its lining.
functions: Making the skull lighter
Adding resonance to the voice
Producing mucus that drains into the nose
Helping to cushion the face against blows
connections: Nasal cavity, through an opening in its inner wall
Eye socket (orbit) above
Roots of the upper premolars and molars below
clinical: Sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinus lining, usually follows a cold.
Because upper back-tooth roots are close to its floor, dental problems can sometimes affect the sinus.
maxillary_sinus.lateralization: There is one on each side; they are usually similar in size.
maxillary_sinus.fact: It is the first sinus to develop and is already present, though small, at birth.
maxillary_sinus.blood_supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, including the infraorbital and superior alveolar arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

heart.name: Heart
heart.tagline: A fist-sized muscular pump that keeps blood moving through the whole body.
heart.overview: The heart sits in the middle of the chest between the lungs, tilted so that its tip points to the left. It has four chambers: two upper atria that receive blood and two lower ventricles that pump it out. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body. One-way valves keep the flow going in the right direction.
functions: Pumping blood to the lungs (right side)
Pumping blood to the body (left side)
Generating its own electrical rhythm
Keeping blood flowing one way with four valves
Releasing hormones that help regulate fluid balance
connections: Great vessels: aorta, pulmonary trunk and the venae cavae
Pulmonary veins from the lungs
Pericardium, the protective sac around it
Autonomic nerves that speed it up or slow it down
clinical: Narrowing of the coronary arteries can reduce blood flow to the heart muscle.
Valve problems or rhythm disturbances can affect how well the heart pumps.
On CT the size and outline of the heart can be seen, but its function needs dedicated tests.
heart.lateralization: A single midline organ that lies mostly left of centre; its right and left sides serve different circulations.
heart.fact: The heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day.
heart.blood_supply: Right and left coronary arteries, the first branches of the aorta.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §19.1 Heart Anatomy
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

atrial_appendage.name: Left atrial appendage
atrial_appendage.tagline: A small ear-shaped pouch off the left upper chamber of the heart.
atrial_appendage.overview: The left atrial appendage is a small, finger- or ear-shaped pouch that projects forward from the left atrium, next to the start of the pulmonary trunk. Its inner wall is ridged by small muscle bands. It is a leftover of the early embryonic atrium and holds a little blood with each heartbeat.
functions: Part of the left atrium's blood reservoir
Adds a little to atrial filling and emptying
Releases natriuretic peptide, a fluid-balancing hormone
Helps the atrium adapt to changes in pressure
connections: Opens into the left atrium
Lies beside the pulmonary trunk and the left coronary artery
clinical: When the atria beat irregularly, blood can pool in the appendage and form clots.
Some heart procedures close off the appendage to lower that risk.
atrial_appendage.lateralization: Only the left appendage is segmented here; the right atrium has its own, broader appendage.
atrial_appendage.fact: Its shape varies a lot between people and is sometimes described as 'chicken wing' or 'windsock'.
atrial_appendage.blood_supply: Branches of the left coronary artery, mainly the circumflex artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §19.1 Heart Anatomy
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

pericardium.name: Pericardium
pericardium.tagline: The tough, two-layered sac that wraps and protects the heart.
pericardium.overview: The pericardium is a double-walled sac around the heart and the roots of the great vessels. Its tough outer fibrous layer anchors the heart to the diaphragm and breastbone. Inside, a thin serous membrane lines the sac and the heart surface, with a film of fluid between them that lets the heart beat with little friction.
functions: Protecting the heart
Holding the heart in position in the chest
Reducing friction as the heart beats
Limiting sudden over-stretching of the heart
connections: Attached below to the central tendon of the diaphragm
Blends with the outer walls of the great vessels
Lies between the two lungs in the middle mediastinum
clinical: Inflammation of the pericardium (pericarditis) can cause sharp chest pain.
Fluid collecting inside the sac can press on the heart if it builds up quickly.
pericardium.fact: 'Peri-cardium' simply means 'around the heart' in Greek.
pericardium.blood_supply: Pericardiacophrenic and other small branches of the internal thoracic artery, plus branches from the aorta.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §19.1 Heart Anatomy
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

aorta.name: Aorta
aorta.tagline: The body's main artery, carrying oxygen-rich blood from the heart.
aorta.overview: The aorta leaves the left ventricle, rises a short way, arches backwards over the left lung root, then runs down in front of the spine through the chest and abdomen. Around the level of the navel it divides into the two common iliac arteries. Along the way it gives branches to the heart, head, arms, chest wall, gut, kidneys and legs.
functions: Carrying oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle
Supplying every major organ through its branches
Its elastic wall smooths the pulsing flow into steadier flow
Housing pressure sensors that help regulate blood pressure
connections: Left ventricle via the aortic valve
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries from the arch
Coeliac, mesenteric and renal arteries in the abdomen
Divides into the common iliac arteries
clinical: The wall can weaken and widen over time (aneurysm).
A tear in the inner wall (dissection) is a medical emergency.
Hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis) often affects the aorta.
aorta.lateralization: A single midline vessel; the arch usually curves to the left.
aorta.fact: In adults the aorta is about as wide as a garden hose, roughly 2–3 cm.
aorta.blood_supply: Its own wall is nourished by tiny vessels (vasa vasorum) from its branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

brachiocephalic_trunk.name: Brachiocephalic trunk
brachiocephalic_trunk.tagline: The first branch of the aortic arch, feeding the right arm and right side of the head.
brachiocephalic_trunk.overview: The brachiocephalic trunk is the largest branch of the aortic arch. It runs up and to the right behind the breastbone for a few centimetres, then splits behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
functions: Carrying blood towards the right arm
Carrying blood towards the right side of the head and neck
Supplying part of the brain via the right carotid and vertebral arteries
Supplying the right upper chest wall
connections: Arises from the aortic arch
Divides into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries
clinical: Atherosclerosis here can reduce flow to the right arm or brain.
Its position in front of the trachea matters during neck and chest surgery.
brachiocephalic_trunk.lateralization: There is only one, on the right; on the left the carotid and subclavian arteries arise separately from the arch.
brachiocephalic_trunk.fact: 'Brachio-cephalic' means 'arm-head', describing the two regions it feeds.
brachiocephalic_trunk.blood_supply: Its wall is fed by small vasa vasorum.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

subclavian_artery.name: Subclavian artery
subclavian_artery.tagline: The artery arching over the first rib to supply the arm, with branches to brain and chest.
subclavian_artery.overview: Each subclavian artery curves over the top of the lung and the first rib, passing behind the collarbone. On the right it starts from the brachiocephalic trunk, on the left directly from the aortic arch. At the outer edge of the first rib it continues as the axillary artery into the armpit.
functions: Main blood supply to the arm
Gives the vertebral artery to the back of the brain
Gives the internal thoracic artery to the front chest wall
Supplies the thyroid, neck and shoulder muscles through branches
connections: Right: from the brachiocephalic trunk; left: from the aortic arch
Continues as the axillary artery
Passes between the anterior and middle scalene muscles
clinical: Narrowing near its start can make blood 'steal' from the brain to the arm during arm exercise.
It can be compressed where it crosses the first rib (thoracic outlet).
subclavian_artery.lateralization: Paired; the left and right arteries have different origins.
subclavian_artery.fact: Blood pressure is usually measured in the arm because it reflects pressure in this artery system.
subclavian_artery.blood_supply: Its wall is fed by small vasa vasorum.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Upper limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

common_carotid_artery.name: Common carotid artery
common_carotid_artery.tagline: The main neck artery on each side, splitting into the internal and external carotids.
common_carotid_artery.overview: Each common carotid artery runs up the side of the neck inside a sheath shared with the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve. It gives no branches in the neck. At about the level of the top of the thyroid cartilage it divides into the internal carotid artery, which goes to the brain and eye, and the external carotid artery, which supplies the face and scalp.
functions: Carrying blood from the chest up to the head
Feeding the brain through the internal carotid
Feeding the face, scalp and neck through the external carotid
Its fork houses sensors for blood pressure and oxygen
connections: Right: from the brachiocephalic trunk; left: from the aortic arch
Divides into internal and external carotid arteries
Travels with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve in the carotid sheath
clinical: Plaque often builds up at the fork, which can narrow flow to the brain.
The pulse can be felt beside the windpipe, under the angle of the jaw.
common_carotid_artery.lateralization: Paired; the right starts in the neck, the left starts inside the chest.
common_carotid_artery.fact: 'Carotid' comes from a Greek word linked to deep sleep, as pressing it was thought to cause fainting.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

internal_carotid_artery.name: Internal carotid artery
internal_carotid_artery.tagline: The neck-to-skull artery that supplies most of the brain's front and middle parts.
internal_carotid_artery.overview: The internal carotid artery begins at the fork of the common carotid in the neck and climbs to the base of the skull without branching. It enters the skull through the carotid canal, curves through the cavernous sinus beside the pituitary, and ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
functions: Supplying most of each cerebral hemisphere
Supplying the eye via the ophthalmic artery
Contributing to the circle of Willis at the brain's base
Supplying the pituitary gland region
connections: Starts from the common carotid artery
Ends as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries
Joins the posterior circulation via the posterior communicating artery
clinical: Narrowing at its origin in the neck is a common cause of stroke.
Its course through the skull base is important in head and neck surgery.
internal_carotid_artery.lateralization: Paired; each mainly supplies the hemisphere on its own side.
internal_carotid_artery.fact: Its S-shaped bends inside the skull are called the carotid siphon.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

iliac_artery.name: Iliac artery
iliac_artery.tagline: The pelvic arteries that carry blood from the aorta to the pelvis and legs.
iliac_artery.overview: The aorta divides in the lower abdomen into the right and left common iliac arteries. Each runs down and outwards along the pelvic brim and splits into an internal iliac artery, which feeds the pelvic organs and buttock, and an external iliac artery, which passes under the groin ligament to become the femoral artery of the thigh. The segmentation covers the common and external parts.
functions: Carrying blood from the aorta to the leg
Supplying the pelvic organs via the internal iliac branch
Supplying the buttock muscles
Supplying the lower abdominal wall
connections: Arises from the end of the aorta
Continues as the femoral artery in the thigh
Lies close to the iliac vein and the ureter
clinical: Narrowing of these arteries can cause leg pain on walking.
Aneurysms of the aorta can extend into the iliac arteries.
iliac_artery.fact: The ureter crosses in front of the iliac artery near its fork, a landmark surgeons use.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

pulmonary_vein.name: Pulmonary veins
pulmonary_vein.tagline: The veins that bring freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
pulmonary_vein.overview: Usually four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium. Unlike most veins, they carry the most oxygenated blood in the body. Their entry points into the left atrium are important landmarks for heart rhythm procedures.
functions: Returning oxygenated blood from the lungs
Filling the left atrium
Completing the pulmonary circulation
Their muscle sleeves can trigger extra heartbeats
connections: Drain each lung
Open into the left atrium
clinical: Abnormal electrical signals near the veins are a common trigger of atrial fibrillation.
The number and pattern of the veins vary between people.
pulmonary_vein.lateralization: Paired, typically two per lung; this label shows them together.
pulmonary_vein.fact: They are the only veins in an adult that carry oxygen-rich blood.
pulmonary_vein.blood_supply: Their walls are nourished by bronchial vessels and the blood they carry.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §19.1 Heart Anatomy
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

lung_arteries.name: Pulmonary arteries (in the lung)
lung_arteries.tagline: Branching arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood into the lungs to pick up oxygen.
lung_arteries.overview: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries. Inside each lung these branch again and again alongside the airways, down to tiny capillaries around the air sacs where blood gives up carbon dioxide and takes up oxygen.
functions: Carrying oxygen-poor blood from the right heart
Delivering blood to the air sacs for gas exchange
Following the branching pattern of the airways
Filtering small clots out of the circulation
connections: From the pulmonary trunk and right ventricle
Run beside the bronchi and end in alveolar capillaries
clinical: A clot lodged in these arteries (pulmonary embolism) blocks blood flow to part of the lung.
Raised pressure in these vessels strains the right side of the heart.
lung_arteries.fact: Spread out, the capillaries of the lungs would cover a surface roughly the size of a tennis court.
lung_arteries.blood_supply: These arteries carry blood to the lungs; the lung tissue itself is also fed by bronchial arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.2 The Lungs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

lung_veins.name: Pulmonary veins (in the lung)
lung_veins.tagline: The veins inside the lungs that collect oxygen-rich blood and return it to the heart.
lung_veins.overview: Small veins gather oxygenated blood from the capillaries around the air sacs. They run mostly between the lung segments rather than beside the airways, joining into larger veins that leave each lung as the pulmonary veins and drain into the left atrium.
functions: Collecting oxygen-rich blood from the air sacs
Draining blood between lung segments
Returning blood to the left atrium
Completing the lung circulation
connections: Begin at alveolar capillaries
Join to form the main pulmonary veins
clinical: When the left heart struggles, pressure backs up into these veins and fluid can leak into the lung.
On imaging they are told apart from arteries by their course between, not beside, the airways.
lung_veins.fact: Arteries follow the airways while veins run between lung segments: a useful rule for telling them apart.
lung_veins.blood_supply: The bronchial circulation nourishes their walls.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.2 The Lungs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

lung_vessels.name: Lung vessels
lung_vessels.tagline: All blood vessels inside the lungs, arteries and veins together.
lung_vessels.overview: This label combines the pulmonary arteries and veins within the lungs into one structure. Together they form a dense, tree-like network that brings oxygen-poor blood to the air sacs and carries oxygen-rich blood back towards the heart.
functions: Bringing blood to the air sacs
Returning oxygenated blood to the heart
Providing a huge surface for gas exchange
Holding a reserve of blood that can shift with posture
connections: Pulmonary trunk and right ventricle (arteries)
Pulmonary veins and left atrium (veins)
clinical: Clots, raised pressure or heart failure can change these vessels.
Vessel patterns on CT help readers understand the anatomy of each lung segment.
lung_vessels.fact: The lungs receive the entire output of the right heart with every beat.
lung_vessels.blood_supply: Lung tissue also has a separate small supply from the bronchial arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.2 The Lungs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax

superior_vena_cava.name: Superior vena cava
