superior_vena_cava.tagline: The large vein returning blood from the head, neck and arms to the heart.
superior_vena_cava.overview: The superior vena cava is a short, wide vein in the upper right chest. It is formed behind the right first costal cartilage where the left and right brachiocephalic veins join, and it runs down to open into the top of the right atrium. Just before it enters the heart it receives the azygos vein from the chest wall.
functions: Returning blood from the head and neck
Returning blood from the arms
Receiving blood from the chest wall via the azygos vein
Filling the right atrium
connections: Formed by the two brachiocephalic veins
Opens into the right atrium
Receives the azygos vein
clinical: Pressure on it from nearby masses can cause swelling of the face and arms.
It is a common destination for central venous lines placed from the neck or arm.
superior_vena_cava.lateralization: A single vessel on the right side of the chest.
superior_vena_cava.fact: It carries roughly a third of the blood returning to the heart.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

inferior_vena_cava.name: Inferior vena cava
inferior_vena_cava.tagline: The body's largest vein, returning blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen.
inferior_vena_cava.overview: The inferior vena cava forms in the lower abdomen where the two common iliac veins join. It runs upwards on the right side of the aorta, in front of the spine, receives the kidney and liver veins, passes through the diaphragm and opens into the bottom of the right atrium.
functions: Returning blood from the legs and pelvis
Collecting blood from the kidneys
Collecting blood from the liver via the hepatic veins
Filling the right atrium
connections: Formed by the common iliac veins
Receives renal and hepatic veins
Opens into the right atrium
clinical: Clots from the leg veins travel through it towards the lungs.
Its width changes with breathing and fluid status.
inferior_vena_cava.lateralization: A single vessel to the right of the aorta.
inferior_vena_cava.fact: It passes through its own opening in the diaphragm at about the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

brachiocephalic_vein.name: Brachiocephalic vein
brachiocephalic_vein.tagline: Large neck-to-chest veins that join to form the superior vena cava.
brachiocephalic_vein.overview: On each side, the internal jugular vein from the head and the subclavian vein from the arm join behind the inner end of the collarbone to form a brachiocephalic vein. The left one is longer and crosses the upper chest in front of the aortic branches; the right one is short and nearly vertical. They unite to form the superior vena cava.
functions: Draining the head and neck
Draining the arm
Receiving lymph from the thoracic duct (left) and right lymphatic duct
Forming the superior vena cava
connections: Formed by the internal jugular and subclavian veins
Join to form the superior vena cava
clinical: The left vein can be narrowed by long-term intravenous lines.
Its course matters when placing central venous catheters.
brachiocephalic_vein.lateralization: Paired; the left is about twice as long as the right.
brachiocephalic_vein.fact: The body's main lymph vessel empties into the venous system right where the left vein begins.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

internal_jugular_vein.name: Internal jugular vein
internal_jugular_vein.tagline: The main vein draining blood from the brain, face and neck.
internal_jugular_vein.overview: The internal jugular vein begins at the base of the skull as the continuation of the sigmoid venous sinus, which drains the brain. It runs down the side of the neck in the carotid sheath, beside the carotid artery, collecting veins from the face and neck, and joins the subclavian vein behind the collarbone.
functions: Draining blood from the brain
Draining the face and neck
Carrying blood towards the superior vena cava
Its pulse reflects pressure in the right heart
connections: Continues from the sigmoid sinus at the jugular foramen
Joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein
Runs beside the carotid artery and vagus nerve
clinical: It is a common site for placing central venous lines.
Doctors look at its pulsation in the neck as an indirect sign of heart pressures.
internal_jugular_vein.lateralization: Paired; the right is often larger.
internal_jugular_vein.fact: The internal jugular is much larger than the external jugular vein seen under the skin.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

iliac_vena.name: Iliac vein
iliac_vena.tagline: The pelvic veins returning blood from the legs and pelvis towards the vena cava.
iliac_vena.overview: The femoral vein of the thigh continues above the groin as the external iliac vein. It joins the internal iliac vein from the pelvic organs to form the common iliac vein, and the two common iliac veins unite in the lower abdomen to form the inferior vena cava. The segmentation covers the common and external parts.
functions: Returning blood from the leg
Collecting blood from the pelvic organs
Forming the inferior vena cava
Draining the lower abdominal wall
connections: Continues from the femoral vein
Join to form the inferior vena cava
Runs close to the iliac artery
clinical: Deep vein clots can extend into these veins.
The left common iliac vein can be pressed between the right iliac artery and the spine.
iliac_vena.fact: Because the vena cava lies on the right, the left common iliac vein is longer than the right.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.name: Portal and splenic veins
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.tagline: Veins that carry blood from the gut and spleen to the liver for processing.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.overview: The splenic vein runs from the spleen behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein, which drains the intestines, to form the portal vein behind the neck of the pancreas. The portal vein then travels to the liver, where it branches so that nutrient-rich blood from the gut passes through the liver before reaching the rest of the body.
functions: Carrying nutrient-rich blood from the intestines to the liver
Draining the spleen
Draining the stomach and pancreas
Supplying about three-quarters of the liver's blood flow
connections: Formed by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins
Branches inside the liver
Runs with the hepatic artery and bile duct to the liver
clinical: Scarring of the liver can raise pressure in the portal system (portal hypertension).
A clot can form in the portal or splenic vein.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.lateralization: Single midline system; the splenic vein crosses from the left.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.fact: The portal vein is called a 'portal' system because it links two capillary beds: gut and liver.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.blood_supply: Its wall has small vasa vasorum; the liver also receives arterial blood from the hepatic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion: The Liver, Pancreas, and Gallbladder
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis

liver_vessels.name: Liver vessels
liver_vessels.tagline: The branching veins and arteries inside the liver.
liver_vessels.overview: Inside the liver, branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery bring blood in, and the hepatic veins carry it out to the inferior vena cava. This label shows these vessels inside the liver as one network. Their branching pattern is what divides the liver into its eight functional segments.
functions: Bringing gut blood into the liver via portal branches
Bringing oxygen-rich blood via hepatic artery branches
Draining processed blood through the hepatic veins
Defining the liver's functional segments
connections: Portal vein and hepatic artery (inflow)
Hepatic veins draining into the inferior vena cava
clinical: Surgeons map these vessels before liver operations.
Liver scarring can change their shape and flow.
liver_vessels.lateralization: A single network within the liver, which lies mainly on the right.
liver_vessels.fact: The liver receives blood from two sources at once, which is rare among organs.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion: The Liver, Pancreas, and Gallbladder
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis

esophagus.name: Oesophagus
esophagus.tagline: The muscular food pipe that carries swallowed food from throat to stomach.
esophagus.overview: The oesophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long. It starts in the neck behind the trachea, runs down through the chest in front of the spine and passes through the diaphragm to join the stomach. Waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis) push food along, so swallowing works even when lying down.
functions: Carrying food and liquid to the stomach
Pushing food with waves of muscle (peristalsis)
Keeping stomach contents from flowing back via its lower sphincter
Relaxing at the top to let swallowed food in
connections: Pharynx above
Stomach below
Trachea in front in the neck
Aorta beside it in the chest
clinical: Acid reflux happens when stomach contents flow back up into the oesophagus.
Difficulty swallowing is a symptom doctors may investigate with a camera test (endoscopy).
esophagus.lateralization: Midline, bending slightly to the left at its lower end.
esophagus.fact: Food takes only about 5 to 10 seconds to travel the length of the oesophagus.
esophagus.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior thyroid arteries, the aorta and the left gastric artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.tagline: A stretchy muscular bag that stores, churns and begins digesting food.
stomach.overview: The stomach lies in the upper left abdomen, under the diaphragm. It is a J-shaped bag that can expand to hold a large meal. Its muscular wall churns food with acid and enzymes into a thick liquid, which it releases a little at a time into the duodenum through a valve called the pylorus.
functions: Storing food after a meal
Mixing food with acid and digestive enzymes
Starting protein digestion
Killing many swallowed germs with acid
Releasing food gradually to the small intestine
Making intrinsic factor needed to absorb vitamin B12
connections: Oesophagus above
Duodenum through the pylorus
Liver, spleen and pancreas nearby
clinical: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining.
Ulcers can form where acid damages the lining, often linked to H. pylori bacteria or some painkillers.
stomach.lateralization: Mostly on the left side of the upper abdomen.
stomach.fact: The stomach lining replaces its surface cells every few days to protect itself from its own acid.
stomach.blood_supply: Branches of the coeliac trunk: left and right gastric, gastro-omental and short gastric arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

duodenum.name: Duodenum
duodenum.tagline: The first, C-shaped part of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice enter.
duodenum.overview: The duodenum is about 25 cm long and curves in a C shape around the head of the pancreas. It receives partly digested food from the stomach. Bile from the liver and digestive juice from the pancreas enter it through a small opening, neutralising stomach acid and continuing digestion.
functions: Receiving food from the stomach
Mixing in bile and pancreatic juice
Neutralising stomach acid
Absorbing iron and other nutrients
Releasing hormones that control digestion
connections: Stomach through the pylorus
Bile duct and pancreatic duct
Jejunum, the next part of the small intestine
clinical: Duodenal ulcers are a common type of peptic ulcer.
A gallstone blocking the shared bile and pancreatic opening can affect both organs.
duodenum.lateralization: Mostly to the right of the midline, wrapping around the pancreas.
duodenum.fact: Its name comes from Latin for 'twelve finger-widths', its approximate length.
duodenum.blood_supply: Gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

small_bowel.name: Small intestine
small_bowel.tagline: The long, coiled tube where most nutrients are absorbed into the blood.
small_bowel.overview: After the duodenum the small intestine continues as the jejunum and ileum, together several metres long, coiled in the middle of the abdomen. Its inner surface is covered in folds and tiny finger-like villi that give it a huge area for absorbing digested food. It hangs from the back wall on a fan-shaped fold (mesentery).
functions: Finishing digestion of food
Absorbing sugars, proteins and fats
Absorbing vitamins, minerals and water
Absorbing vitamin B12 and bile salts in the ileum
Housing immune tissue (Peyer's patches)
connections: Duodenum at the start
Colon at the ileocaecal valve
Mesentery carrying its vessels and nerves
clinical: Coeliac disease is a reaction to gluten that damages the villi.
Crohn's disease is a long-term inflammation that often affects the end of the ileum.
small_bowel.lateralization: Fills the central and lower abdomen on both sides.
small_bowel.fact: Its folds, villi and microvilli give it an absorptive surface of around 200 square metres.
small_bowel.blood_supply: Branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

colon.name: Colon
colon.tagline: The large intestine, which absorbs water and forms stool.
colon.overview: The colon frames the abdomen: it rises on the right (ascending colon), crosses under the liver and stomach (transverse colon), descends on the left and forms an S-shaped loop (sigmoid colon) before the rectum. It absorbs water and salts from what remains after the small intestine and stores waste until it is passed.
functions: Absorbing water and salts
Forming and storing stool
Hosting gut bacteria that ferment fibre
Absorbing some vitamins made by bacteria
Moving waste along with slow muscle waves
connections: Small intestine via the caecum
Appendix attached to the caecum
Rectum below the sigmoid colon
clinical: Diverticula are small pouches in the colon wall, common with age.
Colonoscopy is a camera test used to look at the inside of the colon.
colon.lateralization: Ascending colon on the right, descending colon on the left; transverse colon crosses between them.
colon.fact: The colon holds trillions of bacteria, which outnumber many of the body's own cells.
colon.blood_supply: Superior mesenteric artery for the right half; inferior mesenteric artery for the left half.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

liver.name: Liver
liver.tagline: The body's largest internal organ: chemical factory, store and filter.
liver.overview: The liver sits in the upper right abdomen under the diaphragm, protected by the lower ribs. It receives blood from the gut through the portal vein and processes what has been absorbed. It makes bile, proteins and clotting factors, stores energy and vitamins, and breaks down medicines and toxins.
functions: Making bile to help digest fats
Processing nutrients from the gut
Storing glycogen, iron and vitamins
Making blood proteins and clotting factors
Breaking down medicines, alcohol and toxins
connections: Portal vein and hepatic artery bringing blood
Hepatic veins draining into the inferior vena cava
Bile ducts leading to the gallbladder and duodenum
clinical: Fatty liver is a common condition linked to weight, diet and alcohol.
Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver, often caused by viruses.
liver.lateralization: Mostly on the right, extending across the midline into the upper left abdomen.
liver.fact: The liver can regrow to its original size after part of it is removed.
liver.blood_supply: About three quarters from the portal vein and one quarter from the hepatic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

liver_segment_1.name: Liver segment 1
liver_segment_1.tagline: Liver segment 1: the caudate lobe, tucked behind against the vena cava.
liver_segment_1.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 1 is the caudate lobe, a small part at the back of the liver wrapped around the inferior vena cava. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_1.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_1.fact: Segment 1 drains straight into the inferior vena cava through its own small veins.
liver_segment_1.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_2.name: Liver segment 2
liver_segment_2.tagline: Liver segment 2: the upper, back part of the left lateral liver.
liver_segment_2.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 2 is the upper, back part of the left lateral liver. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_2.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_2.fact: Segments 2 and 3 together are sometimes used for liver donation to children.
liver_segment_2.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_3.name: Liver segment 3
liver_segment_3.tagline: Liver segment 3: the lower, front part of the left lateral liver.
liver_segment_3.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 3 is the lower, front part of the left lateral liver. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_3.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_3.fact: Segment 3 lies just under the left lower ribs near the stomach.
liver_segment_3.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_4.name: Liver segment 4
liver_segment_4.tagline: Liver segment 4: the inner part of the left liver, beside the gallbladder.
liver_segment_4.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 4 is the medial part of the left liver, beside the gallbladder (often split into 4a above and 4b below). Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_4.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_4.fact: Although it belongs to the left liver functionally, segment 4 lies right of the falciform ligament.
liver_segment_4.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_5.name: Liver segment 5
liver_segment_5.tagline: Liver segment 5: the lower front part of the right liver, by the gallbladder.
liver_segment_5.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 5 is the lower, front part of the right liver, under the gallbladder area. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_5.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_5.fact: The gallbladder rests against the underside of segments 4b and 5.
liver_segment_5.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_6.name: Liver segment 6
liver_segment_6.tagline: Liver segment 6: the lower back part of the right liver, above the kidney.
liver_segment_6.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 6 is the lower, back part of the right liver, close to the right kidney. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_6.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_6.fact: Segment 6 is often the lowest part of the liver, reaching towards the right kidney.
liver_segment_6.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_7.name: Liver segment 7
liver_segment_7.tagline: Liver segment 7: the upper back part of the right liver, under the diaphragm.
liver_segment_7.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 7 is the upper, back part of the right liver, under the dome of the diaphragm. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_7.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_7.fact: Segment 7 is tucked high under the right diaphragm, behind the lower ribs.
liver_segment_7.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

liver_segment_8.name: Liver segment 8
liver_segment_8.tagline: Liver segment 8: the upper front part of the right liver, under the diaphragm.
liver_segment_8.overview: Surgeons and radiologists divide the liver into eight Couinaud segments, numbered in a clockwise spiral. Segment 8 is the upper, front part of the right liver, under the diaphragm. Each segment has its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, so it can work, and be surgically removed, largely on its own.
functions: Processing nutrients from the gut
Making bile
Storing glycogen and vitamins
Making blood proteins
Breaking down medicines and toxins
connections: Its own portal vein and hepatic artery branch
Its own bile duct branch
Hepatic veins running between segments
clinical: Segments give a shared map for describing where something lies in the liver.
Because segments are self-contained, surgeons can remove one or more and spare the rest.
liver_segment_8.lateralization: A single segment of one liver; numbering follows the same pattern in every person, with natural variation.
liver_segment_8.fact: Segment 8 is one of the largest segments and meets the hepatic veins near the heart.
liver_segment_8.blood_supply: A segmental branch of the portal vein and of the hepatic artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen
Couinaud C., Le foie: etudes anatomiques et chirurgicales (1957)

gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
gallbladder.tagline: A small pouch under the liver that stores and concentrates bile.
gallbladder.overview: The gallbladder is a pear-shaped sac tucked under the liver. Between meals it stores bile made by the liver and concentrates it by removing water. After a fatty meal it squeezes, sending bile through the bile duct into the duodenum to help digest fats.
functions: Storing bile between meals
Concentrating bile
Releasing bile after eating
Helping digest and absorb fats
connections: Liver above
Cystic duct joining the common bile duct
Duodenum, where bile is delivered
clinical: Gallstones form when substances in bile harden; many cause no symptoms.
The gallbladder can be removed (cholecystectomy) and people digest normally without it.
gallbladder.lateralization: On the right, under the liver.
gallbladder.fact: The hormone cholecystokinin, released when fat reaches the duodenum, tells the gallbladder to contract.
gallbladder.blood_supply: Cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.tagline: A gland behind the stomach that makes digestive juice and insulin.
pancreas.overview: The pancreas is a soft, elongated gland lying across the back of the upper abdomen, behind the stomach. Its head sits in the curve of the duodenum and its tail reaches the spleen. Most of it makes digestive enzymes; scattered islands of cells (islets) release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
functions: Making enzymes that digest fats, proteins and carbohydrates
Releasing bicarbonate to neutralise acid
Producing insulin to lower blood sugar
Producing glucagon to raise blood sugar
Sending its juice to the duodenum through the pancreatic duct
connections: Duodenum around its head
Spleen at its tail
Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vessels behind it
clinical: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas, often linked to gallstones or alcohol.
Diabetes involves problems with insulin made by the pancreas or how the body responds to it.
pancreas.lateralization: Crosses the midline, with the head on the right and the tail on the left.
pancreas.fact: Its islets make up only a small percentage of the pancreas but control blood sugar for the whole body.
pancreas.blood_supply: Branches of the splenic artery and the pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 23 The Digestive System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 17 The Endocrine System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

parotid_gland.name: Parotid gland
parotid_gland.tagline: The largest salivary gland, in front of the ear, emptying into the cheek.
parotid_gland.overview: Each parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear, over the back of the jaw. It makes a watery saliva that flows through the parotid duct, which crosses the cheek and opens inside the mouth opposite the upper second molar. The facial nerve, which moves the muscles of facial expression, branches as it passes through the gland.
functions: Producing saliva
Moistening food so it can be chewed and swallowed
Starting the digestion of starch with the enzyme amylase
Protecting teeth and gums with antibacterial proteins
connections: Parotid duct opening opposite the upper second molar
Facial nerve passing through it
Masseter muscle and the back of the lower jaw beneath it
clinical: Mumps is a viral infection that classically causes painful swelling of the parotid glands.
Most lumps that arise in the parotid are benign, but any lump is assessed by a doctor.
parotid_gland.lateralization: There is one on each side of the face.
parotid_gland.fact: Together the salivary glands make around a litre of saliva a day.
parotid_gland.blood_supply: Branches of the external carotid artery, which runs through the gland.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

submandibular_gland.name: Submandibular gland
submandibular_gland.tagline: A salivary gland under the jaw that makes most of the saliva at rest.
submandibular_gland.overview: Each submandibular gland lies just under the lower jaw, towards the back, partly wrapping around a muscle of the floor of the mouth. Its duct runs forward under the tongue and opens on a small bump beside the frenulum. It makes a mixed watery and slightly thick saliva and produces most of the saliva when a person is not eating.
functions: Producing saliva
Moistening food so it can be chewed and swallowed
Starting the digestion of starch with the enzyme amylase
Protecting teeth and gums with antibacterial proteins
connections: Submandibular duct opening under the tongue
Floor of the mouth (mylohyoid muscle)
Lingual nerve nearby
clinical: Salivary stones form most often in this gland because its saliva is thicker and its duct runs uphill.
A blocked duct can make the gland swell around mealtimes.
submandibular_gland.lateralization: There is one on each side under the jaw.
submandibular_gland.fact: Although the parotid is larger, the submandibular glands make most of the resting saliva.
submandibular_gland.blood_supply: Facial artery and its submental branch.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

tongue.name: Tongue
tongue.tagline: A muscular organ for taste, chewing, swallowing and speech.
tongue.overview: The tongue is a mass of interlacing muscle covered by a lining that carries the taste buds. Its front two-thirds lie in the mouth and its back third faces the throat. Muscles inside it change its shape, and muscles attached to the jaw, hyoid bone and skull move it as a whole.
functions: Tasting food
Moving food between the teeth while chewing
Pushing food back to start swallowing
Forming speech sounds
Cleaning the teeth and mouth
connections: Hyoid bone and lower jaw (mandible) where its muscles attach
Hypoglossal nerve (movement)
Floor of the mouth and the oropharynx
clinical: Damage to one hypoglossal nerve makes the tongue point towards the weak side when stuck out.
During deep sleep the relaxed tongue can fall back and narrow the airway.
tongue.lateralization: Left and right halves are separated by a midline fibrous partition; each half is moved by its own nerve.
tongue.fact: The tongue's taste buds are replaced roughly every one to two weeks.
tongue.blood_supply: The lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

hard_palate.name: Hard palate
hard_palate.tagline: The bony front part of the roof of the mouth, separating mouth from nose.
hard_palate.overview: The hard palate forms the front two-thirds of the roof of the mouth. It is made of the palatine processes of the upper jaw bones in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind, covered by firm, ridged lining. It is the floor of the nasal cavity above and the roof of the mouth below.
functions: Separating the mouth from the nasal cavity
Giving the tongue a firm surface to press food against
Helping to shape speech sounds
Allowing breathing through the nose while chewing
connections: Soft palate at its back edge
Upper teeth and upper jaw bone (maxilla) around its edge
Nasal cavity above
clinical: A cleft palate is a gap present from birth that can affect feeding and speech and is repaired surgically.
A bony bump in the middle of the palate (torus palatinus) is a common harmless variant.
hard_palate.lateralization: A single midline structure formed by left and right halves joined in the middle.
hard_palate.fact: The two halves of the palate normally fuse before birth, around the end of the first trimester.
hard_palate.blood_supply: Greater palatine arteries, branches of the maxillary artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

soft_palate.name: Soft palate
soft_palate.tagline: The movable muscular back of the roof of the mouth, ending in the uvula.
soft_palate.overview: The soft palate hangs from the back edge of the hard palate. It is a flexible sheet of muscle covered by moist lining, with the small uvula hanging from its middle. During swallowing it lifts to close off the nasal part of the throat, and during speech it controls how much air passes through the nose.
functions: Sealing off the nasopharynx during swallowing
Stopping food and drink from entering the nose
Controlling nasal airflow in speech
Taking part in the gag reflex
connections: Hard palate in front
Tongue and pharynx through muscular arches (the palatal arches)
Nasopharynx above and behind
clinical: Its vibration contributes to snoring.
Weakness or a cleft of the soft palate can make speech sound nasal.
soft_palate.lateralization: A midline structure moved by paired muscles on both sides.
soft_palate.fact: The uvula's Latin name means 'little grape'.
soft_palate.blood_supply: Lesser palatine arteries and the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

oropharynx.name: Oropharynx
oropharynx.tagline: The middle part of the throat, behind the mouth, where air and food both pass.
oropharynx.overview: The oropharynx lies behind the mouth, between the soft palate above and the top of the epiglottis below. It includes the back third of the tongue, the palatine tonsils on each side and the back wall of the throat. Both air and swallowed food travel through it.
functions: Passing air between the nasopharynx and the larynx
Passing food from the mouth towards the oesophagus
Immune defence through the palatine and lingual tonsils
Starting the swallowing reflex
connections: Mouth in front through the opening called the fauces
Nasopharynx above and hypopharynx below
Palatine tonsils in its side walls
clinical: Tonsillitis, an infection of the palatine tonsils, is common in children.
Narrowing of this space during sleep contributes to snoring and sleep apnoea.
oropharynx.lateralization: A single midline space, with a tonsil on each side.
oropharynx.fact: The palatine tonsils are what most people mean by 'the tonsils'.
oropharynx.blood_supply: Branches of the external carotid artery, including the facial, lingual and ascending pharyngeal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

hypopharynx.name: Hypopharynx
hypopharynx.tagline: The lowest part of the throat, behind the larynx, leading into the oesophagus.
hypopharynx.overview: The hypopharynx (laryngopharynx) runs from the top of the epiglottis down to the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage, behind and around the larynx. Food passes through two side gutters (the piriform recesses) on either side of the larynx before entering the oesophagus, while air turns forward into the larynx.
functions: Guiding swallowed food around the larynx into the oesophagus
Passing air forward into the larynx
Squeezing food downwards with its constrictor muscles
Protecting the airway together with the epiglottis
connections: Larynx in front
Oesophagus below
Oropharynx above
clinical: Small swallowed objects such as fish bones can lodge in the piriform recesses.
Swallowing difficulty can come from problems with the muscles or nerves of this region.
hypopharynx.lateralization: A single midline space with a piriform recess on each side.
hypopharynx.fact: The upper oesophageal sphincter at its lower end stays closed between swallows.
hypopharynx.blood_supply: Branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries and the ascending pharyngeal artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

pharynx.name: Pharynx
pharynx.tagline: The muscular tube behind nose and mouth shared by air and food.
pharynx.overview: The pharynx is a funnel-shaped muscular tube about 12 to 14 cm long that runs from the base of the skull to the level of the cricoid cartilage, where it continues as the oesophagus. It has three parts: the nasopharynx behind the nose, the oropharynx behind the mouth and the hypopharynx (laryngopharynx) behind the larynx.
functions: Carrying air between the nose and the larynx
Carrying food and drink from the mouth to the oesophagus
Squeezing food downwards during swallowing
Shaping the sound of the voice
connections: Nasal cavity and mouth in front
Larynx and oesophagus below
Pharyngeal constrictor muscles in its wall
clinical: Sore throat (pharyngitis) is usually caused by common viral infections.
Problems with the swallowing muscles can let food or drink go the wrong way.
pharynx.fact: Air and food cross paths in the pharynx; swallowing briefly stops breathing to keep them apart.
pharynx.blood_supply: Branches of the external carotid artery, mainly the ascending pharyngeal artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

teeth_upper.name: Upper teeth
teeth_upper.tagline: All the teeth set in the upper jaw, shown together as one arch.
teeth_upper.overview: In an adult the upper arch normally holds up to 16 permanent teeth: on each side two incisors, one canine, two premolars and up to three molars. They sit in sockets in the upper jaw bone (maxilla) and are covered at the neck by the gums. Shown as one shape, this layer gives an overview of the arch rather than each tooth.
functions: Biting and cutting with the front teeth
Crushing and grinding with the back teeth
Helping to form speech sounds
Supporting the lips and cheeks and the shape of the lower face
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the lower arch when the mouth closes
clinical: Missing teeth are common and can let neighbouring teeth drift or tilt over time.
How the upper and lower arches meet (the bite, or occlusion) varies a lot between people.
teeth_upper.lateralization: The left and right halves of the arch are normally mirror images.
teeth_upper.fact: Children have 20 baby (primary) teeth; adults have up to 32 permanent teeth.
teeth_upper.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

teeth_lower.name: Lower teeth
teeth_lower.tagline: All the teeth set in the lower jaw, shown together as one arch.
teeth_lower.overview: In an adult the lower arch normally holds up to 16 permanent teeth: on each side two incisors, one canine, two premolars and up to three molars. They sit in sockets in the lower jaw bone (mandible) and are covered at the neck by the gums. Shown as one shape, this layer gives an overview of the arch rather than each tooth.

Crushing and grinding with the back teeth
Helping to form speech sounds
Supporting the lips and cheeks and the shape of the lower face
connections: Lower jaw bone (mandible)
Inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the upper arch when the mouth closes
clinical: Missing teeth are common and can let neighbouring teeth drift or tilt over time.
How the upper and lower arches meet (the bite, or occlusion) varies a lot between people.
teeth_lower.lateralization: The left and right halves of the arch are normally mirror images.
teeth_lower.fact: Children have 20 baby (primary) teeth; adults have up to 32 permanent teeth.
teeth_lower.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior alveolar artery, which runs through the lower jaw from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

upper_central_incisor_fdi11.name: Upper right central incisor (FDI 11)
upper_central_incisor_fdi11.tagline: Thin, chisel-shaped front tooth for biting and cutting food.
upper_central_incisor_fdi11.overview: This is the permanent central incisor on the right side of the upper jaw, numbered 11 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 7 to 8 years and has one cone-shaped root. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Biting into and cutting food
Shaping sounds such as 'f', 'v' and 'th'
Supporting the lips and the look of the smile
Guiding the lower jaw forward when biting
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower central incisor when biting
clinical: Front teeth are the ones most often chipped or knocked out in falls and sports injuries.
Crowding or gaps between incisors are common and are usually a cosmetic or bite matter.
upper_central_incisor_fdi11.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 21 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_central_incisor_fdi11.fact: Incisors are the first permanent teeth most children notice, often arriving next to the first molars.
upper_central_incisor_fdi11.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

upper_central_incisor_pulp_fdi111.name: Pulp of upper right central incisor (FDI 11)
upper_central_incisor_pulp_fdi111.tagline: The soft living core of the tooth, with its nerves and blood vessels.
upper_central_incisor_pulp_fdi111.overview: The pulp is the soft tissue inside tooth 11 (upper right central incisor). It fills the pulp chamber in the crown and continues down the root canal(s) to small openings at the root tips, where nerves and vessels enter. The cells lining it keep making dentine slowly throughout life, so the pulp space gradually narrows with age.
functions: Keeping the tooth alive and nourished
Sensing heat, cold and pressure (felt as pain)
Laying down new dentine, including repair dentine after irritation
Helping the tooth respond to infection
connections: Surrounded by the dentine of tooth 11
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
clinical: Deep decay or a crack that reaches the pulp can make it inflamed and painful.
Root canal treatment removes the pulp and seals the canals while keeping the tooth.
upper_central_incisor_pulp_fdi111.lateralization: Each tooth has its own pulp; this one belongs to the right upper central incisor.
upper_central_incisor_pulp_fdi111.fact: The pulp space is widest in young people and becomes narrower with age as dentine is added.
upper_central_incisor_pulp_fdi111.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

upper_lateral_incisor_fdi12.name: Upper right lateral incisor (FDI 12)
upper_lateral_incisor_fdi12.tagline: Thin, chisel-shaped front tooth for biting and cutting food.
upper_lateral_incisor_fdi12.overview: This is the permanent lateral incisor on the right side of the upper jaw, numbered 12 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 8 to 9 years and has one slender root. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.

upper_canine_fdi13.name: Upper right canine (FDI 13)
upper_canine_fdi13.tagline: Pointed 'eye tooth' at the corner of the mouth for gripping and tearing.
upper_canine_fdi13.overview: This is the permanent canine on the right side of the upper jaw, numbered 13 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 11 to 12 years and has one very long root, usually the longest in the mouth. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Gripping and tearing food
Guiding the jaw during side-to-side movements (canine guidance)
Supporting the corner of the lips and the shape of the face
Withstanding strong forces thanks to its long root
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower canine when biting
clinical: Upper canines are among the teeth that most often fail to come through on their own and stay buried (impacted).
Because of their long roots, canines are often among the last teeth to be lost in later life.
upper_canine_fdi13.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 23 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_canine_fdi13.fact: The upper canine is often called the 'eye tooth' because its long root reaches up towards the eye socket region.
upper_canine_fdi13.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

upper_first_premolar_fdi14.name: Upper right first premolar (FDI 14)
upper_first_premolar_fdi14.tagline: Two-cusped tooth between canine and molars that crushes and tears food.
upper_first_premolar_fdi14.overview: This is the permanent first premolar on the right side of the upper jaw, numbered 14 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 10 to 11 years and has usually two roots, one towards the cheek and one towards the palate. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Crushing and tearing food
Passing food back towards the molars
Sharing chewing load between front and back teeth
Supporting the cheeks and the width of the smile
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower first premolar when biting
clinical: Premolars are the teeth most often removed to make space during orthodontic (brace) treatment.
The upper premolar roots sit close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.
upper_first_premolar_fdi14.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 24 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_first_premolar_fdi14.fact: Premolars have no baby-tooth version of the same kind: they replace the primary molars.
upper_first_premolar_fdi14.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.

upper_first_molar_fdi16.name: Upper right first molar (FDI 16)
upper_first_molar_fdi16.tagline: Broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food before swallowing.
upper_first_molar_fdi16.overview: This is the permanent first molar on the right side of the upper jaw, numbered 16 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 6 to 7 years and has three roots, two towards the cheek and one towards the palate. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.

Holding the height of the bite between the jaws
Mixing food with saliva

Meets the opposing lower first molar when biting
clinical: The deep grooves on the chewing surface of molars are a common place for tooth decay to start.
Molar roots in the upper jaw can lie very close to the maxillary sinus; in the lower jaw, near the nerve canal.
upper_first_molar_fdi16.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 26 on the other side of the same jaw.

upper_second_molar_pulp_fdi117.tagline: The soft living core of the tooth, with its nerves and blood vessels.
upper_second_molar_pulp_fdi117.overview: The pulp is the soft tissue inside tooth 17 (upper right second molar). It fills the pulp chamber in the crown and continues down the root canal(s) to small openings at the root tips, where nerves and vessels enter. The cells lining it keep making dentine slowly throughout life, so the pulp space gradually narrows with age.
functions: Keeping the tooth alive and nourished
Sensing heat, cold and pressure (felt as pain)
Laying down new dentine, including repair dentine after irritation
Helping the tooth respond to infection
connections: Surrounded by the dentine of tooth 17
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
clinical: Deep decay or a crack that reaches the pulp can make it inflamed and painful.
Root canal treatment removes the pulp and seals the canals while keeping the tooth.
upper_second_molar_pulp_fdi117.lateralization: Each tooth has its own pulp; this one belongs to the right upper second molar.
upper_second_molar_pulp_fdi117.fact: The pulp space is widest in young people and becomes narrower with age as dentine is added.
upper_second_molar_pulp_fdi117.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

upper_third_molar_fdi18.name: Upper right third molar (FDI 18)
upper_third_molar_fdi18.tagline: Broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food before swallowing.
upper_third_molar_fdi18.overview: This is the permanent third molar on the right side of the upper jaw, numbered 18 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through usually in the late teens or twenties, if at all and has roots that vary a lot and are often fused. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Grinding and mashing food
Bearing most of the chewing force
Holding the height of the bite between the jaws
Mixing food with saliva
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower third molar when biting
clinical: Third (wisdom) molars are often missing, only partly erupted, or stay buried in the jaw (impacted).
A partly erupted wisdom tooth can trap food and let the gum around it become inflamed.
upper_third_molar_fdi18.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 28 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_third_molar_fdi18.fact: Molar comes from the Latin 'mola', meaning millstone.
upper_third_molar_fdi18.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

upper_central_incisor_fdi21.name: Upper left central incisor (FDI 21)
upper_central_incisor_fdi21.tagline: Thin, chisel-shaped front tooth for biting and cutting food.
upper_central_incisor_fdi21.overview: This is the permanent central incisor on the left side of the upper jaw, numbered 21 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 7 to 8 years and has one cone-shaped root. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Biting into and cutting food
Shaping sounds such as 'f', 'v' and 'th'
Supporting the lips and the look of the smile
Guiding the lower jaw forward when biting
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower central incisor when biting
clinical: Front teeth are the ones most often chipped or knocked out in falls and sports injuries.
Crowding or gaps between incisors are common and are usually a cosmetic or bite matter.
upper_central_incisor_fdi21.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 11 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_central_incisor_fdi21.fact: Incisors are the first permanent teeth most children notice, often arriving next to the first molars.
upper_central_incisor_fdi21.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.

upper_canine_fdi23.name: Upper left canine (FDI 23)
upper_canine_fdi23.tagline: Pointed 'eye tooth' at the corner of the mouth for gripping and tearing.
upper_canine_fdi23.overview: This is the permanent canine on the left side of the upper jaw, numbered 23 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 11 to 12 years and has one very long root, usually the longest in the mouth. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Gripping and tearing food
Guiding the jaw during side-to-side movements (canine guidance)
Supporting the corner of the lips and the shape of the face
Withstanding strong forces thanks to its long root
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower canine when biting
clinical: Upper canines are among the teeth that most often fail to come through on their own and stay buried (impacted).
Because of their long roots, canines are often among the last teeth to be lost in later life.
upper_canine_fdi23.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 13 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_canine_fdi23.fact: The upper canine is often called the 'eye tooth' because its long root reaches up towards the eye socket region.
upper_canine_fdi23.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

upper_first_premolar_fdi24.name: Upper left first premolar (FDI 24)
upper_first_premolar_fdi24.tagline: Two-cusped tooth between canine and molars that crushes and tears food.
upper_first_premolar_fdi24.overview: This is the permanent first premolar on the left side of the upper jaw, numbered 24 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 10 to 11 years and has usually two roots, one towards the cheek and one towards the palate. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Crushing and tearing food
Passing food back towards the molars
Sharing chewing load between front and back teeth
Supporting the cheeks and the width of the smile
connections: Upper jaw bone (maxilla)
Superior alveolar nerves (maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing lower first premolar when biting
clinical: Premolars are the teeth most often removed to make space during orthodontic (brace) treatment.
The upper premolar roots sit close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.
upper_first_premolar_fdi24.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 14 on the other side of the same jaw.
upper_first_premolar_fdi24.fact: Premolars have no baby-tooth version of the same kind: they replace the primary molars.
upper_first_premolar_fdi24.blood_supply: Branches of the superior alveolar arteries, which come from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

lower_lateral_incisor_fdi42.name: Lower right lateral incisor (FDI 42)
lower_lateral_incisor_fdi42.tagline: Thin, chisel-shaped front tooth for biting and cutting food.
lower_lateral_incisor_fdi42.overview: This is the permanent lateral incisor on the right side of the lower jaw, numbered 42 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 7 to 8 years and has one narrow, flattened root. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Biting into and cutting food
Shaping sounds such as 'f', 'v' and 'th'
Supporting the lips and the look of the smile
Guiding the lower jaw forward when biting
connections: Lower jaw bone (mandible)
Inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing upper lateral incisor when biting
clinical: Front teeth are the ones most often chipped or knocked out in falls and sports injuries.
Crowding or gaps between incisors are common and are usually a cosmetic or bite matter.
lower_lateral_incisor_fdi42.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 32 on the other side of the same jaw.
lower_lateral_incisor_fdi42.fact: Incisors are the first permanent teeth most children notice, often arriving next to the first molars.
lower_lateral_incisor_fdi42.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior alveolar artery, which runs through the lower jaw from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

lower_lateral_incisor_pulp_fdi142.name: Pulp of lower right lateral incisor (FDI 42)
lower_lateral_incisor_pulp_fdi142.tagline: The soft living core of the tooth, with its nerves and blood vessels.
lower_lateral_incisor_pulp_fdi142.overview: The pulp is the soft tissue inside tooth 42 (lower right lateral incisor). It fills the pulp chamber in the crown and continues down the root canal(s) to small openings at the root tips, where nerves and vessels enter. The cells lining it keep making dentine slowly throughout life, so the pulp space gradually narrows with age.
functions: Keeping the tooth alive and nourished
Sensing heat, cold and pressure (felt as pain)
Laying down new dentine, including repair dentine after irritation
Helping the tooth respond to infection
connections: Surrounded by the dentine of tooth 42
Inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve)
clinical: Deep decay or a crack that reaches the pulp can make it inflamed and painful.
Root canal treatment removes the pulp and seals the canals while keeping the tooth.
lower_lateral_incisor_pulp_fdi142.lateralization: Each tooth has its own pulp; this one belongs to the right lower lateral incisor.
lower_lateral_incisor_pulp_fdi142.fact: The pulp space is widest in young people and becomes narrower with age as dentine is added.
lower_lateral_incisor_pulp_fdi142.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior alveolar artery, which runs through the lower jaw from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus

lower_canine_fdi43.name: Lower right canine (FDI 43)
lower_canine_fdi43.tagline: Pointed 'eye tooth' at the corner of the mouth for gripping and tearing.
lower_canine_fdi43.overview: This is the permanent canine on the right side of the lower jaw, numbered 43 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 9 to 10 years and has one long root. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Gripping and tearing food
Guiding the jaw during side-to-side movements (canine guidance)
Supporting the corner of the lips and the shape of the face
Withstanding strong forces thanks to its long root
connections: Lower jaw bone (mandible)
Inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing upper canine when biting
clinical: Upper canines are among the teeth that most often fail to come through on their own and stay buried (impacted).
Because of their long roots, canines are often among the last teeth to be lost in later life.
lower_canine_fdi43.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 33 on the other side of the same jaw.
lower_canine_fdi43.fact: The upper canine is often called the 'eye tooth' because its long root reaches up towards the eye socket region.
lower_canine_fdi43.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior alveolar artery, which runs through the lower jaw from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

lower_first_premolar_fdi44.tagline: Two-cusped tooth between canine and molars that crushes and tears food.
lower_first_premolar_fdi44.overview: This is the permanent first premolar on the right side of the lower jaw, numbered 44 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 10 to 12 years and has usually one root. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Crushing and tearing food
Passing food back towards the molars
Sharing chewing load between front and back teeth
Supporting the cheeks and the width of the smile
connections: Lower jaw bone (mandible)
Inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing upper first premolar when biting
clinical: Premolars are the teeth most often removed to make space during orthodontic (brace) treatment.
The upper premolar roots sit close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.
lower_first_premolar_fdi44.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 34 on the other side of the same jaw.
lower_first_premolar_fdi44.fact: Premolars have no baby-tooth version of the same kind: they replace the primary molars.
lower_first_premolar_fdi44.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior alveolar artery, which runs through the lower jaw from the maxillary artery.
sources: Nelson, Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion 11e (2019)

lower_first_molar_fdi46.name: Lower right first molar (FDI 46)
lower_first_molar_fdi46.tagline: Broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food before swallowing.
lower_first_molar_fdi46.overview: This is the permanent first molar on the right side of the lower jaw, numbered 46 in the international FDI system (first digit = quadrant, second = position from the midline). It normally comes through around 6 to 7 years and has two roots, one in front and one behind. Like every tooth it has a hard enamel crown, a dentine body and a soft pulp inside, and it is held in its socket by a ligament.
functions: Grinding and mashing food
Bearing most of the chewing force
Holding the height of the bite between the jaws
Mixing food with saliva
connections: Lower jaw bone (mandible)
Inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve)
Meets the opposing upper first molar when biting
clinical: The deep grooves on the chewing surface of molars are a common place for tooth decay to start.
Molar roots in the upper jaw can lie very close to the maxillary sinus; in the lower jaw, near the nerve canal.
lower_first_molar_fdi46.lateralization: Mirrors tooth 36 on the other side of the same jaw.
lower_first_molar_fdi46.fact: Molar comes from the Latin 'mola', meaning millstone.
lower_first_molar_fdi46.blood_supply: Branches of the inferior alveolar artery, which runs through the lower jaw from the maxillary artery.

Holding the height of the bite between the jaws

A partly erupted wisdom tooth can trap food and let the gum around it become inflamed.

kidney.name: Kidney
kidney.tagline: Bean-shaped organs that filter the blood and make urine.
kidney.overview: The two kidneys lie against the back wall of the abdomen on either side of the spine, partly protected by the lowest ribs. Each contains about a million tiny filters (nephrons) that clean the blood, keep its salt and water in balance and produce urine, which drains down the ureter to the bladder.
functions: Filtering waste from the blood
Balancing water and salts
Helping control blood pressure
Making the hormone erythropoietin that boosts red blood cells
Activating vitamin D
Keeping the blood's acid level steady
connections: Renal artery and vein
Ureter to the bladder
Adrenal gland sitting on top
clinical: Kidney stones are hard crystals that can block urine flow and cause pain.
Long-term high blood pressure and diabetes are common causes of reduced kidney function.
kidney.lateralization: Paired; the right kidney usually sits slightly lower because the liver is above it.
kidney.fact: Together the kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid a day but return almost all of it to the blood.
kidney.blood_supply: Renal arteries, coming directly from the aorta; they receive about a fifth of the heart's output.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 25 The Urinary System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

urinary_bladder.name: Urinary bladder
urinary_bladder.tagline: A stretchy muscular bag in the pelvis that stores urine.
urinary_bladder.overview: The bladder sits low in the pelvis behind the pubic bone. Urine arrives from the kidneys through the two ureters and is stored until it is convenient to empty. Its wall is a layer of muscle that stretches as it fills and squeezes to push urine out through the urethra.
functions: Storing urine
Stretching as it fills
Signalling fullness to the brain
Emptying through the urethra
Preventing backflow into the ureters
connections: Ureters from the kidneys
Urethra below
Prostate below it in males; uterus behind it in females
clinical: Bladder infections (cystitis) are common, especially in women.
Overactive bladder causes a frequent, sudden need to pass urine.
urinary_bladder.fact: The urge to urinate usually begins when the bladder holds a few hundred millilitres, well before it is full.
urinary_bladder.blood_supply: Superior and inferior vesical arteries from the internal iliac arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 25 The Urinary System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Pelvis and perineum

adrenal_gland.name: Adrenal gland
adrenal_gland.tagline: Small glands on top of each kidney that make stress and salt hormones.
adrenal_gland.overview: Each adrenal gland is a small, flattened gland sitting like a cap on the upper pole of a kidney. Its outer layer (cortex) makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone. Its core (medulla) releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in response to stress or danger.
functions: Making cortisol, which helps the body handle stress
Making aldosterone to keep salt and water balance
Releasing adrenaline for the fight-or-flight response
Making small amounts of sex hormones
Helping control blood pressure and blood sugar
connections: Top of each kidney
Inferior vena cava beside the right gland
Nerve signals from the sympathetic nervous system
clinical: Small, harmless lumps in the adrenal glands are often found by chance on scans.
Too much or too little cortisol causes conditions such as Cushing's syndrome or Addison's disease.
adrenal_gland.lateralization: Paired; the right is roughly triangular and the left more crescent-shaped.
adrenal_gland.fact: Adrenaline from the gland can raise the heart rate within seconds of a fright.
adrenal_gland.blood_supply: Three small adrenal arteries on each side, from the aorta, renal artery and inferior phrenic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 17 The Endocrine System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

thyroid_gland.name: Thyroid gland
thyroid_gland.tagline: A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that sets the body's metabolic pace.
thyroid_gland.overview: The thyroid lies in the front of the neck, wrapped around the trachea just below the voice box. It has a right and a left lobe joined by a narrow bridge (isthmus). Using iodine from food, it makes thyroid hormones that set how fast the body's cells use energy.
functions: Making thyroid hormones (T4 and T3)
Setting the body's metabolic rate
Supporting growth and brain development
Helping regulate heart rate and body temperature
Making calcitonin, involved in calcium balance
connections: Trachea behind it
Larynx above it
Parathyroid glands on its back surface
Carotid arteries on either side
clinical: An underactive thyroid can cause tiredness and weight gain; an overactive one can cause a fast heartbeat.
A goitre is an enlarged thyroid, historically common where diets lacked iodine.
thyroid_gland.lateralization: Two lobes, right and left, joined across the midline.
thyroid_gland.fact: Iodised salt was introduced in many countries to prevent thyroid problems caused by iodine shortage.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 17 The Endocrine System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Neck

spleen.name: Spleen
spleen.tagline: A fist-sized organ in the upper left abdomen that filters blood and fights infection.
spleen.overview: The spleen sits high in the left abdomen, behind the stomach and under the lower left ribs. It is soft and full of blood. It removes old or damaged red blood cells, stores some platelets and white cells, and acts as a large lymph node for the blood, helping fight certain infections.
functions: Filtering old red blood cells
Recycling iron from broken-down cells
Storing platelets and white cells
Fighting blood-borne infections
Making antibodies
connections: Splenic artery and vein
Stomach in front
Left kidney and tail of the pancreas nearby
clinical: The spleen can enlarge in some infections, such as glandular fever.
It can be injured in a blow to the left side; people can live without a spleen but need extra protection against some infections.
spleen.fact: Small extra spleens (accessory spleens) are present in a fair number of people and are harmless.
spleen.blood_supply: Splenic artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 21 The Lymphatic and Immune System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

prostate.name: Prostate
prostate.tagline: A walnut-sized male gland below the bladder that adds fluid to semen.
prostate.overview: The prostate is a gland found only in males, lying just below the bladder and in front of the rectum. The urethra, which carries urine and semen, passes through its centre. The prostate makes a thin fluid that forms part of semen and helps sperm move.
functions: Producing part of the fluid in semen
Helping sperm survive and move
Helping control urine flow with its muscle fibres
Closing the bladder outlet during ejaculation
connections: Bladder above
Urethra running through it
Rectum behind it
Seminal vesicles joining it from behind
clinical: The prostate commonly grows larger with age (benign prostatic enlargement), which can slow urine flow.
Prostate cancer is common in older men; doctors decide on any testing together with the person.
prostate.fact: Because it lies right in front of the rectum, a doctor can feel the back of the prostate during an examination.
prostate.blood_supply: Branches of the internal iliac arteries, mainly the inferior vesical artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 27 The Reproductive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Pelvis and perineum

breast.name: Breast
breast.tagline: Glandular and fatty tissue on the front of the chest; in women it can produce milk.
breast.overview: Each breast lies on the front of the chest over the pectoralis major muscle. It is made of milk-producing glands and ducts set in fat and supportive tissue, with the nipple at the centre. Breasts are present in everyone but develop much more in females at puberty; their make-up changes with age and hormones.
functions: Producing milk after childbirth (lactation)
Carrying milk to the nipple through ducts
Responding to hormonal changes
Storing fat
connections: Pectoralis major muscle behind it
Lymph nodes in the armpit
Skin and nipple in front
clinical: Breast tissue often feels lumpy and can change through the menstrual cycle.
Mammography and ultrasound are common ways to examine breast tissue.
breast.lateralization: Paired; slight differences in size between the two sides are normal.
breast.fact: Most lymph from the breast drains towards the lymph nodes of the armpit.
breast.blood_supply: Internal thoracic artery branches and branches of the lateral thoracic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 27 The Reproductive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

skull.name: Skull
skull.tagline: The bony case of the head: protects the brain and frames the face.
skull.overview: The skull is made of 22 bones. Eight form the cranium, the vault and base that enclose the brain; the rest form the face, including the eye sockets, nose and upper jaw. Except for the lower jaw, the bones are locked together by wavy fibrous joints called sutures. Holes in the skull base let nerves and blood vessels pass in and out.
functions: Protecting the brain
Housing the eyes, inner ears and nasal cavity
Forming the face and supporting the teeth
Giving attachment to chewing and neck muscles
Providing openings (foramina) for nerves and vessels
connections: Brain and its coverings (meninges)
First cervical vertebra (atlas) at the base
Lower jaw (mandible) at the jaw joints
Cranial nerves and the carotid and vertebral arteries
clinical: Skull fractures can follow head injury; the thin temple region (pterion) overlies an important artery.
In infants the soft gaps between bones (fontanelles) close over the first two years.
Early fusion of a suture in babies (craniosynostosis) can change head shape.
skull.lateralization: Mostly a midline structure built from paired and unpaired bones.
skull.fact: The stapes in the middle ear, the smallest bone of the body, sits inside the temporal bone of the skull.
skull.blood_supply: Mainly the middle meningeal artery for the cranial bones, plus branches of the external carotid artery for the face.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head

mandible.name: Mandible
mandible.tagline: The movable lower jaw that holds the lower teeth.
