mandible.overview: The mandible is the U-shaped lower jaw, the largest and strongest bone of the face and the only skull bone that moves freely. Its horizontal body carries the lower teeth, and a vertical branch (ramus) rises on each side to the jaw joint in front of the ear. A canal inside it carries the nerve and vessels to the lower teeth.
functions: Holding the lower teeth
Opening and closing the mouth
Chewing and biting
Supporting speech and swallowing
Giving attachment to chewing muscles and the tongue's base
connections: Temporal bones at the two jaw joints (temporomandibular joints)
Masseter, temporalis and pterygoid muscles
Inferior alveolar nerve and vessels
clinical: The mandible is one of the most commonly broken facial bones, often at the angle or near the joint.
Problems of the jaw joint can cause clicking, pain or limited mouth opening.
Bone in the tooth-bearing part slowly thins after teeth are lost.
mandible.lateralization: A single midline bone with a left and right half joined at the chin.
mandible.fact: The two halves of the mandible fuse at the chin during the first year of life.
mandible.blood_supply: Mainly the inferior alveolar artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, plus vessels from the overlying muscles.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head

upper_jawbone.name: Upper jawbone
upper_jawbone.tagline: The fixed upper jaw that holds the upper teeth and forms the mid-face.
upper_jawbone.overview: The upper jaw is formed by the two maxillae, joined in the midline. They carry the upper teeth, form most of the roof of the mouth (hard palate), the floor of the eye sockets and the sides of the nose. Each maxilla contains a large air space, the maxillary sinus. In dental cone-beam CT the label covers the tooth-bearing bone.
functions: Holding the upper teeth
Forming the front of the hard palate
Forming the floor of the eye socket
Shaping the nose and cheeks
Containing the maxillary sinus
connections: Upper teeth
Maxillary sinus
Nasal, zygomatic and palatine bones
Superior alveolar nerves and vessels
clinical: Mid-face fractures after facial injury often involve the maxilla.
Roots of upper back teeth lie close to the maxillary sinus, so tooth and sinus problems can affect each other.
A cleft palate results when the two halves do not fuse fully before birth.
upper_jawbone.lateralization: Formed from a left and right maxilla joined in the midline.
upper_jawbone.fact: The maxillae are sometimes called the keystone of the face because most facial bones meet them.
upper_jawbone.blood_supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, mainly the superior alveolar and infraorbital arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head

lower_jawbone.name: Lower jawbone
lower_jawbone.tagline: The movable lower jaw that holds the lower teeth.
lower_jawbone.overview: The mandible is the U-shaped lower jaw, the largest and strongest bone of the face and the only skull bone that moves freely. Its horizontal body carries the lower teeth, and a vertical branch (ramus) rises on each side to the jaw joint in front of the ear. A canal inside it carries the nerve and vessels to the lower teeth. In dental cone-beam CT the label covers the tooth-bearing bone around the roots.
functions: Holding the lower teeth
Opening and closing the mouth
Chewing and biting
Supporting speech and swallowing
Giving attachment to chewing muscles and the tongue's base
connections: Temporal bones at the two jaw joints (temporomandibular joints)
Masseter, temporalis and pterygoid muscles
Inferior alveolar nerve and vessels
clinical: The mandible is one of the most commonly broken facial bones, often at the angle or near the joint.
Problems of the jaw joint can cause clicking, pain or limited mouth opening.
Bone in the tooth-bearing part slowly thins after teeth are lost.
lower_jawbone.lateralization: A single midline bone with a left and right half joined at the chin.
lower_jawbone.fact: The two halves of the mandible fuse at the chin during the first year of life.
lower_jawbone.blood_supply: Mainly the inferior alveolar artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, plus vessels from the overlying muscles.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head

zygomatic_arch.name: Zygomatic arch
zygomatic_arch.tagline: The bony bridge of the cheek running from the cheekbone back toward the ear.
zygomatic_arch.overview: The zygomatic arch is a slender bar of bone on the side of the face, formed where a projection of the cheekbone (zygomatic bone) meets a projection of the temporal bone. It can be felt just in front of the ear. The temporalis muscle passes beneath it, and the masseter muscle hangs from its lower edge.
functions: Forming the prominence of the cheek
Giving origin to the masseter muscle
Protecting the temporalis muscle passing beneath it
Bracing the side of the face
connections: Zygomatic bone in front
Temporal bone behind
Masseter and temporalis muscles
clinical: A direct blow to the side of the face can break the arch and sometimes limits mouth opening.
Its shape and height largely set the width of the face.
zygomatic_arch.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
zygomatic_arch.fact: 'Zygoma' comes from the Greek for 'yoke', after its bridge-like shape.
zygomatic_arch.blood_supply: Small branches of the superficial temporal and transverse facial arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head

styloid_process.name: Styloid process
styloid_process.tagline: A thin bony spike below the ear that anchors muscles and ligaments of the throat.
styloid_process.overview: The styloid process is a slender, pointed projection from the underside of the temporal bone, just below and in front of the ear. Three small muscles and two ligaments attach to it, linking the skull base to the tongue, the hyoid bone and the throat. Its length varies a lot between people.
functions: Anchoring the styloglossus muscle of the tongue
Anchoring the stylohyoid muscle to the hyoid
Anchoring the stylopharyngeus muscle of the throat
Attaching the stylohyoid and stylomandibular ligaments
connections: Hyoid bone via the stylohyoid ligament
Tongue and pharynx muscles
Nearby internal carotid artery and jugular vein
clinical: An unusually long styloid process or calcified ligament can occasionally cause throat or neck pain (Eagle syndrome).
It lies close to major vessels and cranial nerves at the skull base.
styloid_process.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
styloid_process.fact: 'Styloid' means 'pen-like', from the Greek stylos, a writing stylus.
styloid_process.blood_supply: Small branches of the occipital and ascending pharyngeal arteries.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Neck
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull

hyoid.name: Hyoid bone
hyoid.tagline: A small U-shaped neck bone that anchors the tongue and helps swallowing.
hyoid.overview: The hyoid is a horseshoe-shaped bone in the front of the neck, at the level of the third cervical vertebra, between the jaw and the voice box. It is unusual because it does not form a joint with any other bone; it is slung in place by muscles and ligaments. It moves up and forward each time you swallow.
functions: Anchoring the base of the tongue
Raising the voice box during swallowing
Giving attachment to muscles above and below it
Helping keep the upper airway open
Supporting speech
connections: Tongue and floor-of-mouth muscles
Thyroid cartilage via the thyrohyoid membrane
Styloid process via the stylohyoid ligament
Strap muscles of the neck
clinical: A hyoid fracture is uncommon and usually follows direct force to the neck.
It is a useful landmark in the neck, above the thyroid cartilage.
hyoid.fact: The hyoid is the only bone in the body that does not articulate with another bone.
hyoid.blood_supply: Branches of the lingual and superior thyroid arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Neck

inferior_alveolar_canal.name: Inferior alveolar canal
inferior_alveolar_canal.tagline: A tunnel inside the lower jaw carrying the nerve and vessels to the lower teeth.
inferior_alveolar_canal.overview: The inferior alveolar canal runs through the mandible from an opening on the inner side of each ramus, down and forward below the roots of the lower teeth, to the mental foramen under the premolars. It carries the inferior alveolar nerve, artery and vein, which supply the lower teeth, gums and, through the chin branch, the lower lip.
functions: Protecting the inferior alveolar nerve
Carrying the artery and vein of the lower teeth
Supplying sensation to the lower teeth
Leading to the mental nerve for the chin and lower lip
connections: Mandibular foramen at its start
Mental foramen near the premolars
Roots of the lower molars and premolars
clinical: Dentists locate it before removing lower wisdom teeth or placing implants to avoid injuring the nerve.
Irritation of the nerve can cause numbness or tingling of the lower lip and chin.
inferior_alveolar_canal.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
inferior_alveolar_canal.fact: The 'numb lip' after a lower dental injection comes from anaesthetic placed near the entrance of this canal.
inferior_alveolar_canal.blood_supply: Inferior alveolar artery, from the maxillary artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head

mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi103.name: Mandibular incisive canal (left)
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi103.tagline: The small left front continuation of the jaw canal toward the lower incisors.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi103.overview: Beyond the mental foramen, a small branch of the inferior alveolar canal continues forward inside the front of the lower jaw toward the canine and incisor teeth. It carries the incisive branch of the nerve and vessels. This label marks the left canal; the numbers 103/104 are a dental-dataset convention, not FDI tooth codes.
functions: Carrying the incisive nerve to the lower front teeth
Carrying small vessels to the front of the jaw
Supplying sensation to the lower canine and incisors
Linking with the opposite side near the midline
connections: Inferior alveolar canal behind it
Roots of the lower canine and incisors
clinical: Surgeons check its position before placing implants in the front of the lower jaw.
Its size varies widely and it is not visible on every scan.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi103.lateralization: Paired: this is the left one.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi103.fact: The canal is often too thin to see on ordinary X-rays but can show on cone-beam CT.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi103.blood_supply: Incisive branch of the inferior alveolar artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head
Dental CBCT labelling convention (ToothFairy3 dataset)

mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi104.name: Mandibular incisive canal (right)
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi104.tagline: The small right front continuation of the jaw canal toward the lower incisors.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi104.overview: Beyond the mental foramen, a small branch of the inferior alveolar canal continues forward inside the front of the lower jaw toward the canine and incisor teeth. It carries the incisive branch of the nerve and vessels. This label marks the right canal; the numbers 103/104 are a dental-dataset convention, not FDI tooth codes.
functions: Carrying the incisive nerve to the lower front teeth
Carrying small vessels to the front of the jaw
Supplying sensation to the lower canine and incisors
Linking with the opposite side near the midline
connections: Inferior alveolar canal behind it
Roots of the lower canine and incisors
clinical: Surgeons check its position before placing implants in the front of the lower jaw.
Its size varies widely and it is not visible on every scan.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi104.lateralization: Paired: this is the right one.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi104.fact: The canal is often too thin to see on ordinary X-rays but can show on cone-beam CT.
mandibular_incisive_canal_fdi104.blood_supply: Incisive branch of the inferior alveolar artery.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Head
Dental CBCT labelling convention (ToothFairy3 dataset)

lingual_canal.name: Lingual canal
aka: Lingual foramen and canal of the mandible
lingual_canal.tagline: A tiny channel on the tongue side of the chin carrying small vessels into the jaw.
lingual_canal.overview: On the inner (tongue-facing) surface of the mandible, near the midline behind the chin, there are one or more small openings called lingual foramina. Short canals lead from them into the bone and carry small branches of the arteries of the floor of the mouth, and sometimes a nerve twig.
functions: Carrying small arteries into the front of the jaw
Draining small veins from the bone
Contributing to the blood supply of the chin region
Sometimes carrying a small sensory nerve branch
connections: Floor of the mouth (sublingual and submental arteries)
Genial tubercles where tongue muscles attach
clinical: Surgeons consider these vessels when placing implants in the front of the lower jaw, as bleeding into the floor of the mouth can be serious.
Their number and size vary between people.
lingual_canal.lateralization: Usually midline; there may be one or several.
lingual_canal.fact: These canals were little noticed until cone-beam CT made them easy to see.
lingual_canal.blood_supply: Branches of the sublingual and submental arteries.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and Neck
Dental CBCT labelling convention (ToothFairy3 dataset)

clavicula.name: Clavicle
clavicula.tagline: The collarbone: a strut that holds the shoulder out from the chest.
clavicula.overview: The clavicle is an S-shaped bone lying horizontally at the base of the neck, easily felt under the skin. Its inner end joins the breastbone and its outer end joins the shoulder blade. It acts as a strut that keeps the arm away from the body, and it shelters the large vessels and nerves passing from the neck to the arm.
functions: Holding the shoulder out to the side so the arm can swing freely
Passing forces from the arm to the trunk
Protecting the vessels and nerves that run to the arm
Giving attachment to neck, chest and shoulder muscles
connections: Sternum at the sternoclavicular joint
Scapula at the acromioclavicular joint
Subclavian vessels and brachial plexus beneath it
Sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, deltoid and pectoralis major
clinical: The clavicle is one of the most commonly broken bones, often from a fall on the shoulder or outstretched hand.
Shoulder-tip injuries can strain or separate the joint at its outer end.
clavicula.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
clavicula.fact: The clavicle is the first bone to begin hardening in the embryo and among the last to finish growing.
clavicula.blood_supply: Branches of the suprascapular and thoracoacromial arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §8.1 The Pectoral Girdle
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Upper Limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Upper Limb

scapula.name: Scapula
scapula.tagline: The shoulder blade: a flat, triangular bone that forms the socket of the shoulder.
scapula.overview: The scapula is a thin, triangular bone lying over the back of the upper ribs. It is held to the chest wall mainly by muscles, so it can glide and rotate. A shallow socket (glenoid) on its outer corner receives the head of the upper-arm bone, and a bony ridge (spine) ends in the acromion, the point of the shoulder.
functions: Forming the shoulder socket
Allowing the arm to be raised above the head by rotating
Anchoring the rotator cuff muscles
Linking the arm to the trunk through the clavicle and muscles
Giving attachment to about 17 muscles
connections: Humerus at the shoulder joint
Clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint
Rotator cuff, deltoid, trapezius and serratus anterior muscles
clinical: Scapular fractures are uncommon because the bone is well padded by muscle.
Weakness of the muscles that hold it can make the inner edge stick out ('winged scapula').
Wear or injury of the rotator cuff tendons attached to it is a common cause of shoulder pain.
scapula.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
scapula.fact: The scapula is the only large bone joined to the trunk almost entirely by muscles rather than joints.
scapula.blood_supply: Suprascapular, dorsal scapular and circumflex scapular arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §8.1 The Pectoral Girdle
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Upper Limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Upper Limb

humerus.name: Humerus
humerus.tagline: The long bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow.
humerus.overview: The humerus is the only bone of the upper arm. Its rounded head fits into the shallow socket of the shoulder blade, giving the shoulder its wide range of movement. The shaft carries a groove for the radial nerve, and the lower end widens to form the elbow joint with the two forearm bones.
functions: Forming the ball of the shoulder joint
Forming the upper part of the elbow joint
Acting as a lever for the biceps, triceps and deltoid
Housing bone marrow
Transmitting forces between the forearm and the trunk
connections: Scapula at the shoulder
Radius and ulna at the elbow
Radial, axillary and ulnar nerves close to the bone
clinical: Fractures of the upper end (surgical neck) are common in older people after a fall.
A break of the mid-shaft can injure the radial nerve that runs in a groove on the bone.
The shoulder is the joint that dislocates most often, the humeral head usually slipping forward.
humerus.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
humerus.fact: The 'funny bone' is not a bone: it is the ulnar nerve running behind the lower end of the humerus.
humerus.blood_supply: Branches of the brachial artery, including a nutrient artery, and the circumflex humeral arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Upper Limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Upper Limb

sternum.name: Sternum
sternum.tagline: The breastbone: a flat bone in the front of the chest that anchors the ribs.
sternum.overview: The sternum is a flat, dagger-shaped bone in the middle of the front of the chest. It has three parts: the manubrium at the top, the long body, and the small xiphoid process at the bottom. The clavicles and the cartilages of the upper seven ribs attach to it, closing the front of the ribcage over the heart.
functions: Protecting the heart and great vessels
Anchoring the clavicles and the upper ribs
Moving with the ribs during breathing
Containing red bone marrow
Giving attachment to chest and abdominal muscles
connections: Clavicles at the sternoclavicular joints
Costal cartilages of ribs 1-7
Heart and pericardium behind it
Pectoralis major and the diaphragm
clinical: It can break in strong frontal impacts, such as from a steering wheel or seat belt.
Heart surgery is commonly performed by dividing the sternum lengthwise (sternotomy), which then heals.
The angle between the manubrium and body is a landmark for counting ribs.
sternum.fact: The xiphoid process stays cartilage for years and usually only turns to bone in middle age.
sternum.blood_supply: Internal thoracic arteries running down just beside it.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_1.name: Rib 1
rib_1.tagline: The first rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_1.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The first rib is the shortest, broadest and most curved. It lies almost flat under the clavicle, joins only the first thoracic vertebra, and carries grooves for the subclavian artery and vein.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Supporting the subclavian vessels and the scalene muscles
connections: At the back: the first thoracic vertebra (T1)
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
An extra rib from the seventh neck vertebra (cervical rib) or a tight first-rib outlet can press on arm nerves or vessels.
rib_1.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_1.fact: The first rib is hard to feel because the clavicle lies over it.
rib_1.blood_supply: Supreme (superior) intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk, and the internal thoracic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_2.name: Rib 2
rib_2.tagline: The second rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_2.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The second rib is longer and thinner than the first and has a roughened area for the serratus anterior muscle. Its cartilage joins the sternum at the sternal angle, a landmark used for counting ribs.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Marking the sternal angle used to count ribs
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T1 and T2
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Rib counting from the sternal angle starts at the second rib.
rib_2.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_2.fact: The second rib is the first one that can easily be felt below the clavicle.
rib_2.blood_supply: Supreme (superior) intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk, and the internal thoracic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_3.name: Rib 3
rib_3.tagline: The third rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_3.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The third rib is a typical 'true' rib: its own cartilage joins the sternum directly. Its head meets the bodies of the second and third thoracic vertebrae, and a groove under its lower edge shelters the intercostal nerve and vessels.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Joining the sternum through its own cartilage
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T2 and T3
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Needles or drains are placed just above a rib, away from the vessels under its lower edge.
rib_3.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_3.fact: Ribs 3 to 9 share a similar 'typical' design with a head, neck, tubercle and shaft.
rib_3.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_4.name: Rib 4
rib_4.tagline: The fourth rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_4.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The fourth rib is a typical 'true' rib: its own cartilage joins the sternum directly. Its head meets the bodies of the third and fourth thoracic vertebrae, and a groove under its lower edge shelters the intercostal nerve and vessels.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Joining the sternum through its own cartilage
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T3 and T4
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Needles or drains are placed just above a rib, away from the vessels under its lower edge.
rib_4.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_4.fact: Ribs 3 to 9 share a similar 'typical' design with a head, neck, tubercle and shaft.
rib_4.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_5.name: Rib 5
rib_5.tagline: The fifth rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_5.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The fifth rib is a typical 'true' rib: its own cartilage joins the sternum directly. Its head meets the bodies of the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, and a groove under its lower edge shelters the intercostal nerve and vessels.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Joining the sternum through its own cartilage
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T4 and T5
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Needles or drains are placed just above a rib, away from the vessels under its lower edge.
rib_5.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_5.fact: Ribs 3 to 9 share a similar 'typical' design with a head, neck, tubercle and shaft.
rib_5.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_6.name: Rib 6
rib_6.tagline: The sixth rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_6.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The sixth rib is a typical 'true' rib: its own cartilage joins the sternum directly. Its head meets the bodies of the fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae, and a groove under its lower edge shelters the intercostal nerve and vessels.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Joining the sternum through its own cartilage
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T5 and T6
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Needles or drains are placed just above a rib, away from the vessels under its lower edge.
rib_6.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_6.fact: Ribs 3 to 9 share a similar 'typical' design with a head, neck, tubercle and shaft.
rib_6.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_7.name: Rib 7
rib_7.tagline: The seventh rib, a true rib of the ribcage.
rib_7.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The seventh rib is a typical 'true' rib: its own cartilage joins the sternum directly. Its head meets the bodies of the sixth and seventh thoracic vertebrae, and a groove under its lower edge shelters the intercostal nerve and vessels.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Joining the sternum through its own cartilage
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T6 and T7
At the front: the sternum through its own costal cartilage
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Needles or drains are placed just above a rib, away from the vessels under its lower edge.
rib_7.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_7.fact: The seventh is the lowest rib whose cartilage reaches the sternum directly.
rib_7.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_8.name: Rib 8
rib_8.tagline: The eighth rib, a false rib of the ribcage.
rib_8.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The eighth rib is a 'false' rib: its cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above rather than the sternum, helping form the curved lower edge of the ribcage.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Forming part of the costal margin
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T7 and T8
At the front: the cartilage of the rib above
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Lower rib fractures can be associated with injury to the liver or spleen beneath them.
rib_8.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_8.fact: A loose tip of a false-rib cartilage can occasionally slip and click ('slipping rib').
rib_8.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_9.name: Rib 9
rib_9.tagline: The ninth rib, a false rib of the ribcage.
rib_9.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The ninth rib is a 'false' rib: its cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above rather than the sternum, helping form the curved lower edge of the ribcage.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Forming part of the costal margin
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebrae T8 and T9
At the front: the cartilage of the rib above
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Lower rib fractures can be associated with injury to the liver or spleen beneath them.
rib_9.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_9.fact: A loose tip of a false-rib cartilage can occasionally slip and click ('slipping rib').
rib_9.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta, plus anterior intercostal branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_10.name: Rib 10
rib_10.tagline: The tenth rib, a false rib of the ribcage.
rib_10.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The tenth rib is a 'false' rib: its cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above rather than the sternum, helping form the curved lower edge of the ribcage. It often has a single joint facet on its head.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Forming part of the costal margin
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebra T10
At the front: the cartilage of the rib above
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Lower rib fractures can be associated with injury to the liver or spleen beneath them.
rib_10.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_10.fact: A loose tip of a false-rib cartilage can occasionally slip and click ('slipping rib').
rib_10.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal (rib 10-11) or subcostal (rib 12) arteries from the aorta.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_11.name: Rib 11
rib_11.tagline: The eleventh rib, a floating rib of the ribcage.
rib_11.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The eleventh rib is a 'floating' rib: short, with a single joint on its head, no neck or tubercle, and a free tip of cartilage that ends in the muscles of the flank without reaching the front.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Protecting the back of the kidney and upper abdomen
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebra T11
At the front: flank muscles (free front tip)
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Its free front end makes it more mobile and less often broken than the ribs above.
rib_11.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_11.fact: Floating ribs are joined to the spine at the back only.
rib_11.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal (rib 10-11) or subcostal (rib 12) arteries from the aorta.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

rib_12.name: Rib 12
rib_12.tagline: The twelfth rib, a floating rib of the ribcage.
rib_12.overview: The ribs are 12 pairs of curved bones that, with the spine and sternum, form the ribcage around the chest. The twelfth rib is a 'floating' rib: short, with a single joint on its head, no neck or tubercle, and a free tip of cartilage that ends in the muscles of the flank without reaching the front. The twelfth is the shortest rib and lies behind the kidney.
functions: Protecting the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs
Moving up and out with each breath
Anchoring the intercostal muscles between the ribs
Protecting the back of the kidney and upper abdomen
connections: At the back: thoracic vertebra T12
At the front: flank muscles (free front tip)
Intercostal muscles, nerves and vessels
clinical: Rib fractures are common after chest injury and make deep breathing painful; most heal in weeks.
Its free front end makes it more mobile and less often broken than the ribs above.
rib_12.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
rib_12.fact: The twelfth rib can be very short or even absent in some people.
rib_12.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal (rib 10-11) or subcostal (rib 12) arteries from the aorta.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

costal_cartilages.name: Costal cartilages
costal_cartilages.tagline: Flexible bars of cartilage joining the front ends of the ribs to the breastbone.
costal_cartilages.overview: Each rib ends at the front in a bar of hyaline cartilage. The cartilages of ribs 1-7 reach the sternum directly; those of ribs 8-10 join the cartilage above and form the curved lower edge of the ribcage (costal margin); ribs 11 and 12 have only short tips. Their flexibility lets the chest expand when breathing in.
functions: Joining the ribs to the sternum
Giving the ribcage elasticity for breathing
Forming the costal margin of the lower chest
Absorbing shocks to the front of the chest
connections: Ribs 1-12 at their front ends
Sternum
Internal and external intercostal muscles
clinical: The cartilages often calcify with age and may then look bright on CT.
Inflammation where the cartilages meet the sternum (costochondritis) is a common cause of harmless chest-wall pain.
costal_cartilages.lateralization: Paired on both sides of the sternum.
costal_cartilages.fact: Surgeons sometimes use costal cartilage to rebuild a nose or ear.
costal_cartilages.blood_supply: Branches of the internal thoracic and anterior intercostal arteries reach the surrounding membrane; the cartilage itself has no vessels.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.4 The Thoracic Cage
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

hip.name: Hip bone
hip.tagline: The large hip bone: forms the pelvis and the socket of the hip joint.
hip.overview: Each hip bone is formed from three bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse during the teenage years at the cup-shaped hip socket (acetabulum). The two hip bones meet at the front (pubic symphysis) and join the sacrum at the back, forming the pelvic ring that carries the weight of the upper body to the legs.
functions: Forming the socket of the hip joint
Carrying body weight from the spine to the legs
Supporting and protecting the pelvic organs
Anchoring the large muscles of the hip, thigh and abdomen
Containing red bone marrow
connections: Sacrum at the sacroiliac joint
Femur at the hip joint
The other hip bone at the pubic symphysis
Gluteal, iliopsoas and abdominal wall muscles
clinical: Pelvic fractures usually follow high-energy injury, while minor pubic fractures can follow falls in older people.
Wear of the hip socket cartilage is a common part of hip osteoarthritis.
The iliac crest is a common site for taking bone marrow samples.
hip.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
hip.fact: The female pelvis is typically wider with a rounder inlet, an adaptation for childbirth.
hip.blood_supply: Branches of the internal iliac artery (iliolumbar, obturator, gluteal) plus the deep circumflex iliac artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §8.3 The Pelvic Girdle and Pelvis
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Pelvis and Perineum

femur.name: Femur
femur.tagline: The thigh bone: the longest and strongest bone in the body.
femur.overview: The femur runs from the hip to the knee. Its ball-shaped head fits deep into the hip socket, and an angled neck joins it to the shaft. Two bony knobs near the top (the greater and lesser trochanters) anchor powerful hip muscles. At the lower end, two rounded condyles form the upper part of the knee joint.
functions: Carrying body weight in standing and walking
Forming the ball of the hip joint
Forming the upper part of the knee joint
Acting as a lever for the thigh and hip muscles
Containing bone marrow
connections: Hip bone at the hip joint
Tibia and patella at the knee
Gluteal, quadriceps, hamstring and adductor muscles
clinical: Fractures of the femoral neck ('hip fractures') are common in older people with thin bones.
The blood supply of the femoral head is delicate, so some neck fractures can damage it.
Breaking the shaft usually needs high-energy force because the bone is so strong.
femur.lateralization: Paired: one on the left and one on the right.
femur.fact: The femur is about a quarter of a person's height.
femur.blood_supply: Medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries for the head and neck, and perforating branches of the deep femoral artery for the shaft.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §8.4 Bones of the Lower Limb
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Lower Limb

vertebrae.name: Vertebrae
vertebrae.tagline: All the vertebrae of the spine shown together as one structure.
vertebrae.overview: The vertebral column is a flexible stack of 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (lower back), 5 fused sacral and about 4 small coccygeal. Discs between them act as cushions. Seen from the side it has four gentle curves that help absorb shocks, and its central canal shelters the spinal cord. This label (used by MR segmentation) covers all the vertebrae together without separating levels.
functions: Supporting the head and trunk
Protecting the spinal cord
Allowing bending and twisting
Carrying weight down to the pelvis
Anchoring back muscles and the ribs
connections: Skull at the top
Ribs along the thoracic part
Hip bones through the sacrum
Spinal cord and nerve roots inside the canal
clinical: Back pain is very common and usually comes from muscles, joints or discs rather than serious disease.
Bone thinning can lead to vertebral compression fractures, especially in the thoracic and lumbar spine.
Abnormal curves can develop sideways (scoliosis) or as an exaggerated rounding (kyphosis).
vertebrae.lateralization: A midline column; nerves leave it in pairs to the left and right.
vertebrae.fact: Whether a giraffe or a human, almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae.
vertebrae.blood_supply: Segmental branches of the vertebral, intercostal, lumbar and sacral arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

vertebrae_body.name: Vertebral bodies
vertebrae_body.tagline: The weight-bearing front blocks of the vertebrae, without their arches.
vertebrae_body.overview: Each vertebra has a solid, drum-shaped front part, the body, and a bony arch behind it that encloses the spinal canal. The bodies, stacked with discs between them, carry most of the load of the spine and grow larger from the neck down to the lower back. This label covers the bodies of all levels, without the arches.
functions: Bearing the body's weight
Transferring load to the discs between them
Containing red bone marrow
Forming the front wall of the spinal canal
connections: Intervertebral discs above and below
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
Vertebral arches behind (pedicles)
clinical: Bone thinning can lead to collapse of a vertebral body (compression fracture), often in the mid-back.
Small bony spurs on the edges of the bodies are a common sign of age-related wear.
vertebrae_body.fact: Vertebral bodies are among the main sites of red blood-cell production in adults.
vertebrae_body.blood_supply: Segmental arteries (from the vertebral, intercostal and lumbar arteries) entering through small holes in the body.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

intervertebral_discs.name: Intervertebral discs
intervertebral_discs.tagline: The cushions between the vertebrae, shown together as one structure.
intervertebral_discs.overview: Intervertebral discs are the cushions between the vertebral bodies, from the second neck vertebra down to the sacrum. Each has a tough outer ring of fibrous cartilage (annulus fibrosus) around a soft, gel-like centre (nucleus pulposus). Together they make up about a quarter of the spine's length. This label shows all discs together.
functions: Absorbing shocks between vertebrae
Allowing the spine to bend and twist
Spreading load evenly over the vertebral bodies
Keeping space for the nerve roots to exit
Holding the vertebrae together
connections: Vertebral bodies above and below (through the endplates)
Longitudinal ligaments in front and behind
Spinal nerve roots close behind them
clinical: With age the discs lose water and height, a normal process often called disc degeneration.
Part of the soft centre can bulge or push out (disc herniation) and press on a nerve root, causing leg or arm pain.
Disc changes are very common on scans of people without any symptoms.
intervertebral_discs.lateralization: Midline structures, one between each pair of vertebrae.
intervertebral_discs.fact: You are slightly taller in the morning because the discs regain water while you lie down.
intervertebral_discs.blood_supply: Adult discs have almost no blood vessels; they are nourished by diffusion through the vertebral endplates.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Back

sacrum.name: Sacrum
sacrum.tagline: The triangular base of the spine, made of five fused vertebrae, wedged into the pelvis.
sacrum.overview: The sacrum forms from five sacral vertebrae that fuse in early adulthood into one triangular bone. It sits between the two hip bones like a keystone, joined to them at the sacroiliac joints, and passes the weight of the upper body into the pelvis. Rows of holes on its front and back let the sacral nerves out, and the tailbone hangs below it.
functions: Carrying the weight of the spine into the pelvis
Forming the back wall of the pelvis
Letting the sacral nerves out to the pelvis and legs
Anchoring the gluteus maximus and back muscles
Supporting the tailbone (coccyx)
connections: Fifth lumbar vertebra above
Hip bones at the sacroiliac joints
Coccyx below
Sacral nerve roots
clinical: Irritation of the sacroiliac joints is one cause of low back and buttock pain.
Insufficiency fractures of the sacrum can occur in older people with thin bones.
The first sacral segment is sometimes partly separate (lumbarised), a harmless variant that affects level counting.
sacrum.fact: 'Sacrum' comes from the Latin os sacrum, 'sacred bone', a name of uncertain origin.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §8.3 The Pelvic Girdle and Pelvis
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Pelvis and Perineum

temporalis.name: Temporalis
temporalis.tagline: A fan-shaped chewing muscle on the side of the head.
temporalis.overview: The temporalis is a broad, fan-shaped muscle that fills the shallow hollow on the side of the skull above the cheekbone. Its fibres converge into a tendon that passes under the zygomatic arch to attach to the lower jaw. You can feel it tighten at the temple when you clench your teeth.
functions: Closing the jaw
Pulling the jaw backwards
Holding the jaw at rest
Helping side-to-side grinding
connections: From the temporal fossa of the skull
To the coronoid process of the mandible
Supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
clinical: Tension in this muscle is one cause of headache at the temples.
It can be involved in jaw joint (temporomandibular) disorders.
temporalis.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
temporalis.fact: Its strength helps humans bite with a force of several hundred newtons at the back teeth.
temporalis.blood_supply: Deep temporal branches of the maxillary artery and the superficial temporal artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

masseter.name: Masseter
masseter.tagline: The thick cheek muscle that powers chewing.
masseter.overview: The masseter is a thick, rectangular muscle on the side of the face, running from the cheekbone down to the angle of the lower jaw. It is one of the strongest muscles for its size and is easy to feel bulging when the teeth are clenched.
functions: Closing the jaw with force
Crushing food between the back teeth
Pushing the jaw slightly forward
Helping hold the jaw closed
connections: From the zygomatic arch and cheekbone
To the outer surface of the angle and ramus of the mandible
Supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
clinical: Habitual teeth grinding can enlarge the masseter.
Spasm of the jaw muscles limits mouth opening.
masseter.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
masseter.fact: Relative to its size, the masseter is often called the strongest muscle in the body.
masseter.blood_supply: Masseteric branch of the maxillary artery, plus facial and transverse facial arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

lateral_pterygoid.name: Lateral pterygoid
lateral_pterygoid.tagline: A deep jaw muscle that pulls the jaw forward and helps open the mouth.
lateral_pterygoid.overview: The lateral pterygoid lies deep in the face, behind the cheekbone, running almost horizontally from the skull base to the neck of the lower jaw and the jaw joint. Unlike most chewing muscles, it helps open rather than close the mouth.
functions: Pulling the jaw forward
Helping open the mouth
Moving the jaw side to side
Guiding the jaw joint disc
connections: From the greater wing of the sphenoid and the lateral pterygoid plate
To the neck of the mandible and the jaw joint capsule
Supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
clinical: Overactivity is thought to contribute to clicking of the jaw joint.
It can be tender in jaw joint disorders.
lateral_pterygoid.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
lateral_pterygoid.fact: Using the left and right muscles in turn produces the grinding movement of chewing.
lateral_pterygoid.blood_supply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

medial_pterygoid.name: Medial pterygoid
medial_pterygoid.tagline: A deep chewing muscle on the inner side of the lower jaw.
medial_pterygoid.overview: The medial pterygoid lies on the inner surface of the lower jaw, roughly mirroring the masseter on the outside. Together the two muscles form a sling around the angle of the jaw.
functions: Closing the jaw
Pushing the jaw forward
Moving the jaw side to side
Helping grind food
connections: From the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and the maxilla
To the inner surface of the angle of the mandible
Supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
clinical: Inflammation or injections near it can cause temporary difficulty opening the mouth.
It may be tender in jaw-clenching habits.
medial_pterygoid.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
medial_pterygoid.fact: With the masseter, it forms a muscular sling that cradles the angle of the jaw.
medial_pterygoid.blood_supply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

digastric.name: Digastric
digastric.tagline: A two-bellied muscle under the jaw that helps open the mouth and lift the hyoid.
digastric.overview: The digastric has two fleshy bellies joined by a rounded tendon that slides through a loop attached to the hyoid bone. The front belly runs to the chin and the back belly to the mastoid area behind the ear. The two bellies are supplied by different nerves because they develop from different embryonic arches.
functions: Opening the mouth (lowering the jaw)
Raising the hyoid bone during swallowing
Steadying the hyoid during speech
Helping pull the jaw back
connections: Front belly: inner side of the chin; back belly: mastoid notch of the temporal bone
Intermediate tendon linked to the hyoid
Front belly by the mylohyoid nerve (CN V3); back belly by the facial nerve (CN VII)
clinical: It is an important landmark in neck surgery.
Its two bellies with two nerve supplies are a classic example of embryology shaping anatomy.
digastric.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
digastric.blood_supply: Submental branch of the facial artery (front) and occipital and posterior auricular arteries (back).
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

superior_rectus_muscle.name: Superior rectus
superior_rectus_muscle.tagline: The eye muscle that mainly turns the eye upwards.
superior_rectus_muscle.overview: The superior rectus is one of six muscles that move the eyeball. It runs forward along the roof of the orbit from the back of the eye socket and attaches to the top of the eyeball, just behind the coloured part of the eye.
functions: Turning the eye upwards
Turning the eye slightly inwards
Rotating the top of the eye inwards
Working with the other eye's muscles to keep vision single
connections: From the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit
To the upper surface of the eyeball
Supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
clinical: Weakness can cause double vision when looking up.
It lies just under the muscle that lifts the eyelid and shares its nerve.
superior_rectus_muscle.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
superior_rectus_muscle.fact: Because the orbit points outwards, this muscle pulls at an angle and also turns the eye slightly inwards.
superior_rectus_muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

inferior_rectus_muscle.name: Inferior rectus
inferior_rectus_muscle.tagline: The eye muscle that mainly turns the eye downwards.
inferior_rectus_muscle.overview: The inferior rectus runs forward along the floor of the orbit and attaches to the underside of the eyeball. It is the main muscle for looking down, which we use constantly when reading or walking downstairs.
functions: Turning the eye downwards
Turning the eye slightly inwards
Rotating the top of the eye outwards
Coordinating with the other eye for single vision
connections: From the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit
To the lower surface of the eyeball
Supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
clinical: A fracture of the thin orbital floor can trap this muscle and limit upward gaze.
It is often enlarged in thyroid-related eye disease.
inferior_rectus_muscle.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
inferior_rectus_muscle.fact: It sits right above the thin floor of the orbit, which separates the eye from the maxillary sinus.
inferior_rectus_muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

medial_rectus_muscle.name: Medial rectus
medial_rectus_muscle.tagline: The eye muscle that turns the eye towards the nose.
medial_rectus_muscle.overview: The medial rectus runs along the inner wall of the orbit and attaches to the nose side of the eyeball. It is the largest of the eye muscles and pulls both eyes inwards together when we focus on something close.
functions: Turning the eye towards the nose
Turning both eyes in for near vision (convergence)
Balancing the lateral rectus
Keeping the eyes aligned
connections: From the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit
To the nasal surface of the eyeball
Supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
clinical: Imbalance with the lateral rectus is one cause of a squint (strabismus).
Squint surgery often adjusts this muscle.
medial_rectus_muscle.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
medial_rectus_muscle.fact: It is the strongest of the six muscles that move the eye.
medial_rectus_muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

lateral_rectus_muscle.name: Lateral rectus
lateral_rectus_muscle.tagline: The eye muscle that turns the eye outwards, away from the nose.
lateral_rectus_muscle.overview: The lateral rectus runs along the outer wall of the orbit and attaches to the outer side of the eyeball. It has its own nerve, the abducens nerve, which has a long path inside the skull.
functions: Turning the eye outwards
Balancing the medial rectus
Helping both eyes track sideways
Keeping the eyes aligned
connections: From the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit
To the outer surface of the eyeball
Supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI)
clinical: Weakness causes double vision when looking to that side.
Its nerve can be affected by raised pressure inside the skull.
lateral_rectus_muscle.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
lateral_rectus_muscle.fact: A memory aid for the eye muscle nerves is 'LR6 SO4, the rest 3'.
lateral_rectus_muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

superior_oblique_muscle.name: Superior oblique
superior_oblique_muscle.tagline: A pulley-guided eye muscle that turns the eye down and out.
superior_oblique_muscle.overview: The superior oblique runs forward along the upper inner wall of the orbit, then its tendon loops through a small cartilage pulley (the trochlea) near the inner corner of the eyebrow and turns back to attach to the top of the eyeball. This pulley changes its direction of pull.
functions: Turning the eye downwards when it looks inward
Turning the eye outwards
Rotating the top of the eye inwards
Important for looking down while reading
connections: From the sphenoid bone above the common ring
Tendon passes through the trochlea to the upper back of the eyeball
Supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV)
clinical: Weakness can cause double vision when walking downstairs.
People may tilt their head to compensate for a weak superior oblique.
superior_oblique_muscle.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
superior_oblique_muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

inferior_oblique_muscle.name: Inferior oblique
inferior_oblique_muscle.tagline: The eye muscle that turns the eye up and out.
inferior_oblique_muscle.overview: The inferior oblique is the only eye muscle that does not start at the back of the orbit. It arises from the front of the orbit floor near the nose and runs backwards and outwards under the eyeball to attach to its outer back part.
functions: Turning the eye upwards when it looks inward
Turning the eye outwards
Rotating the top of the eye outwards
Balancing the superior oblique
connections: From the front of the orbital floor (maxilla)
To the outer back surface of the eyeball
Supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
clinical: Overaction of this muscle is a common pattern in childhood squints.
Its nerve branch also carries fibres for the pupil.
inferior_oblique_muscle.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
inferior_oblique_muscle.fact: It is the only eye-moving muscle that starts at the front of the orbit.
inferior_oblique_muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

levator_palpebrae_superioris.name: Levator palpebrae superioris
levator_palpebrae_superioris.tagline: The muscle that lifts the upper eyelid.
levator_palpebrae_superioris.overview: This thin, triangular muscle runs forward above the superior rectus and spreads into a broad sheet of tendon in the upper eyelid. It holds the eyelid open while we are awake and relaxes when we close our eyes or sleep.
functions: Lifting the upper eyelid
Keeping the eye open while awake
Raising the lid further when looking up
Working with a small smooth muscle that adds extra lift
connections: From the lesser wing of the sphenoid above the optic canal
To the skin and tarsal plate of the upper eyelid
Supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
clinical: A drooping eyelid (ptosis) can come from weakness of this muscle or its nerve.
With age its tendon can stretch, lowering the lid.
levator_palpebrae_superioris.lateralization: Paired, one set for each eye; the two eyes' muscles work together so both eyes point at the same target.
levator_palpebrae_superioris.fact: Its name simply means 'lifter of the upper eyelid' in Latin.
levator_palpebrae_superioris.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

sternocleidomastoid.name: Sternocleidomastoid
sternocleidomastoid.tagline: The prominent strap muscle on the side of the neck that turns and bends the head.
sternocleidomastoid.overview: The sternocleidomastoid runs diagonally across the side of the neck from the breastbone and collarbone up to the bony bump behind the ear. It stands out clearly when the head is turned. It divides the side of the neck into front and back triangles, which doctors use as landmarks.
functions: Turning the head to the opposite side
Tilting the head towards the same shoulder
Bending the neck forward (both sides)
Helping lift the ribcage in deep breathing
connections: From the top of the sternum and the inner part of the clavicle
To the mastoid process of the skull
Supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI)
clinical: Tightness of this muscle in infants can cause a head tilt (torticollis).
It is a key landmark for structures in the neck.
sternocleidomastoid.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
sternocleidomastoid.fact: Its long name lists its three attachments: sternum, clavicle and mastoid.
sternocleidomastoid.blood_supply: Branches of the occipital and superior thyroid arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

platysma.name: Platysma
platysma.tagline: A thin sheet of muscle just under the skin of the neck.
platysma.overview: The platysma is a very thin, broad sheet of muscle lying in the fat just beneath the skin of the neck. It runs from the upper chest over the collarbone to the lower jaw and the corners of the mouth. It belongs to the facial expression muscles.
functions: Tensing the skin of the neck
Pulling the corners of the mouth down
Helping lower the jaw
Contributing to expressions of strain or fear
connections: From the skin and fascia over the upper chest
To the lower border of the mandible and skin around the mouth
Supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
clinical: Its bands can become more visible with age.
Surgeons repair it carefully when closing neck incisions.
platysma.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
platysma.fact: It is a remnant of a skin muscle that, in many animals, lets them twitch their skin.
platysma.blood_supply: Branches of the submental and suprascapular arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

trapezius.name: Trapezius
trapezius.tagline: A large diamond-shaped back muscle that moves the shoulder blade and steadies the neck.
trapezius.overview: The trapezius is a broad, flat muscle covering the back of the neck and upper back. Left and right together form a diamond (trapezium) shape. Its upper fibres shrug the shoulders, its middle fibres pull the shoulder blades together and its lower fibres draw them down.
functions: Shrugging the shoulders
Pulling the shoulder blades together
Rotating the shoulder blade to raise the arm overhead
Extending and steadying the neck
Drawing the shoulder blades down
connections: From the base of the skull and the spines of the cervical and thoracic vertebrae
To the clavicle and the acromion and spine of the scapula
Supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI)
clinical: Tension in the upper trapezius is a common source of neck and shoulder ache.
Injury to its nerve makes it hard to lift the arm above the head.
trapezius.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
trapezius.fact: It is named after the trapezium shape formed by the left and right muscles together.
trapezius.blood_supply: Transverse cervical artery, plus occipital and dorsal scapular branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

levator_scapulae.name: Levator scapulae
levator_scapulae.tagline: A strap-like neck muscle that lifts the shoulder blade.
levator_scapulae.overview: The levator scapulae runs down the side and back of the neck, under the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, from the upper neck vertebrae to the upper inner corner of the shoulder blade.
functions: Lifting the shoulder blade
Tilting the shoulder blade downwards
Bending the neck to the same side
Helping steady the neck
connections: From the transverse processes of the upper four cervical vertebrae
To the upper medial border of the scapula
Supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and cervical nerves C3–C4
clinical: It is a frequent source of a stiff neck after sleeping awkwardly.
Tender spots at its lower end are common in desk workers.
levator_scapulae.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
levator_scapulae.fact: Its name means 'lifter of the shoulder blade'.
levator_scapulae.blood_supply: Dorsal scapular and transverse cervical arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

anterior_scalene.name: Anterior scalene
anterior_scalene.tagline: A side-of-neck muscle that bends the neck and lifts the upper ribs.
anterior_scalene.overview: The scalene muscles are three muscles on each side of the neck running from the neck vertebrae down to the first two ribs. The anterior scalene is the front one; the subclavian vein passes in front of it and the subclavian artery behind it.
functions: Bending the neck to the same side
Lifting the upper ribs during deep breathing
Steadying the neck
Helping rotate the neck slightly
connections: From the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae
To the scalene tubercle of the first rib
Supplied by branches of the cervical spinal nerves
clinical: The nerves and artery to the arm pass close to the scalenes and can be squeezed here (thoracic outlet).
They work harder during laboured breathing.
anterior_scalene.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
anterior_scalene.fact: The phrenic nerve, which drives the diaphragm, runs down across its front surface.
anterior_scalene.blood_supply: Ascending cervical artery and other branches of the subclavian artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

middle_scalene.name: Middle scalene
middle_scalene.tagline: A side-of-neck muscle that bends the neck and lifts the upper ribs.
middle_scalene.overview: The scalene muscles are three muscles on each side of the neck running from the neck vertebrae down to the first two ribs. The middle scalene is the largest and longest; the nerves to the arm pass between it and the anterior scalene.
functions: Bending the neck to the same side
Lifting the upper ribs during deep breathing
Steadying the neck
Helping rotate the neck slightly
connections: From the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae
To the upper surface of the first rib, behind the subclavian artery groove
Supplied by branches of the cervical spinal nerves
clinical: The nerves and artery to the arm pass close to the scalenes and can be squeezed here (thoracic outlet).
They work harder during laboured breathing.
middle_scalene.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
middle_scalene.fact: The gap between the anterior and middle scalenes carries the brachial plexus and subclavian artery.
middle_scalene.blood_supply: Ascending cervical artery and other branches of the subclavian artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

posterior_scalene.name: Posterior scalene
posterior_scalene.tagline: A side-of-neck muscle that bends the neck and lifts the upper ribs.
posterior_scalene.overview: The scalene muscles are three muscles on each side of the neck running from the neck vertebrae down to the first two ribs. The posterior scalene is the smallest and deepest, lying behind the middle scalene.
functions: Bending the neck to the same side
Lifting the upper ribs during deep breathing
Steadying the neck
Helping rotate the neck slightly
connections: From the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae
To the outer surface of the second rib
Supplied by branches of the cervical spinal nerves
clinical: The nerves and artery to the arm pass close to the scalenes and can be squeezed here (thoracic outlet).
They work harder during laboured breathing.
posterior_scalene.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
posterior_scalene.fact: It is the only scalene that reaches the second rib.
posterior_scalene.blood_supply: Ascending cervical artery and other branches of the subclavian artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

prevertebral.name: Prevertebral muscles
prevertebral.tagline: Deep muscles lying on the front of the neck spine that bend and steady the neck.
prevertebral.overview: The prevertebral muscles, mainly longus colli and longus capitis, lie directly on the front of the cervical vertebrae, behind the throat and oesophagus. They act like an inner support for the neck, counterbalancing the strong muscles at the back.
functions: Bending the head and neck forward
Steadying the neck spine
Supporting the natural curve of the neck
Helping bend the neck to the side
connections: From the bodies and transverse processes of the cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae
To the base of the skull and upper vertebrae
Supplied by the anterior branches of cervical spinal nerves
clinical: They are often strained in whiplash injuries.
Swelling in the space in front of them can be seen on neck imaging.
prevertebral.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
prevertebral.fact: Exercises that tuck the chin are designed to strengthen these deep neck flexors.
prevertebral.blood_supply: Ascending cervical, inferior thyroid and vertebral arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

sterno_thyroid.name: Sternothyroid
sterno_thyroid.tagline: A thin strap muscle in front of the neck that pulls the voice box down.
sterno_thyroid.overview: The sternothyroid is one of the 'strap muscles' below the hyoid bone. It runs from the back of the breastbone up to the thyroid cartilage of the voice box, lying over the thyroid gland.
functions: Pulling the larynx down after swallowing
Lowering the larynx for deep voice notes
Steadying the larynx
Working with other strap muscles during speech
connections: From the back of the manubrium of the sternum
To the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1–C3)
clinical: Surgeons move these strap muscles aside to reach the thyroid gland.
They can be enlarged or displaced by a large thyroid.
sterno_thyroid.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
sterno_thyroid.fact: It lies deeper than the sternohyoid, another strap muscle of the neck.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

thyrohyoid.name: Thyrohyoid
thyrohyoid.tagline: A short strap muscle linking the voice box to the hyoid bone.
thyrohyoid.overview: The thyrohyoid is a small, four-sided muscle that continues upwards from the sternothyroid, running from the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. Depending on which end is fixed, it lowers the hyoid or raises the larynx.
functions: Lowering the hyoid bone
Raising the larynx during swallowing
Helping close the airway entrance while swallowing
Adjusting the larynx position for voice
connections: From the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
To the lower border of the hyoid bone
Supplied by C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve
clinical: It helps protect the airway during swallowing.
It is a landmark in surgery of the larynx.
thyrohyoid.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
thyrohyoid.fact: Its nerve fibres come from the first cervical nerve but hitch a ride with the hypoglossal nerve.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

superior_pharyngeal_constrictor.name: Superior pharyngeal constrictor
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor.tagline: A curved throat muscle that squeezes food down during swallowing.
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor.overview: Three curved constrictor muscles overlap like stacked cups to form the back and side walls of the throat (pharynx). The superior constrictor is the top one, behind the nose and mouth. When we swallow they contract in sequence from top to bottom, pushing food towards the oesophagus.
functions: Squeezing food and drink down the throat
Contracting in a wave during swallowing
Helping shape the throat for speech
Keeping the throat walls firm
connections: From the pterygoid plate, a ligament behind the cheek and the jaw near the last molar
Meets its partner from the other side at a midline seam behind the throat
Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (mainly vagus nerve, CN X)
clinical: Weak coordination of these muscles can cause difficulty swallowing.
Their action is checked in swallowing studies.
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor.lateralization: A left and right half that meet in the middle behind the throat; usually shown as one structure.
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor.fact: It helps the soft palate seal off the nose when we swallow.
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal and tonsillar branches of the external carotid system.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

middle_pharyngeal_constrictor.name: Middle pharyngeal constrictor
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor.tagline: A curved throat muscle that squeezes food down during swallowing.
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor.overview: Three curved constrictor muscles overlap like stacked cups to form the back and side walls of the throat (pharynx). The middle constrictor is fan-shaped and lies behind the mouth at the level of the hyoid bone. When we swallow they contract in sequence from top to bottom, pushing food towards the oesophagus.
functions: Squeezing food and drink down the throat
Contracting in a wave during swallowing
Helping shape the throat for speech
Keeping the throat walls firm
connections: From the horns of the hyoid bone and the stylohyoid ligament
Meets its partner from the other side at a midline seam behind the throat
Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (mainly vagus nerve, CN X)
clinical: Weak coordination of these muscles can cause difficulty swallowing.
Their action is checked in swallowing studies.
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor.lateralization: A left and right half that meet in the middle behind the throat; usually shown as one structure.
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor.fact: Its upper fibres overlap the superior constrictor like roof tiles.
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery and branches of the lingual and facial arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
