OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

inferior_pharyngeal_constrictor.name: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor
inferior_pharyngeal_constrictor.tagline: A curved throat muscle that squeezes food down during swallowing.
inferior_pharyngeal_constrictor.overview: Three curved constrictor muscles overlap like stacked cups to form the back and side walls of the throat (pharynx). The inferior constrictor is the thickest, wrapped around the voice box; its lowest part acts as the upper sphincter of the oesophagus. When we swallow they contract in sequence from top to bottom, pushing food towards the oesophagus.
functions: Squeezing food and drink down the throat
Contracting in a wave during swallowing
Helping shape the throat for speech
Keeping the throat walls firm
connections: From the thyroid and cricoid cartilages of the larynx
Meets its partner from the other side at a midline seam behind the throat
Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (mainly vagus nerve, CN X)
clinical: Weak coordination of these muscles can cause difficulty swallowing.
Their action is checked in swallowing studies.
inferior_pharyngeal_constrictor.lateralization: A left and right half that meet in the middle behind the throat; usually shown as one structure.
inferior_pharyngeal_constrictor.fact: A weak spot between its two parts is where a throat pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) can form.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

pectoralis_major.name: Pectoralis major
pectoralis_major.tagline: The large fan-shaped chest muscle that moves the arm across the body.
pectoralis_major.overview: The pectoralis major covers most of the upper front of the chest. Its fibres run from the collarbone, breastbone and upper rib cartilages and converge into a tendon that attaches to the upper arm bone, forming the front fold of the armpit.
functions: Bringing the arm across the chest
Rotating the arm inwards
Raising the arm forward (upper part)
Pulling the raised arm down (lower part)
Helping lift the ribs in forced breathing
connections: From the clavicle, sternum and upper costal cartilages
To the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus
Supplied by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves
clinical: It can tear near its tendon during heavy lifting.
It lies directly behind the breast, which matters in breast surgery.
pectoralis_major.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
pectoralis_major.fact: Rarely, part of this muscle is missing from birth (Poland syndrome).
pectoralis_major.blood_supply: Pectoral branches of the thoraco-acromial artery and perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Upper limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

serratus_anterior.name: Serratus anterior
serratus_anterior.tagline: A saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest that holds the shoulder blade to the ribs.
serratus_anterior.overview: The serratus anterior wraps around the side of the ribcage. It starts from the outer surfaces of the upper eight or nine ribs with finger-like slips, which give it a serrated look, and runs back under the shoulder blade to its inner border.
functions: Pulling the shoulder blade forward (punching)
Holding the shoulder blade flat against the ribs
Rotating the shoulder blade to lift the arm overhead
Helping in forced breathing
connections: From the outer surfaces of the upper 8–9 ribs
To the medial border of the scapula
Supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7)
clinical: Injury to its nerve makes the shoulder blade stick out ('winged scapula').
Its nerve runs on the side of the chest and can be at risk in surgery there.
serratus_anterior.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
serratus_anterior.fact: It is called the 'boxer's muscle' because it pushes the arm forward in a punch.
serratus_anterior.blood_supply: Lateral thoracic, thoracodorsal and superior thoracic arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Upper limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

latissimus_dorsi.name: Latissimus dorsi
latissimus_dorsi.tagline: The broadest back muscle, pulling the arm down and back.
latissimus_dorsi.overview: The latissimus dorsi is a large, flat, triangular muscle covering the lower and middle back. It runs from the lower spine and back of the pelvis up and outwards, narrowing to a tendon that wraps around to the front of the upper arm bone.
functions: Pulling the arm down from above the head
Pulling the arm back behind the body
Rotating the arm inwards
Helping in climbing and rowing movements
Assisting forced breathing such as coughing
connections: From the spines of the lower thoracic vertebrae, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and lower ribs
To the floor of the intertubercular groove of the humerus
Supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8)
clinical: Surgeons sometimes move part of this muscle to rebuild other areas, such as the breast.
Strain can occur in throwing and pulling sports.
latissimus_dorsi.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
latissimus_dorsi.fact: 'Latissimus dorsi' means 'broadest muscle of the back' in Latin.
latissimus_dorsi.blood_supply: Thoracodorsal artery, plus posterior intercostal and lumbar artery branches.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

rectus_abdominis.name: Rectus abdominis
rectus_abdominis.tagline: The long vertical muscle down the front of the belly that bends the trunk forward.
rectus_abdominis.overview: The rectus abdominis is a pair of long, strap-like muscles running vertically on either side of the midline from the pubic bone to the lower ribs and breastbone. Tendinous bands cross each muscle, creating the segmented 'six-pack' look. Each muscle lies inside a sheath formed by the tendons of the flat abdominal muscles.
functions: Bending the trunk forward
Tilting the pelvis backwards
Supporting the abdominal organs
Raising pressure inside the abdomen (coughing, straining)
connections: From the pubic crest and symphysis
To the xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5–7
Supplied by the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7–T12)
clinical: The two muscles can drift apart, especially after pregnancy (diastasis recti).
Surgeons often make incisions along or through its sheath.
rectus_abdominis.lateralization: Paired, one on each side of the midline (linea alba).
rectus_abdominis.fact: The tendinous bands usually create three or four segments on each side above the navel.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

external_oblique.name: External oblique
external_oblique.tagline: The outermost flat muscle of the side of the belly.
external_oblique.overview: The external oblique is the largest and most superficial of the three flat muscles of the side abdominal wall. Its fibres run downwards and forwards, like hands in the front pockets, from the lower ribs to the pelvis and to a broad tendon sheet in front of the belly. Its lower edge forms the groin ligament.
functions: Bending the trunk forward (both sides)
Rotating the trunk to the opposite side
Bending the trunk sideways
Compressing the abdomen
Helping forceful breathing out
connections: From the outer surfaces of ribs 5–12
To the iliac crest, pubic tubercle and linea alba via its aponeurosis
Supplied by the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, and iliohypogastric nerve
clinical: Its lower edge forms the inguinal ligament, a key landmark for groin hernias.
It can be strained in twisting sports.
external_oblique.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
external_oblique.fact: Its fibres run in the same direction as the external intercostal muscles between the ribs.
external_oblique.blood_supply: Lower posterior intercostal, subcostal and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

internal_oblique.name: Internal oblique
internal_oblique.tagline: The middle flat muscle of the side of the belly, under the external oblique.
internal_oblique.overview: The internal oblique lies just beneath the external oblique. Its fibres fan upwards and forwards, roughly at right angles to those of the external oblique, from the hip bone and lower back fascia to the lower ribs and the central tendon of the belly.
functions: Bending the trunk forward (both sides)
Rotating the trunk to the same side
Bending the trunk sideways
Compressing the abdomen and supporting the organs
connections: From the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and inguinal ligament
To the lower ribs and the linea alba via its aponeurosis
Supplied by the lower intercostal, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal nerves
clinical: Its lowest fibres help form the inguinal canal, important in hernias.
Strains can cause pain on the side of the abdomen.
internal_oblique.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
internal_oblique.fact: The external oblique of one side and internal oblique of the other work as a team to twist the trunk.
internal_oblique.blood_supply: Lower intercostal, subcostal, superior and inferior epigastric, and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

quadratus_lumborum.name: Quadratus lumborum
quadratus_lumborum.tagline: A deep, square-shaped muscle of the lower back beside the spine.
quadratus_lumborum.overview: The quadratus lumborum is a flat, four-sided muscle in the back wall of the abdomen, lying beside the lumbar spine between the lowest rib and the top of the pelvis. It sits behind the kidney and next to the psoas muscle.
functions: Bending the trunk to the same side
Steadying the lowest rib during breathing in
Helping keep the pelvis level when walking
Extending the lower back (both sides)
connections: From the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament
To the 12th rib and the transverse processes of L1–L4
Supplied by anterior branches of T12–L4 nerves
clinical: It is a common source of one-sided low back pain.
It forms part of the back wall of the abdomen seen on CT.
quadratus_lumborum.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
quadratus_lumborum.fact: Its name simply means 'square muscle of the loins'.
quadratus_lumborum.blood_supply: Lumbar arteries, plus branches of the iliolumbar and subcostal arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

autochthon.name: Deep back muscles
autochthon.tagline: The deep muscle columns along the spine that keep the back upright.
autochthon.overview: 'Autochthon' is the name TotalSegmentator uses for the intrinsic (deep) back muscles that lie in the grooves on either side of the spinous processes, from the pelvis up to the skull. They include the erector spinae and transversospinalis groups. Unlike the superficial back muscles, they develop in the back itself and are supplied by the back branches of the spinal nerves.
functions: Holding the spine upright
Bending the spine backwards
Bending the spine to the side
Rotating the spine
Fine control of posture between vertebrae
connections: Run from the sacrum and pelvis up to the base of the skull
Attach to vertebrae and ribs along the way
Supplied by the posterior branches of the spinal nerves
clinical: Strain of these muscles is one of the most common causes of back pain.
Their size and fat content can be estimated on CT or MRI.
autochthon.lateralization: Paired columns, one on each side of the spine.
autochthon.fact: 'Autochthonous' means 'native to the place': these muscles develop in the back itself.
autochthon.blood_supply: Posterior branches of the intercostal, lumbar and vertebral arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

erector_spinae.name: Erector spinae
erector_spinae.tagline: Three long muscle columns that straighten and support the back.
erector_spinae.overview: The erector spinae is a large group of deep back muscles arranged in three columns on each side: iliocostalis (outer), longissimus (middle) and spinalis (inner). They run from a thick tendon over the sacrum and pelvis up along the ribs and vertebrae, some reaching the skull.
functions: Straightening the back from a bent position
Holding the spine upright when standing
Bending the spine backwards
Bending the spine to the side
Controlling forward bending
connections: From the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spinous processes
To the ribs, vertebrae and the base of the skull
Supplied by the posterior branches of the spinal nerves
clinical: They are often involved in muscular low back pain.
Keeping them strong helps posture and lifting.
erector_spinae.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
erector_spinae.fact: They work hardest not when you stand still but when you lower and raise your trunk while bending.
erector_spinae.blood_supply: Posterior branches of the intercostal and lumbar arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

transversospinalis.name: Transversospinalis
transversospinalis.tagline: Short deep back muscles linking neighbouring vertebrae for fine control.
transversospinalis.overview: The transversospinalis group lies beneath the erector spinae, filling the groove between the spinous and transverse processes. It includes semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores, which run upwards and inwards from transverse processes to spinous processes a few levels above.
functions: Stabilising individual vertebrae
Rotating the spine
Extending the spine
Fine-tuning posture
connections: From transverse processes of the vertebrae
To spinous processes one to six levels above
Supplied by the posterior branches of the spinal nerves
clinical: The multifidus often becomes weaker and fattier in long-standing back pain.
Rehabilitation exercises target these stabilising muscles.
transversospinalis.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
transversospinalis.fact: Multifidus is thickest in the lower back, where stability is most needed.
transversospinalis.blood_supply: Posterior branches of the intercostal and lumbar arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

iliopsoas.name: Iliopsoas
iliopsoas.tagline: The main hip flexor, running from the lower spine and pelvis to the thigh bone.
iliopsoas.overview: The iliopsoas combines two muscles: the psoas major, which runs down beside the lumbar spine, and the iliacus, which lines the inside of the hip bone. They join and pass under the groin ligament to a shared tendon on the inner upper thigh bone.
functions: Bending the hip (lifting the thigh)
Bending the trunk forward at the hip (sitting up)
Helping keep the trunk upright when standing
Steadying the lower spine
connections: Psoas from the lumbar vertebrae; iliacus from the iliac fossa
To the lesser trochanter of the femur
Supplied by lumbar nerves (L1–L3) and the femoral nerve
clinical: Inflammation or collections near the psoas can cause pain on extending the hip.
Tightness after long sitting may tilt the pelvis forward.
iliopsoas.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
iliopsoas.fact: It is the strongest muscle for lifting the thigh, used in every step and stair climb.
iliopsoas.blood_supply: Lumbar arteries, iliolumbar artery and branches of the femoral and external iliac arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Pelvic girdle and lower limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

psoas_major.name: Psoas major
psoas_major.tagline: A long muscle beside the lumbar spine that bends the hip.
psoas_major.overview: The psoas major is a long, thick muscle lying on either side of the lumbar spine in the back of the abdomen. It runs down over the pelvic brim to join the iliacus and attach to the thigh bone. The nerves of the lumbar plexus run through and around it.
functions: Bending the hip
Bending the trunk forward
Bending the lumbar spine to the side
Steadying the lumbar spine
connections: From the bodies, discs and transverse processes of T12–L5
Joins the iliacus to insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur
Supplied by anterior branches of L1–L3
clinical: Its outline on imaging is used as a rough guide to overall muscle mass.
Infections from the spine can track down inside its sheath.
psoas_major.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
psoas_major.fact: In meat cuts, the psoas is the tenderloin.
psoas_major.blood_supply: Lumbar arteries and branches of the iliolumbar artery.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

gluteus_maximus.name: Gluteus maximus
gluteus_maximus.tagline: The large buttock muscle that straightens the hip for climbing and rising.
gluteus_maximus.overview: The gluteus maximus is the largest and most superficial buttock muscle, giving the buttock its shape. It runs from the back of the pelvis, sacrum and coccyx downwards and outwards to the thigh bone and the iliotibial band on the outer thigh.
functions: Straightening the hip (rising from sitting, climbing stairs)
Rotating the thigh outwards
Stabilising the pelvis and knee via the iliotibial band
Keeping the trunk upright when bending forward
connections: From the back of the ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament
To the gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial tract
Supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2)
clinical: Weakness makes climbing stairs and standing up harder.
Injections are given in the upper outer part of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve.
gluteus_maximus.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
gluteus_maximus.fact: It is usually the largest single muscle in the human body by mass.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Pelvic girdle and lower limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

gluteus_medius.name: Gluteus medius
gluteus_medius.tagline: A hip muscle that keeps the pelvis level when you stand on one leg.
gluteus_medius.overview: The gluteus medius is a fan-shaped muscle on the outer surface of the pelvis, partly covered by the gluteus maximus. It runs from the outer hip bone to the bony bump at the top of the thigh bone (greater trochanter).
functions: Moving the thigh out to the side
Keeping the pelvis level when standing on one leg
Rotating the thigh inwards (front fibres)
Stabilising the hip when walking
connections: From the outer surface of the ilium
To the greater trochanter of the femur
Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
clinical: Weakness causes the pelvis to drop on the opposite side when walking (Trendelenburg sign).
Its tendon can become painful at the outer hip.
gluteus_medius.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
gluteus_medius.fact: Without it, each step would make the pelvis tilt noticeably.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Pelvic girdle and lower limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

gluteus_minimus.name: Gluteus minimus
gluteus_minimus.tagline: The smallest and deepest buttock muscle, steadying the hip joint.
gluteus_minimus.overview: The gluteus minimus is a small, fan-shaped muscle lying underneath the gluteus medius, close to the hip joint. It shares the same nerve and many actions with the gluteus medius.
functions: Moving the thigh out to the side
Rotating the thigh inwards
Keeping the pelvis level when walking
Holding the head of the thigh bone in the hip socket
connections: From the outer surface of the ilium, below the gluteus medius
To the front of the greater trochanter of the femur
Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
clinical: Its tendon can be involved in outer hip pain.
It is close to the hip joint and is considered in hip surgery approaches.
gluteus_minimus.lateralization: Paired, one on each side; each side can act alone or both together.
gluteus_minimus.fact: Despite its name, it is still a fairly substantial muscle about the size of a palm.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Pelvic girdle and lower limb
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

head.name: Head
head.tagline: The whole head as one outline: skull, face and soft tissues.
head.overview: This region is the overall outline of the head, including the scalp, skull, face, jaws and the soft tissues around them. It is useful as a frame of reference for the structures inside it, such as the brain, eyes, sinuses and teeth. The head sits on the neck, balanced on the top two vertebrae.
functions: Housing and protecting the brain
Holding the main sense organs: eyes, ears, nose and tongue
Taking in food and air
Facial expression and speech
connections: Neck and cervical spine below
Brain, eyes and sinuses inside
Jaws and teeth at the front
clinical: The scalp has a rich blood supply, so even small cuts can bleed a lot.
Head size and shape vary widely between healthy people.
head.lateralization: Broadly symmetrical left and right, though no face is perfectly symmetrical.
head.fact: A newborn's head is about a quarter of its body length; an adult's is about an eighth.
head.blood_supply: Branches of the external carotid arteries (face and scalp) and the internal carotid and vertebral arteries (brain).
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §1.6 Anatomical Terminology
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.2 The Skull
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

body_trunc.name: Trunk
body_trunc.tagline: The central part of the body: chest, abdomen and pelvis, without head or limbs.
body_trunc.overview: The trunk is the main body region between the neck and the hips. It contains the chest (thorax), the abdomen and the pelvis, and holds most of the internal organs. This surface shows the outer shape of the trunk, including its skin, fat and muscle, separated from the arms and legs.
functions: Housing and protecting the internal organs
Supporting the head and limbs
Providing the base for breathing movements
Anchoring the muscles that move the spine
Storing much of the body's fat
connections: Neck and head above
Arms at the shoulders
Legs at the hips
clinical: The amount of fat around the trunk is linked to heart and metabolic health.
Trunk muscles are important for posture and preventing back pain.
body_trunc.lateralization: Roughly symmetrical, though organs inside are not.
body_trunc.fact: Waist measurement is one simple way doctors estimate fat around the trunk.
body_trunc.blood_supply: Branches of the aorta, including intercostal and lumbar arteries for the body wall.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 1 An Introduction to the Human Body (Anatomical Terminology)
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax; Abdomen and pelvis

body_extremities.name: Limbs
body_extremities.tagline: The arms and legs, shown as their outer shape.
body_extremities.overview: The extremities are the upper limbs (shoulders, arms, forearms and hands) and lower limbs (hips, thighs, legs and feet). Each is built around long bones, moved by groups of muscles and supplied by its own major artery, vein and nerves. This surface shows their outer shape separated from the trunk.
functions: Reaching, grasping and fine hand movements
Standing, walking and running
Bearing body weight through the legs
Sensing the environment through touch
Returning blood to the heart through muscle pumping in the legs
connections: Trunk at the shoulders and hips
Major limb arteries and veins
Nerve plexuses in the neck and lower back
clinical: Limb fractures are among the most common injuries.
Leg veins can form clots, especially after long periods of not moving.
body_extremities.lateralization: Paired left and right; most people have a dominant hand.
body_extremities.fact: Calf muscles act as a second heart, squeezing leg veins to push blood upwards.
body_extremities.blood_supply: Subclavian-axillary-brachial arteries for the arms; iliac-femoral arteries for the legs.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 1 An Introduction to the Human Body (Anatomical Terminology)
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Upper limb and Lower limb

thoracic_cavity.name: Thoracic cavity
thoracic_cavity.tagline: The space inside the ribcage that holds the lungs and heart.
thoracic_cavity.overview: The thoracic cavity is the space enclosed by the ribs, spine and breastbone, closed below by the diaphragm. It contains the two lungs, each in its own pleural sac, and the central compartment (mediastinum) with the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus. Its size changes with every breath.
functions: Housing and protecting the heart and lungs
Changing volume to drive breathing
Creating the low pressure that draws air in
Helping venous blood return to the heart
connections: Ribcage and spine around it
Diaphragm below, separating it from the abdomen
Neck above through the thoracic inlet
clinical: Air or fluid in the chest cavity outside the lungs can make breathing harder.
Chest injuries are assessed carefully because of the vital organs inside.
thoracic_cavity.lateralization: Divided into right and left pleural cavities with the mediastinum in between.
thoracic_cavity.fact: The diaphragm does most of the work of quiet breathing by flattening and enlarging the cavity.
thoracic_cavity.blood_supply: Intercostal and internal thoracic arteries for the walls.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 1 An Introduction to the Human Body (Anatomical Terminology)
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

mediastinum.name: Mediastinum
mediastinum.tagline: The central compartment of the chest between the lungs, holding the heart.
mediastinum.overview: The mediastinum is the middle region of the chest, running from the neck down to the diaphragm and from the breastbone back to the spine. It contains the heart in its pericardial sac, the great blood vessels, the trachea, the oesophagus, the thymus, lymph nodes and important nerves.
functions: Holding the heart and great vessels
Providing a passage for the trachea and oesophagus
Carrying nerves such as the vagus and phrenic nerves
Containing lymph nodes that drain the lungs
Housing the thymus, important for immunity in childhood
connections: Lungs and pleura on either side
Neck above
Diaphragm below
clinical: Enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum can be seen on chest scans in various conditions.
Doctors often describe the mediastinum as superior, anterior, middle and posterior parts.
mediastinum.lateralization: Midline, but the heart within it bulges more to the left.
mediastinum.fact: The thymus in the mediastinum is large in children and gradually replaced by fat in adults.
mediastinum.blood_supply: Many small branches of the aorta and internal thoracic arteries.
sources: Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Thorax

abdominal_cavity.name: Abdominal cavity
abdominal_cavity.tagline: The large space below the diaphragm holding the digestive organs, kidneys and more.
abdominal_cavity.overview: The abdominal cavity lies below the diaphragm and continues down into the pelvis. It is lined by a thin membrane (peritoneum) and holds the stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen and, at the back, the kidneys. Its front and sides are formed by muscles rather than bone, allowing it to expand.
functions: Housing and cushioning the digestive organs
Letting the intestines move and shift
Allowing expansion after meals and in pregnancy
Helping with breathing, coughing and pushing via abdominal pressure
connections: Diaphragm above
Pelvic cavity below
Abdominal wall muscles in front and at the sides
Spine behind
clinical: Doctors often divide the abdomen into quadrants to describe where pain or a finding is.
Fluid can collect in the abdominal cavity in some liver, heart or kidney conditions.
abdominal_cavity.lateralization: Organs are arranged asymmetrically: liver mainly right, stomach and spleen mainly left.
abdominal_cavity.fact: The peritoneum lining the cavity has a surface area similar to that of the skin.
abdominal_cavity.blood_supply: Branches of the abdominal aorta: coeliac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), Ch. 1 An Introduction to the Human Body (Anatomical Terminology)
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018), Abdomen

frontal.name: Frontal lobe
frontal.tagline: The front of the brain: planning, decisions, movement and speech.
frontal.overview: The frontal lobe is the largest lobe, lying behind the forehead and in front of the central sulcus. Its back part controls movement, and its front part, the prefrontal cortex, supports planning, judgement, self-control and personality. On the language-dominant side it also contains Broca's area for speech production.
functions: Voluntary movement
Planning and decision making
Working memory and attention
Speech production
Personality and social behaviour
clinical: Damage can cause weakness on the opposite side, speech difficulty or changes in behaviour.
It is commonly affected in head injuries.
frontal.fact: The frontal lobes make up roughly a third of the cerebral cortex in humans.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

parietal.name: Parietal lobe
parietal.tagline: Touch, body awareness and knowing where things are.
parietal.overview: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, under the crown of the head. Its front strip receives touch and body-position signals, and the areas behind combine touch, vision and hearing. It helps us know where our body and objects are, and supports reading, writing and numbers.
functions: Touch, pain and body position
Spatial awareness
Guiding movements toward objects
Reading, writing and calculation
Attention
clinical: Damage on the right can cause people to ignore the left side of space (neglect).
Damage on the left can affect language, reading, writing and calculation.
parietal.fact: 'Parietal' comes from the Latin for 'wall', after the parietal bones of the skull above it.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

temporal.name: Temporal lobe
temporal.tagline: Hearing, language understanding, memory and recognising things.
temporal.overview: The temporal lobe lies on the side of the brain, below the lateral sulcus and near the temples. It contains the hearing cortex and, on the language-dominant side, Wernicke's area for understanding speech. Its lower and inner parts help recognise objects and faces and work with the hippocampus to form memories.
functions: Hearing
Understanding language
Recognising objects and faces
Memory
Knowledge of meanings
clinical: Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common type of focal epilepsy in adults.
Damage on the language-dominant side can impair understanding of speech.
temporal.fact: The hippocampus and amygdala, key structures for memory and emotion, lie folded inside the inner part of the temporal lobe.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

occipital.name: Occipital lobe
occipital.tagline: The back of the brain, dedicated mainly to vision.
occipital.overview: The occipital lobe is the rearmost lobe, at the back of the head. It contains the primary visual cortex and surrounding areas that process shape, colour and motion. Each side processes the opposite half of what we see.
functions: Receiving visual signals from the eyes
Processing shape and edges
Processing colour
Processing motion
Passing visual information to other lobes
clinical: Damage on one side causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes.
Strokes of the posterior cerebral artery are a common cause of occipital damage.
occipital.fact: 'Occipital' comes from the Latin occiput, meaning the back of the head.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

insular.name: Insular lobe
insular.tagline: A hidden lobe that senses the body's inner state.
insular.overview: The insula is a lobe of cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. It brings together signals from inside the body with taste, pain and emotion. It is sometimes counted as part of the limbic system.
functions: Awareness of the body's internal state
Taste
Pain
Emotion
Regulating heart rate and blood pressure
clinical: It is often affected in middle cerebral artery strokes.
Seizures can start in the insula.
insular.fact: The insula can only be seen when the overlying opercula are pulled apart.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020)

limbic.name: Limbic lobe
limbic.tagline: A ring of structures for emotion, motivation and memory.
limbic.overview: The limbic lobe is a ring of cortex on the inner surface of each hemisphere, curving around the corpus callosum and brainstem. It includes the cingulate and parahippocampal gyri, and is closely tied to the hippocampus and amygdala. Together these form much of the limbic system, which supports emotion, motivation and memory.
functions: Emotion
Memory formation
Motivation
Linking emotion with body responses
clinical: Alzheimer's disease often first affects the hippocampus and nearby areas.
Many temporal lobe seizures start in limbic structures.
limbic.fact: 'Limbic' comes from the Latin limbus, meaning 'border', because it forms a border around the brainstem; the term was used by Paul Broca.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)
Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)

subcortical.name: Deep grey matter
subcortical.tagline: Deep nuclei that relay signals and shape movement and motivation.
subcortical.overview: Deep grey matter is a set of nuclei buried inside the hemispheres beneath the cortex. It includes the thalamus, which relays information to the cortex, and the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus and nucleus accumbens), which help select movements and drive motivation. The hypothalamus, which controls hormones and body balance, also lies here.
functions: Relaying sensory and motor signals
Selecting and starting movements
Learning habits
Reward and motivation
Hormone and body regulation
clinical: Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases affect the basal ganglia.
Small deep strokes and bleeds often affect these structures.
subcortical.fact: The basal ganglia work in loops: signals leave the cortex, pass through these nuclei and the thalamus, and return to the cortex.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

ventricles.name: Ventricles
ventricles.tagline: Fluid-filled spaces inside the brain that make and carry cerebrospinal fluid.
ventricles.overview: The ventricles are four connected cavities inside the brain: two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle and the fourth ventricle. They contain cerebrospinal fluid, which is made mainly by the choroid plexus. The fluid flows out of the fourth ventricle to surround the brain and spinal cord.
functions: Producing cerebrospinal fluid
Cushioning and supporting the brain
Helping clear waste products
Maintaining a stable chemical environment
clinical: Blocked fluid flow causes the ventricles to enlarge (hydrocephalus).
The ventricles naturally become larger with age.
ventricles.fact: The total volume of cerebrospinal fluid in an adult is about 150 millilitres.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020)

white_matter.name: White matter
white_matter.tagline: The brain's wiring: insulated fibres connecting all regions.
white_matter.overview: White matter is made of nerve fibres coated in myelin, a fatty insulation that speeds up signals. It connects areas within each hemisphere, links the two hemispheres through the corpus callosum, and carries signals to and from the brainstem and spinal cord.
functions: Connecting brain regions
Linking the two hemispheres
Carrying signals to and from the body
Speeding up signals
clinical: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin in white matter.
Small-vessel disease, more common with age and high blood pressure, can affect white matter.
white_matter.fact: Myelin continues to be added to white matter through childhood and adolescence.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.tagline: The 'little brain' that coordinates movement and balance.
cerebellum.overview: The cerebellum sits at the back of the head below the cerebrum and behind the brainstem. It compares intended movements with what actually happens and fine-tunes them. It has two hemispheres joined by the midline vermis, and also contributes to timing, learning and some thinking skills.
functions: Coordinating movement
Balance and posture
Learning motor skills
Eye movement control
Contributing to some thinking and language
clinical: Damage causes clumsiness, unsteady walking and slurred speech.
Swelling or bleeding here can press on the brainstem and fourth ventricle.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.tagline: The stalk that links brain and spinal cord and runs vital functions.
brainstem.overview: The brainstem is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. It carries all signals between the brain and body, contains most cranial nerve nuclei, and houses centres that control breathing, heart rate and wakefulness.
functions: Breathing and heart rate
Wakefulness
Eye, face and swallowing control
Carrying signals between brain and body
clinical: Brainstem strokes can cause dizziness, double vision and weakness.
Pressure on the brainstem is a medical emergency.
brainstem.fact: Ten of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves attach to the brainstem.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases 3e (2021)

arteries.name: Arteries
arteries.tagline: The vessels that carry oxygen-rich blood to the brain.
arteries.overview: Four arteries carry blood up the neck to the brain: two internal carotid and two vertebral arteries. They join at the base of the brain in the circle of Willis, which gives rise to the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries.
functions: Delivering oxygen and glucose
Providing back-up routes for blood flow
Supplying each brain region through its own branches
clinical: Blocked arteries cause ischaemic stroke.
Aneurysms can form at branch points and may bleed.
arteries.fact: The brain cannot store much energy, so it depends on a constant blood supply.
sources: Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020)

integument.name: Skin and body surface
integument.tagline: The body's outer covering: protection, temperature control and touch.
integument.overview: The integumentary system is the skin together with hair, nails and skin glands. It is the largest organ of the body and forms a waterproof, flexible barrier between the inside of the body and the outside world. On CT and MR scans its outer edge is used to show the shape of the body.
functions: Protecting deeper tissues from injury, germs and water loss
Helping to control body temperature through sweat and blood flow
Sensing touch, pressure, pain and temperature
Making vitamin D when exposed to sunlight
clinical: Cuts, burns and infections are the most common skin problems.
Many skin conditions are examined by looking at the skin directly rather than on scans.
integument.fact: In an adult the skin covers roughly 1.5 to 2 square metres.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 5 The Integumentary System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Skin and its appendages

skeleton.name: Skeletal system
skeleton.tagline: The bony framework that supports, protects and moves the body.
skeleton.overview: The adult skeleton has about 206 bones, joined by cartilage and ligaments. The axial skeleton (skull, spine, ribs and breastbone) protects the brain, spinal cord and chest organs; the appendicular skeleton (shoulder and hip girdles and the limbs) lets us move. Bone is living tissue that is constantly rebuilt, and it is the brightest tissue on CT.
functions: Supporting the body and giving it shape
Protecting the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs
Acting as levers for muscles to produce movement
Making blood cells in the bone marrow
Storing calcium and phosphate
clinical: Fractures are the most common bone injury and usually heal well.
Bones gradually lose density with age (osteoporosis), which makes fractures more likely.
skeleton.fact: A newborn has nearer 300 bony parts; many fuse together during growth.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 6 Bone Tissue and the Skeletal System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 7 Axial Skeleton
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 8 The Appendicular Skeleton

spinal_column.name: Spinal column
spinal_column.tagline: The stack of vertebrae and discs that holds us upright and guards the cord.
spinal_column.overview: The spinal column (backbone) is a flexible chain of 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (lower back), and the fused sacrum and coccyx. Cushioning intervertebral discs sit between most vertebrae. Together they carry the weight of the upper body, allow bending and twisting, and form a bony canal around the spinal cord.
functions: Carrying the weight of the head and trunk
Allowing the neck and back to bend and twist
Protecting the spinal cord and nerve roots
Anchoring the ribs, muscles and ligaments of the back
clinical: Back and neck pain are very common and often come from muscles, joints or discs.
Discs and joints change with age (degeneration), which is common even in people without symptoms.
spinal_column.fact: The spine has four gentle curves when seen from the side, which help absorb shocks.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §7.3 The Vertebral Column
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Back

nervous_spine.name: Spinal cord and its coverings
nervous_spine.tagline: The nerve cable running down the spine, bathed in protective fluid.
nervous_spine.overview: The spinal cord is the part of the central nervous system inside the spinal canal. It runs from the base of the brain to about the first or second lumbar vertebra, where it tapers and continues as a bundle of nerve roots. It is wrapped in membranes (meninges) and floats in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which cushions it. On MR the cord is grey and the CSF around it is bright on T2-weighted images.
functions: Carrying sensation from the body up to the brain
Carrying movement commands from the brain to the muscles
Running simple reflexes without involving the brain
Cushioning by the surrounding cerebrospinal fluid
clinical: Pressure on the cord or nerve roots can cause pain, numbness or weakness in the arms or legs.
Injuries to the cord can affect movement and feeling below the injured level.
nervous_spine.fact: In adults the spinal cord is only about 45 cm long, shorter than the spine itself.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.2 The Central Nervous System
Purves et al., Neuroscience 6e (2018)

respiratory.name: Respiratory system
respiratory.tagline: The airways and lungs that bring oxygen in and let carbon dioxide out.
respiratory.overview: The respiratory system runs from the nose and mouth through the throat, voice box and windpipe into the two lungs, where the airways branch many times and end in tiny air sacs (alveoli). There, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. Air is dark on CT, so the airways and lungs stand out clearly.
functions: Bringing oxygen into the blood
Removing carbon dioxide
Warming, moistening and filtering the air we breathe
Producing the voice
Helping to keep the blood's acid balance steady
clinical: Infections such as colds, bronchitis and pneumonia are the most common lung problems.
Smoking is the leading avoidable cause of long-term lung disease.
respiratory.fact: The surface of all the air sacs together is roughly the size of a tennis court.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §22.2 The Lungs

cardiovascular.name: Heart and blood vessels
cardiovascular.tagline: The heart pump and the network of arteries and veins it drives.
cardiovascular.overview: The cardiovascular system is the heart and the blood vessels. The right side of the heart pumps blood through the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps it through the aorta and its branches to every organ. Veins bring the blood back to the heart. On CT, vessels are easiest to see when a contrast dye has been injected (CT angiography).
functions: Delivering oxygen and nutrients to every tissue
Carrying away carbon dioxide and waste
Moving hormones and immune cells around the body
Helping to control body temperature
clinical: Narrowing of arteries by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis) is a common cause of heart attack and stroke.
High blood pressure often has no symptoms and is usually found by measuring it.
cardiovascular.fact: The heart beats around 100,000 times a day.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §19.1 Heart Anatomy
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §20.5 Circulatory Pathways

digestive.name: Digestive system
digestive.tagline: From mouth to colon, plus liver and pancreas: turning food into fuel.
digestive.overview: The digestive system is a long tube (mouth, throat, food pipe, stomach, small and large intestine) together with helper organs that add digestive juices: the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas. The teeth and tongue begin digestion by chewing and mixing food. Food is broken down, nutrients are absorbed into the blood, and what remains is passed out.
functions: Chewing, swallowing and moving food along
Breaking food down with acid and enzymes
Absorbing nutrients and water
Processing and storing nutrients in the liver
Removing undigested waste
clinical: Indigestion, constipation and stomach upsets are very common and usually short-lived.
Gallstones and inflammation of the appendix are frequent reasons for abdominal scans.
digestive.fact: The small intestine alone is several metres long, folded to fit inside the abdomen.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 23 The Digestive System
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Abdomen and pelvis

urinary.name: Urinary system
urinary.tagline: Kidneys and bladder: filtering the blood and storing urine.
urinary.overview: The urinary system is made up of the two kidneys, the two ureters that carry urine down, the bladder that stores it, and the urethra that empties it. The kidneys filter the whole blood volume many times a day, keeping the right balance of water and salts and removing waste.
functions: Filtering waste products out of the blood
Balancing water and salts
Helping to control blood pressure
Storing and emptying urine
clinical: Urinary infections are common, especially in women.
Kidney stones are a frequent cause of sudden side or back pain.
urinary.fact: The kidneys filter roughly 180 litres of fluid a day, but only about 1.5 litres leaves as urine.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 25 The Urinary System

endocrine.name: Endocrine system
endocrine.tagline: Glands that release hormones to coordinate the whole body.
endocrine.overview: The endocrine system is a set of glands that release chemical messengers (hormones) into the blood. On body scans the most visible ones are the thyroid gland in the neck and the two adrenal glands on top of the kidneys; others include the pituitary gland, the pancreas islets and the ovaries or testes.
functions: Controlling metabolism and energy use
Managing the stress response
Regulating growth and development
Keeping salt, water and sugar levels steady
clinical: An under- or over-active thyroid is one of the most common hormone problems.
Small lumps in endocrine glands are often found by chance and are usually harmless.
endocrine.fact: Hormones can act on organs far away from the gland that made them.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 17 The Endocrine System

lymphatic.name: Lymphatic and immune organs
lymphatic.tagline: Spleen, lymph nodes and vessels: draining fluid and fighting infection.
lymphatic.overview: The lymphatic system is a network of thin vessels and small lymph nodes that collects excess fluid from the tissues and returns it to the blood, filtering it on the way. The spleen, in the upper left abdomen, is the largest lymphatic organ: it filters the blood and stores immune cells.
functions: Returning tissue fluid to the bloodstream
Filtering germs and debris
Housing and training immune cells
Absorbing fats from the gut
clinical: Lymph nodes often swell for a while during ordinary infections.
The spleen can enlarge in many conditions, including some infections.
lymphatic.fact: Unlike blood, lymph has no central pump; it is moved by muscle movement and breathing.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §21.1 Anatomy of the Lymphatic and Immune Systems

reproductive.name: Reproductive organs
reproductive.tagline: Organs involved in reproduction, such as the prostate and the breast.
reproductive.overview: The reproductive system differs between the sexes. Of its organs, the ones most often outlined on body scans are the prostate gland, which sits below the bladder in men, and the breast, whose glandular tissue can produce milk. The uterus, ovaries and testes also belong to this system.
functions: Producing eggs or sperm
Making sex hormones
Adding fluid to semen (prostate)
Producing milk after childbirth (breast)
clinical: The prostate commonly enlarges with age, which can affect passing urine.
Breast tissue changes naturally with age, hormones and pregnancy.
reproductive.fact: Breast tissue extends up towards the armpit, forming a 'tail'.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 27 The Reproductive System

muscular.name: Skeletal muscles
muscular.tagline: The muscles that move the skeleton, hold posture and help us breathe.
muscular.overview: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons and contract under voluntary control. They move the joints, keep us upright, protect the abdomen and help with breathing, chewing and eye movement. On CT, muscle is mid-grey, between fat (darker) and bone (brighter).
functions: Moving the body and its joints
Maintaining posture
Producing heat
Helping with breathing, chewing and swallowing
clinical: Strains and bruises are the most common muscle injuries.
Muscle mass naturally declines with age and inactivity, and exercise helps maintain it.
muscular.fact: There are more than 600 named skeletal muscles in the human body.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), ch. 11 The Muscular System
Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e (2018)

nervous.name: Nervous system
nervous.tagline: The brain and nerves: sensing, thinking and controlling the body.
nervous.overview: The nervous system is the brain and spinal cord (central nervous system) plus the nerves that connect them to the rest of the body. On body scans the brain is often outlined as a single organ inside the skull; the brain model in this app shows its individual regions. The optic nerve, which carries vision from the eye, is technically an extension of the brain.
functions: Receiving information from the senses
Thinking, memory and emotion
Controlling movement
Running automatic functions such as heartbeat and breathing
clinical: Headaches are very common and usually not caused by a problem visible on a scan.
Strokes happen when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted.
nervous.fact: Signals can travel along some nerves at over 100 metres per second.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.2 The Central Nervous System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §13.4 The Peripheral Nervous System

sensory.name: Sense organs
sensory.tagline: The eyes and ears: gathering light and sound for the brain.
sensory.overview: Sense organs turn light, sound and other stimuli into nerve signals. The eyes sit in bony sockets (orbits) and are moved by six small muscles each; the lens focuses light onto the retina. The ear canal leads from the outer ear to the eardrum, behind which lie the tiny hearing and balance organs of the inner ear.
functions: Seeing (eyes)
Hearing (ears)
Sensing balance and head movement (inner ear)
Protecting delicate sensory tissue inside bony spaces
clinical: Clouding of the lens (cataract) is a very common age-related change.
Wax and infections are common causes of a blocked ear canal.
sensory.fact: The eyeball is about 24 mm across in adults, roughly the size of a large marble.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §14.1 Sensory Perception
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Head and neck

body_regions.name: Body regions and cavities
body_regions.tagline: The head, trunk and limbs, and the large spaces that hold the organs.
body_regions.overview: Anatomists divide the body into regions (head, trunk, arms and legs) and describe large internal spaces called cavities. The chest (thoracic) cavity holds the lungs and, in its central compartment called the mediastinum, the heart and great vessels. Below the diaphragm, the abdominal cavity holds the digestive organs, liver, spleen and kidneys. Segmentation tools outline these as broad shapes to give context to the organs inside them.
functions: Giving a framework for describing where structures lie
Holding and protecting the internal organs
Letting organs move and change size (breathing, digestion)
Providing context when viewing a 3D model
clinical: Doctors describe symptoms and findings by region, such as 'upper abdomen' or 'right chest'.
Fluid or air can sometimes collect in body cavities and is looked for on scans.
body_regions.fact: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle, is the wall between the chest and abdominal cavities.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e (2022), §1.6 Anatomical Terminology
Gray's Anatomy 42e (2020), Thorax; Abdomen and pelvis

arteries.overview: The brain receives blood from two internal carotid arteries at the front and two vertebral arteries at the back, which join to form the basilar artery. At the base of the brain, communicating arteries link these into a ring called the circle of Willis. Its shape varies between people, and incomplete circles are common normal variants.

ica.name: Internal carotid artery
ica.supplies: Most of the front and middle of each hemisphere (through the anterior and middle cerebral arteries) and the eye.
ica.note: Arises from the common carotid artery in the neck and enters the skull without branching in the neck.

mca.name: Middle cerebral artery
mca.supplies: The outer surface of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes, the insula and, through small perforating branches, the basal ganglia.
mca.note: The largest branch of the internal carotid artery and the artery most often involved in stroke.

aca.name: Anterior cerebral artery
aca.supplies: The inner surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg areas of the motor and touch strips, and most of the corpus callosum.
aca.note: The two anterior cerebral arteries are joined by the anterior communicating artery.

pca.name: Posterior cerebral artery
pca.supplies: The occipital lobe, the underside of the temporal lobe, the thalamus and the midbrain.
pca.note: Usually arises from the top of the basilar artery; in some people it is fed mainly by the internal carotid artery (a 'fetal' pattern), which is a normal variant.

basilar.name: Basilar artery
basilar.supplies: The pons and parts of the cerebellum, then divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
basilar.note: Formed where the two vertebral arteries join at the front of the brainstem.

vertebral.name: Vertebral artery
vertebral.supplies: The medulla and lower cerebellum (including via the posterior inferior cerebellar artery), then joins its partner to form the basilar artery.
vertebral.note: Runs up through openings in the neck vertebrae; the two sides are often unequal in size, which is usually normal.

acom.name: Anterior communicating artery
acom.supplies: Small branches to nearby deep structures; mainly connects the two anterior cerebral arteries.
acom.note: A common site of brain aneurysms.

pcom.name: Posterior communicating artery
pcom.supplies: Small branches to the thalamus and hypothalamus; mainly connects the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral artery.
pcom.note: Its size varies widely; an aneurysm here can press on the nerve that moves the eye and lifts the eyelid.

common_carotid.name: Common carotid artery
common_carotid.supplies: Divides in the neck into the internal carotid (brain and eye) and external carotid (face and scalp) arteries.
common_carotid.note: The left usually arises directly from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk.

eca.name: External carotid artery
eca.supplies: The face, scalp, jaw, throat and the coverings of the brain (via the middle meningeal artery).
eca.note: Its branches can form connections with the internal carotid system.

T1.name: T1-weighted MRI
T1.what: An MRI image in which fat appears bright and fluid appears dark, giving a clear picture of anatomy.
T1.why: Shows the shape of brain structures well; often repeated after a contrast injection to look for areas that light up.

T2.name: T2-weighted MRI
T2.what: An MRI image in which fluid appears bright.
T2.why: Good at showing fluid, swelling and many kinds of tissue change.

FLAIR.name: FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery)
FLAIR.what: A T2-type MRI image in which the normal fluid around and inside the brain is made dark.
FLAIR.why: Makes changes near the ventricles and brain surface easier to see, because the bright fluid no longer hides them.

DWI.name: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)
DWI.what: An MRI image that measures how freely water molecules move in tissue.
DWI.why: Very sensitive to early stroke and some other conditions in which water movement is restricted.

ADC.name: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map
ADC.what: A map calculated from diffusion images that shows water movement as a number for each point.
ADC.why: Read together with DWI to confirm whether water movement is truly restricted.

T2STAR.name: T2* gradient echo (GRE)
T2STAR.what: An MRI image that is sensitive to small disturbances in the magnetic field.
T2STAR.why: Shows blood products, calcium and iron as dark spots.

SWI.name: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI)
SWI.what: A refined version of T2* imaging that is even more sensitive to magnetic disturbances.
SWI.why: Detects very small amounts of blood, iron or calcium and shows veins clearly.

TOF.name: Time-of-flight MR angiography (TOF MRA)
TOF.what: An MRI technique in which flowing blood appears bright, without needing a contrast injection.
TOF.why: Shows the arteries of the brain and neck, including the circle of Willis.

STIR.name: STIR (short tau inversion recovery)
STIR.what: An MRI image in which fat is made dark and fluid stays bright.
STIR.why: Useful for showing swelling in bones, the spine and soft tissues.

PD.name: Proton density (PD) MRI
PD.what: An MRI image whose brightness mainly reflects how much water (hydrogen) a tissue contains.
PD.why: Often used for joints, such as the knee, to show cartilage and ligaments.

CT.name: Computed tomography (CT)
CT.what: Cross-sectional X-ray images in which each point's brightness reflects tissue density, measured in Hounsfield units.
CT.why: Fast and widely available; good at showing bone and fresh bleeding.

CTA.name: CT angiography (CTA)
CTA.what: A CT scan timed with an iodine contrast injection so the arteries appear bright.
CTA.why: Shows the arteries in detail, including narrowing or bulges.

CR.name: Computed radiography (CR)
CR.what: A digital X-ray taken with a reusable imaging plate that is read by a scanner.
CR.why: A flat (2D) X-ray picture, for example of the chest or bones.

DX.name: Digital radiography (DX)
DX.what: A digital X-ray taken with a detector that produces the image directly.
DX.why: A flat (2D) X-ray picture, for example of the chest or bones.

MIP.name: Maximum intensity projection (MIP)
MIP.what: A view made by a computer from a stack of images, keeping the brightest point along each line of sight.
MIP.why: Shows bright structures such as vessels in angiography as one picture; it is a processed view, not a separate scan.

PHOTO.name: Photo or scanned document
PHOTO.what: A photograph, scanned film or document page imported as an image.
PHOTO.why: Can be viewed, but it has no real-world scale, so no measurements are possible.
